News.title: Moment police officer borrows bike from passerby then races after ‘thief’ and tackles him to ground
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a police officer borrows a bike from a cyclist and uses it to chase down a suspected thief.

After commandeering the bicycle, bodycam footage shows the cop tackling the man to the ground and shouting: “You’re f****** nicked!”.



The chase began with the officer driving through the streets of Twickenham, south-west London in pursuit of an alleged thief.

Realising he needs to carry on the chase on foot, the Metropolitan Police officer exits his car and starts running.



But he soon passes a member of the public with a bike – who says: “Do you guys want to chase him on this?”.

The grateful officer replies “would you mind?” and tells the cyclist he only needs it for “five minutes”.

He races off, eventually reaching the suspect on a towpath near to the Twickenham Stoop stadium.

He then tackles the man to the ground and shouts: “Get over, get on the ground”.



“You’re f****** nicked!” he adds.

The officer then contacts his team, saying: “Additional officers coming to join me.

“I’m going to have to repatriate this bike to my hero member of the public.”

Insp Jon McLoughlin said of the incident: “The video below shows a recent arrest after a bike was stolen on Whitton High Street and is a great example of the public and police working together.

“In this case, a quick-thinking cyclist lent an officer their bike so they could continue their pursuit of a suspect.



“It’s a brilliant example of how a small act can make a big difference.”

This isn’t the first time an officer has used a member of the public to help catch a suspect.

In June, one armed police officer was helped by a van driver in the middle of a police chase before they catch the suspect fleeing on foot.



The officer clutching a firearm can be seen approaching a mini-roundabout after the suspect evaded attempts to arrest him.

Standing in the middle of the road, he then turns to a passing motorist in a van who stops and urges the officer to “get in the back, get in the back”.

The officer climbs in shouting “go, go, go” and tells the driver to follow the other officers.

In another amusing clip an out of breath bobby is picked up by a driver as he is chasing down two thieving boys.

The woman who filmed the incident said she and her friend were driving home when they saw the chase unfold.



“He opened the door and told us to follow the suspect,” she said.

News.title: Horror moment soapbox cart ploughs into crowd during race when it loses control after jump and injures eight
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a soapbox cart loses control and ploughs into a crowd of spectators during a traditional race, injuring eight.

Horrifying footage shows the cart whizz down a steep street in Ecuador before losing control after a jump and veering into bystanders.



The racer immediately smashes through fences and tyres used as safety barriers sending the cart driver flying into spectators on the pavement.

Horrified witnesses rush to help the wounded as one of the drivers writhes in agony from the impact.



A huge crowd immediately starts pulling the barricades off the injured spectators.

The crash unfolded as 51 teams competed in celebrations marking the 128th anniversary of the San Roque parish, in Imbabura, Ecuador, on August 23.

A cart racing in the “Fuerza Libre” (Open) category was the one to lose control on the two-mile course.

These makeshift vehicles can go faster than 60mph on the dangerous route, which features bumpy hills.



The eight injured in the chaos were rushed to hospitals in Atuntaqui and Ibarra for treatment.

Event organiser Steven Terán said safety measures had been put in place for the race but acknowledged that competitions of this type carry inherent risks.

Fortunately, there were no fatalities.



Soapbox cart racing is very popular in hilly, rally-crazed Ecuador.

The phenomenon, which is dubbed Carrera Coches de Madera – or “wooden car race”, dates back to the 1940s, according to Quito Informa.

Certain events, like the one involving the crash, have carts crewed by two riders.

One is responsible for steering, while others push with their feet in the slower sections.

Riders throw their bodies around to make sharp turns, akin to bobsleigh races.



These high-speed gravity-fuelled street races often draw large crowds of keen spectators.

News.title: PM must find the courage to stop taxing families and small businesses to the hilt to fund freebies for Benefits Street
News.content:
It’s the Taxman

THE next time Andy Burnham gets his guitar out he might as well treat voters to a version of The Beatles classic Taxman.

Because be in no doubt, our Prime Minister is preparing to launch yet another massive Labour cash grab.

Economists reckon the Autumn Budget could swipe another £25billion.



That would be on a par with the pain former Chancellor Rachel Reeves dished out last November which was on TOP of her £40billion of tax rises in 2024. The reason for this doom loop?



Keir Starmer ducked ALL the tough choices while his successor doesn’t seem to have much of a plan either. There are STILL no concrete proposals to slash eye-watering welfare payments.

In just a few weeks this summer, Burnham has already spent billions on small-change help for families such as £45 off their energy bills and two quid bus fares. The PM also has big plans to deliver radical change in social care — but no clue how to pay for it.

Chancellor John Healey rightly wants to ramp up defence spending. But there are already billions missing from Starmer and Reeves’s Defence Investment Plan which fell way short of what military chiefs were demanding.



Meanwhile, backbench Labour MPs refuse to consider any spending cuts.

It means only one thing: massive tax rises. Unless Burnham finds the courage to stop taxing families and small businesses to the hilt to fund freebies for Benefits Street, nothing will change.

He’ll be back for more of your money NEXT year. And the year after, too.

A bitter taste

A CLASSIC example of the consequences of Labour’s addiction to tax and spending is the perilous state of our pubs.



When he was trying to get elected as an MP, Andy Burnham raised hopes that he would halve VAT for boozers.

But as with so many pledges that dripped casually off his tongue, the reality inside No10 is very different.

Treasury ministers now bleakly warn such a move would “cost a lot of money.”

But what’s the cost to our communities when their local pub closes down?

Goodbye Dolly

VERY few people have used their success to help others quite like Dolly Parton.



One of the greatest country stars, it was the way she shared her hard-earned fortune that made her so unique.

More than 150million books have been given to kids thanks to the Dollywood Foundation, inspired by the struggles of her dad who couldn’t read or write.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Famed for her blonde wigs and big boobs, Dolly quipped: “It takes a lot of money to look this cheap.”

But the truth is that nothing about Dolly was cheap. She was solid gold from 9 to 5 — and in every other hour too.

News.title: Kemi Badenoch set to reshuffle her top team ahead of Tory conference after the summer break
News.content:
FRESH FACES Kemi Badenoch set to reshuffle her top team ahead of Tory conference after the summer break

TORY leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to make changes to her top team after the summer break.

She is said to be preparing a reshuffle ahead of the Conservative conference in October.



Energy’s Claire Coutinho is expected to step away from the front bench before maternity leave.

Shadow Solicitor General Helen Grant has asked to stand down.



Julia Lopez could also be moved after PM Andy Burnham scrapped the Science, Innovation and Technology department covered by her brief.

Restless MPs from the 2024 intake are said to be pushing for promotion, , with Katie Lam, Harriet Cross and Aphra Brandreth among those tipped for bigger jobs.

A Tory source said: “A lot of the new intake want jobs because they think the shadow cabinet are lazy and they have to pick up the slack.”

There has also been speculation over the futures of shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Dame Priti Patel but neither is currently expected to be replaced.

Tory sources last night played down suggestions a major overhaul is being planned and stressed some changes would simply be needed because of Labour’s machinery-of-government shake-up, Ms Coutinho’s maternity leave and Ms Grant’s decision to step down.

News.title: Drone flying at height nearly 14 times the legal limit came within just 16ft of crashing into passenger plane
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

NEAR MISS Drone flying at height nearly 14 times the legal limit came within just 16ft of crashing into passenger plane

A DRONE flying at a height nearly 14 times the legal limit came within just 16ft of crashing into a passenger plane.

Virgin Atlantic pilots saw the device at 5,500ft near Woking, Surrey, after leaving Heathrow for Johannesburg on June 8.



The B787 Dreamliner was carrying up to 264 passengers when the horrifying incident happened.

A British Airprox Board report said there was a high risk of collision, and the pilots spotted the drone too late to take avoiding action.



Air traffic controllers were immediately contacted and they alerted other planes in the area.

Its operator was not found but faces five years in jail if caught.

Pilots and aviation experts have long warned of the danger of a drone smashing into a cockpit.

Drones are normally permitted to fly at a maximum height of 400ft in the UK, meaning the device in the incident was being flown far above the legal height.

A Virgin Atlantic spokesperson confirmed the incident.

The spokesperson added: “The safety and security of our customers and crew is always our priority, and the pilots immediately reported the incident to Air Traffic Control in line with our procedures.”

News.title: Teacher ‘who sexually abused two pupils’ was often reluctant to have sex, partner of 36 years tells court
News.content:
TEACHER'S 'PAIN' Teacher ‘who sexually abused two pupils’ was often reluctant to have sex, partner of 36 years tells court

A TEACHER accused of sexually abusing two pupils was often reluctant to have sex, her partner of 36 years told her trial yesterday.

Darren Scotchbrook told jurors he was “always quick” in bed to spare Sally-Anne Bowen discomfort.



The court heard evidence from a consultant gynaecologist that she has a medical condition which makes sex painful.

Mr Scotchbrook told the jury they have continued to have sex but their relationship was “built on much more than that”.



Asked if he enjoyed the sex, Mr Scotchbrook said: “She made me listen to Leonard Cohen.

“It was more enjoyable than that.”



Mr Scotchbrook also told the court that he was “a bit upset” that Bowen did not want to sleep with him after their first date as he had “spent £200 on dinner”.

Bowen, 65, is said to have had sexual relationships with two teenage students at the all-boys Christ’s College in Finchley, North London, in the late 1980s.

Bowen, then in her mid-20s, is said to have “engaged in flirtatious conduct” with the pupils and had sex with one alleged victim “20 to 30 times” over five months.

She also kissed the second boy while allowing him to touch her breasts and place his hand near her crotch in a café as they ate lunch together, it is said.



The court also heard evidence from a former pupil who claimed Bowen spoke about oral sex in class and sat provocatively so boys could see up her skirt.

Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Herts, denies indecent assault.

The trial at Harrow crown court continues.

News.title: Second man charged with murder & 8 counts of attempted murder following deadly house fire that killed woman
News.content:
BLAZE 'MURDER' Second man charged with murder & 8 counts of attempted murder following deadly house fire that killed woman

A SECOND man has been charged with murder following a house fire in West London which killed a woman.

Emergency services descended on Berkley Avenue in Hounslow in the early hours of August 19 following reports of a fire.



A 48-year-old woman later died in hospital while another woman, aged 40, remains in a life-threatening condition.

The woman who died has been named as Anna Kowalsaka and her family are being supported by specialist officers.



The force added that the other six men and one woman who were taken to hospital have since been discharged with minor injuries.

Slawomir Alama, 41, has now been charged with murder alongside eight counts of attempted murder, arson with intent to endanger life, possession of a class B drug and possession of a knife in a public place.



He remains in custody after he was arrested in Leeds earlier today and is due to appear at Willesden Magistrates’ Court tomorrow.

This comes after Pawel Kupla, 34, was charged with one count of murder, eight counts of attempted murder and one count of arson with intent to endanger life.



The Met Police said their investigation “remains ongoing” after they were called to Berkeley Avenue at around 1.14am last Wednesday.

It was also reported at the time how a hero neighbour in his pyjamas battled the raging flames.

Armed with a jet washer, shopkeeper Satwant Singh, 48, rushed outside to fight the blaze, The Sun revealed.

His daughter had spotted the fire from her bedroom window and woken him up in the middle of the night.

He told us: “I told my wife to get all the children outside and then opened up the alleyway side door and brought the jet wash around the front of the house to spray the fire.



“I could see that the door was on fire but there was smoke everywhere else.”

Satwant said he put out “most of the fire”, adding: “I didn’t think about myself, I was just thinking that I needed to help.

“We are Sikhs. My culture says we should help people. It doesn’t matter who you are.”

His wife, Barkash, praised his bravery and said she begged him to move from the flames, but that he continued spraying the house.

She said: “He is very brave. I think the water from the jet wash reduced the smoke coming from the house and helped people get out.”



Another local Shaf Akmal, 40, said he was one of the first people outside.

He said: “I saw two men who stood on the back of a car parked in the driveway of the house and broke the downstairs window to pull two people out.”

Shaf’s ring doorbell footage showed the house suddenly being engulfed in flames.

Officers attended the scene alongside the London Fire Brigade and London Ambulance Service.

Lisa Ramsarran, chief crown prosecutor in London North said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute Pawel Kupla for murder, attempted murder and arson following a fatal fire in Hounslow, west London which resulted in the murder of a 48-year-old woman and the injury of eight others at approximately 1am on Wednesday 19 August.



“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to pursue criminal proceedings.

“We have worked closely with the Metropolitan Police to bring this case to court, and we will continue working with them as their investigation progresses.”

The Met Police have urged anyone with information or footage that may assist their investigation to get in touch.

News.title: Dolly Parton: The life of an iconic country singer
News.content:
Iconic country musician Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80, her family announced on her social media.

"Sadness lies with us, not with Dolly," Parton's nephew Brian Seaver said in a video announcement.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.

Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy."

She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her show business career that spanned more than 60 years.

Follow for live updates and read more about Dolly's life.

News.title: Father's house rammed before son died in A66 crash
News.content:
A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.

Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.

Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.

The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.

There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

News.title: Winter energy prices expected to rise to three-year high
News.content:
Energy bills for millions of households are expected to rise this winter to the highest level for three years, under a price cap to be announced by the industry regulator on Wednesday.

The cap will reflect the rise in the wholesale cost of gas, paid by suppliers and will hit bills just as the colder weather arrives in October until the end of December.

Analysts expect Ofgem to say prices will go up by 4% compared with the current cap, affecting those on variable tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales.

Firms say energy debt has jumped and, with high bills likely to persist, have called for more support for those struggling to pay. The government says VAT is being cut from electricity bills.

The price cap for about 33 million households is expected to rise, driven by volatility in international wholesale gas prices.

The average price of gas has been 61% higher over the past three months compared to late 2025, according to suppliers' trade body Energy UK.

Millions of people have moved on to fixed energy tariffs, some in response to the uncertainty created by the impact of the US-Israeli war with Iran.

Anyone on a fixed deal will not see the price they pay rise, until at least the end of the term of their tariff. About 40% of billpayers have fixed tariffs.

News.title: Why Pride is facing a backlash - from inside and outside the LGBT community
News.content:
Matt left Crewe as soon as he could, aged 18, feeling that he wasn't accepted as a young gay man. The only LGBT scene to mention was a tiny, makeshift bar behind a curtain in the back of an out-of-town pub.

He left in 2015, but this June found himself returning home, for Crewe Pride.

For Matt, it was a significant homecoming. "It really took me back to when I was a kid growing up here, trying to navigate my identity. It felt so important to be there and see how a town that wasn't particularly welcomingâ¦ has changed and flourished."

For many, these small, community Pride events feel a world away from the huge celebrations in the UK's largest cities.

But Matt's happy weekend in Crewe masks a growing culture war over Pride. Over the last few years, a number of councils have withdrawn their support for Pride festivals, while some big brands - perhaps nervous about being seen as too "woke" - have become hesitant to associate themselves with them. On top of all that, there's a long-running complaint from some LGBT campaigners that Pride has become overly commercialised; while the argument over trans issues has also made matters more fraught.

It's leading some to ask: what future do Pride events have?

News.title: Yellow warnings in force as rain and thunderstorms hit parts of UK
News.content:
Downpours and thunderstorms will continue to bring the risk of flooding to parts of the UK on Wednesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms is valid from 03:00 until 22:00 BST, covering much of the Midlands, parts of northern, eastern and southern England, as well as the far east of Wales.

The rain could be heavy enough to bring flash flooding and travel disruption, with lightning and large hail posing additional hazards.

A further Met Office yellow warning has been issued for Thursday with more thunderstorms expected.

For some areas that have seen barely any rain so far this August, the next few days could bring the wettest weather in many weeks.

News.title: Man dies in crash after police pursuit
News.content:
A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.

Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.

A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's 19-year-old male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics.

The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.

Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.

A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said.

Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.

It later reopened.

News.title: As Ukraine hits Russia's refineries, Russia targets Ukraine's petrol pumps
News.content:
"Fill up quickly and move on," Mayor Ihor Terekhov warns drivers in Ukraine's second largest city Kharkiv.

Two petrol stations in the city in Ukraine's north-east were hit by Russian drones on Monday, which local officials say wounded two people. In another attack on a petrol station outside the city of Kryvyi Rih last week, three people were killed.

Russia's campaign of targeting civilian filling stations with drones and missiles began in earnest in April, primarily in regions on the front line, and the attacks are steadily growing more frequent.

At the same time, Russia has endured two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

In total, Russia has hit at least 246 filling stations across Ukraine so far, says Oleksandr Sirenko, an analyst with Ukrainian energy think-tank Nafto Rynok ("Oil Market").

In July alone, the Centre for Information Resilience, an open-source investigation non-profit group, verified 114 Russian strikes on filling stations, compared with 66 the month before.

Given the threat, police have issued special guidance urging motorists to leave petrol stations and, if necessary, to abandon their vehicles whenever air raid alerts sound.

"You can fix your car, but you won't get your life back," says one police force in the Dnipropetrovsk region.

The damage is highly disruptive and puts civilians at considerable risk.

According to Sirenko, initially the attacks were being carried out with smaller, remote-controlled drones, but then Russia started using bigger, more expensive and more destructive Iranian-made Shahed drones.

One Shahed drone is estimated to cost between $20,000 (Â£14,500) and $50,000 (Â£36,000).

"One petrol station took five Shahed hits," Sirenko tells the BBC. "These Shaheds cost more than the petrol station."

News.title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
News.content:
Smokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found.

The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10.

They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine.

And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine, external, which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed.

News.title: Yellow weather warnings issued as thunderstorms and flooding forecast
News.content:
Yellow weather warnings have been issued by the Met Office as heavy rain and thunderstorms are forecast to break out over parts of the UK later this week.

The warnings span Wednesday and Thursday and include parts of east Wales, the Midlands, northern England, East Anglia and southern England - including London.

It is likely to be the one of the most widespread outbreaks of heavy rain across southern and central parts of the UK this summer.

While good news for regions plagued by drought, significant accumulations could lead to flash flooding where the ground is too dry and hard to absorb the downpours. Lightning, large hail and gusty winds are also possible.

News.title: Young care leavers dying early a 'national tragedy'
News.content:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today, report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

News.title: Boy, 3, injured in crocodile attack returns home
News.content:
A three-year-old boy who was seriously injured in a crocodile enclosure has been discharged from hospital and is settling back in at home, his family has said.

The child returned home "a few weeks ago" and is "happy to be home, playing with his toys, sleeping in his own bed and being a big brother", his parents said in an update posted online.

The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, with his family on 18 June when he was attacked by at least one of the animals.

In an update shared on a fundraising page on Monday, the boy's family said it was "nice to have us all back together in the comfort of our own home".

Cambridgeshire Police arrested and bailed a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder after the incident.

News.title: Inspectors to assess police after Henry Nowak murder
News.content:
An inspection into how a police force responds to violent incidents has been launched in the wake of Henry Nowak's murder.

The 18-year-old student was stabbed in Southampton by Vickrum Digwa, who lied to police and insisted he had been the victim of a racist attack.

Hampshire Police officers initially arrested Nowak and placed him in handcuffs as he lay dying.

His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Service (HMICFRS) will assess the force's processes, training and how officers are supported to make sound and impartial judgements.

The inspection was requested by Hampshire Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones, who said the public "must have confidence" in the force.

"This inspection will provide an independent assessment of the force's training, processes and culture, including the handling of allegations of racially aggravated assault," she said.

"Henry's family deserve answers, and the public deserve reassurance that their police service is equipped to recognise victims and provide the highest standard of care when it matters most."

News.title: Legendary rugby league winger Boston dies aged 92
News.content:
Tributes have been led by prime minister Andy Burnham who said he was a "giant of a man in every way".

"Heartbroken to hear my friend Sir Billy Boston has died," he said on social media.

"Billy was one of the greatest rugby league players of all time but also one of the kindest and most down-to-earth people you could ever wish to meet.

"He always had time for people and gave so much to back to his adopted home, Wigan.

"I will miss him greatly and am thinking today of Billy's family, still grieving the recent loss of his beloved wife Joan."

Wigan owner Mike Danson said: "Billy Boston was everybody's hero, including my mum's.

"His achievements in rugby league were extraordinary, and his knighthood was a fitting recognition of a career that brought great credit to Wigan and to the game.

"But Billy's legacy was not simply what he achieved. It was the humility with which he carried it. Despite everything he accomplished, he remained a quiet, dignified and deeply respected man.

"He leaves behind an example that will endure for generations. Our thoughts are with his family and those closest to him.

"A great man, and a true Wigan legend. He will be remembered with pride and affection."

In a statement, Wales Rugby League said: "Today, rugby league has lost one of its greatest-ever players, Wales has lost one of its finest sporting sons, and our sport has lost a truly special gentleman."

The WRU also paid tribute, calling Boston "one of the best loved and most iconic figures in the history of Welsh sport".

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy added: "He was, in my view, the greatest rugby league player of all time and one of the nicest people I've ever had the privilege to know."

News.title: Former police officer charged with raping woman while on duty
News.content:
A former police officer allegedly raped and strangled a woman while on duty, according to the policing watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said ex-constable Rikki Hall had been charged with two counts of rape and one count of non-fatal strangulation.

The 33-year-old is accused of attacking the woman while on duty in Swansea city centre in February 2024.

Hall, who resigned from South Wales Police during the IOPC investigation, has also been charged with possession of a firearm and two counts of misconduct in public office.

He will appear at Bristol Magistrates' Court on Thursday.

The IOPC said its investigation began in February 2024 following a mandatory conduct referral from South Wales Police.

"A substantial file of material was submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service in February 2025 and, following further lines of enquiry being undertaken, charges were authorised by the CPS," it added.

News.title: 'We just want to get home' - dozens stranded in Tunisia after cancelled Belfast flight
News.content:
Dozens of people from Northern Ireland have been left stranded in Tunisia after their EasyJet flight home was cancelled, with the airline telling them it had no other flights available for another 10 days.

One man told BBC News NI he has spent Â£4,000 on travel home for his family-of-five, while another woman, Georgina Doherty, said she and her six children were trying to get home after the death of her mother-in-law.

Others described running out of medication for health issues, while EasyJet were also criticised over a lack of support and communication.

EasyJet has said it is operating an additional direct flight to Belfast on Tuesday night, and that it was "very sorry" for the inconvenience.

BBC News NI understands more than 100 people were booked onto the cancelled flight that was due to leave Enfidha-Hamamet Airport for Belfast International three days ago.

Stuart McCartney, from Dromore, County Down, said he had spent thousands on accommodation and flights to get his family home via a flight to Brussels.

"I'm willing to pay Â£4,000 to get us home, if needs be, and then battle for reimbursement if I have to after that," he said.

"But we shouldn't have to pay. My holiday was a fraction of what I'm paying to get home right now."

McCartney said EasyJet provided two nights of accommodation but then told the family to find alternative accommodation for the rest of the delay.

He said his mother Katherine, who accompanied his wife and children on the trip, relies on heart medication and they have had to keep a close eye on her remaining supply as the delay continued.

An EasyJet spokesperson said that the company "have been doing everything we can to support Mr McCartney, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred".

Georgina Doherty, who is originally from Londonderry but now lives in County Donegal, told BBC News NI the last few days have been an "absolute nightmare" for her family.

Her husband returned home a day before they were due to fly back due to his mother taking ill. She has since died, with Doherty and her six children stranded in Tunisia.

News.title: More than 70,000 social and affordable homes to be built across England over 10 years
News.content:
Ministers have announced where more than 70,000 social and affordable homes will be built in England over the next 10 years as part of an initial allocation of almost Â£10bn in a bid to address the housing crisis.

Funding has been granted to Greater Manchester, the West Midlands, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, North East England, and Liverpool. An additional Â£6bn was previously announced for London.

It is the first part of a wider plan to build 300,000 social and affordable homes, under the government's Â£39bn social housebuilding programme.

Housing charities welcomed the news but said it was still not enough to meet demand, while the Conservatives said it was an "unfunded spending commitment".

Social housing provides affordable homes at a low cost, managed by social landlords. It includes affordable rented properties as well as low-cost home ownership, such as shared ownership, and can be provided by local authorities and housing associations.

Earlier this year, before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham had called for the entire Â£39bn affordable housing budget for England to be spent on homes for social rent - which means the cost of the unit is about half that of market rents, and there are strict criteria for who can apply for it.

"I would actually devote all of it to social housing," Burnham told The Social Housing Podcast in May.

But of the new homes announced on Monday, 60% would be for social rent.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook told BBC Breakfast he did not accept Burnham had failed to meet his previous commitment, saying the government had taken a "pragmatic approach" and wants to "get money out the door".

He said the next tranche of funding would be more focused on council houses - which are usually also classed as homes for social rent.

It is understood ministers decided against giving councils more of the funding announced in the first tranche because they did not believe councils would be in a position to build the required number of social homes.

Chinese artist Gao Zhen was sentenced to three years in prison Tuesday for “infringing upon the reputation of heroes” through his satirical works of art, including statues of China's former leader Mao Zedong.

The U.S.-based Gao, who was part of an artistic duo known internationally as the Gao Brothers, was arrested while visiting family in China in August 2024. He has been in official custody since then.

He was sentenced by the Sanhei People's Court court in northern Hebei province, according to his wife, Zhao Yaliang.

The charges against Gao relate to artistic works that China's authorities deem insulting to revolutionary figures. One was a 2009 statue called Mao’s Guilt that shows the former leader and founder of modern China kneeling in repentance, and another was the Miss Mao series of caricatures depicting Mao with breasts and an engorged nose.

Shane Yi, a researcher at Chinese Human Rights Defenders, who has been advocating for Gao's case, described the sentence as “a very clear case of a violation of a person’s freedom of expression.”

Yi said the artist plans to appeal the sentence and noted that the artworks in question were created before the law Gao was sentenced with had been passed.

The court did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Amnesty International criticized the court sentence, which it described as a deterrent against artistic expression.

“The lengthy pre-trial detention and, ultimately, decision to convict Gao Zhen and sentence him to the maximum three-year prison term under this offense illustrate the authorities’ determination to deter others from engaging in independent artistic expression,” said Amnesty's China Director Sarah Brooks.

“No artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history,” she said.

Zhao said she hopes to be reunited with her husband and be able to return to the U.S., where the family had immigrated.

“I felt two years was my limit, and I was really disappointed and sad. I haven't been able to catch my breath,” she said. She had prepared clothes for her husband hoping that he would be released. Chinese courts often count pretrial detention as time served in a sentence.

The Gao Brothers, whose works addressed themes of authoritarianism and censorship, became famous in a time of relative openness in China and were exhibited both inside the country and abroad.

However, in recent years, the state's increased its controlling grip on certain aspects of expression, especially in regards to political figures with the passage of the law in 2018 that bans criticism of the nation's heroes.

U.S. Sen. Darline Graham has secured the Republican nomination on South Carolina’s general election ballot to replace her late brother, Lindsey Graham.

She defeated U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman during Tuesday’s special Republican primary runoff, two weeks after the pair emerged as the top two candidates from a 10-way primary.

A newcomer to politics, Darline Graham defeated several prominent state figures in the contest triggered by her brother’s sudden death last month. Appointed by Gov. Henry McMaster to complete the remaining months of the term, she quickly secured an endorsement from President Donald Trump, who encouraged her to seek a full term and campaigned with her in South Carolina last week.

open image in gallery Despite being a political unknown, Darline Graham bested some of South Carolina’s top political names in the special election spun up after her brother’s sudden death last month ( Sean Rayford/Getty Images )

Graham will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews in November.

On Monday, MAGA Inc., the super PAC that supports Trump and aligned Republicans — but that has spent little thus far on Trump's picks in this year's midterms — infused nearly $830,000 into Graham's campaign for voter calls and text message blasts.

Among the unknowns going into Tuesday was whether Trump's backing would be enough to boost the novice candidate with the famous last name, but whose political positions were previously unknown, across the finish line to the nomination.

After losing a top Senate advocate when Lindsey Graham died July 11, Trump angled to play a role in picking his successor.

Trump heralded the selection of Darline Graham to serve as her brother’s interim replacement as “a fabulous tribute.” He also urged her to run in the special primary, endorsing her before she’d made her candidacy official.

On Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump reiterated that sentiment to a crowd of several thousand, encouraging people to vote for Graham to preserve tax cuts, among other things.

“I want it to happen,” he said. “Good luck, Darline.”

In forging a relationship with her, Trump could be angling to develop another ally to help steer his agenda through the Senate.

open image in gallery On Friday in Myrtle Beach, Trump reiterated that sentiment to a crowd of several thousand, encouraging people to vote for Graham to preserve tax cuts, among other things ( Win McNamee/Getty Images )

Throughout her brief campaign, Graham did just that. She repeatedly stressed to voters her intent to support Trump’s policy positions and often referenced in particular her co-sponsorship of a voting bill that’s become a key priority for the president.

Casting his ballot for Graham at an early voting location near Trump's rally site, Robert Tropiano said Friday that the president's backing for the candidate was enough to win his support.

“Trump wants her, he's doing a great job and I believe we should give him what he wants,” Tropiano said.

Norman promoted legislative know-how over Graham's inexperience

Fresh off his unsuccessful primary run for governor, Norman entered the Senate contest as one of several politicians more familiar to South Carolina voters. He snapped up endorsements from the likes of Sens. Rick Scott of Florida and Mike Lee of Utah, as well as former South Carolina Sen. Jim DeMint and Turning Point Action, the conservative youth movement founded by the late Charlie Kirk.

During the sprint to the runoff, Norman — one of the most conservative U.S. House members — frequently touted his experience in Washington and willingness to take unpopular stances. That includes at times challenging Trump, whose policies Norman has routinely supported in Congress. But Norman campaigned against Trump in the early part of the 2024 presidential primary, siding instead with former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley.

A wealthy developer before he entered politics, Norman put some of his own fortune toward the campaign, including more than $1 million in the closing week.

open image in gallery Fresh off his unsuccessful primary run for governor, Norman entered the Senate contest as one of several politicians more familiar to South Carolina voters ( AP Photo/Meg Kinnard )

Graham overcomes debate flub

Graham and Norman met for a single runoff debate, and there was one moment from the hourlong face-off that lived on.

Graham stumbled over a question about foreign policy — a signature issue of her late brother — when asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea, a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations.

She struggled to answer before admitting “national security is not my thing” and “I’m not that informed on national security.”

Graham avoided a direct response and instead mentioned her brother’s wealth of experience and her desire to focus on more domestic issues like affordability. Norman called Taiwan “a definite ally” when posed the same question, applauding Trump for “enabling Taiwan to defend themselves against China.” Afterward, he suggested Graham's answer showed her lack of qualifications for the office.

Some of that argument landed with Rock Hill voter Mike Sellers, who said that he voted Tuesday for Norman in part because Graham's experience level “wasn't really cutting it for me."

Sellers also said he wasn't swayed by the notion of supporting Graham as a tribute to her late brother.

“Just because her brother was senator doesn’t give her an easy pass in,” Sellers said. "If she wants to come next time around — maybe challenge (Sen.) Tim Scott — we’ll look at it then.”

No Democrat has won a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina in decades. When Graham last ran in 2020, he defeated his Democratic opponent by a 10 percentage point margin.

That contest was the most expensive in state history and among the country’s most expensive congressional races ever.

A Southern California start-up used high-tech drones to enhance a series of clouds in Alaska over the weekend, generating what it said was approximately 19 million gallons of water in three hours.

The company, Rainmaker, argues the test is a breakthrough and proof that its tech will help fight drought and protect water systems across the country.

“In the future, Rainmaker will protect and restore glaciers with man-made snowfall,” CEO Augustus Doricko wrote on X after the demo. “Immediately, this demonstration shows how Rainmaker will add new water to the Colorado River and Great Salt Lake in the coming months.”

Rainmaker, which says it’s the first private company to “unambiguously prove” its cloud seeding technologies work at scale, conducted the test above Alaska’s Kenai Peninsula. It has previously conducted validated cloud-seeding in Utah, Idaho and Oregon, according to the company.

Rainmaker uses drones and advanced weather-monitoring software to target clouds with silver iodide, which encourages the formation of ice crystals and ultimately precipitation as rain or snow.

open image in gallery Rainmaker, a cloud seeding start-up, used drones in Alaska to generate roughly 19 million gallons of water in a recent test ( Rainmaker )

The company, founded in 2023, has inked contracts with Western states and water systems, and it has raised more than $50 million from investors.

Rainmaker was previously the target of unfounded claims from conspiracy theorists that it caused deadly Texas flooding.

It has spent an estimated $450,000 on federal lobbying in 2025, according to E&E News, and has funded s in Washington, D.C. to make the case to the public and lawmakers about its technology.

“People have had very, very legitimate questions about what cloud seeding is and whether it’s safe and whether it should be allowed at all,” Doricko told the outlet in January.

open image in gallery The company hopes to use its technology to protect glaciers and fill drought-starved Western water systems ( Rainmaker )

“My first priority is just making sure that America and American farms and communities have the option to use this technology,” he added.

Scientists and local officials have been experimenting with cloud-seeding since the mid-1900s.

The climate crisis, coupled with advances in drone, weather monitoring and AI technology, have all helped spur a new wave of companies working on cloud-seeding.

“We’re looking at a really, really kind of dire situation, drastic times and we’ve got to be smart with the water we have,” Joel Ferry, executive director of the Utah Department of Natural Resources, told The Washington Post earlier this year. “We can’t be stuck in kind of the old ways. And a big part of that is using cloud seeding.”

The practice is regarded as a promising tool, though climate experts emphasize that cloud seeding alone cannot offset the impacts of the climate crisis and ongoing megadroughts.

As The Independent has reported, another weather-modification practice, using aerosol particles to block out solar radiation, has also generated considerable investor interest and controversy.

The U.S. military attacked a boat suspected of being used to smuggle drugs in the Caribbean Sea on Tuesday, killing four people, as the Trump administration continues its monthslong campaign against alleged traffickers in Latin America.

The latest attack brings the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the U.S. military to at least 227 in 68 strikes since the Trump administration began targeting those it calls “narcoterrorists” almost a year ago. As with most of the military’s statements on strikes in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, U.S. Southern Command said it targeted the alleged drug traffickers along known smuggling routes.

The military did not provide evidence that the vessel was ferrying drugs. A video posted on X showed an image of what appeared to be a moving boat followed by a flash.

Tuesday's strike came just two days after the U.S. military carried out a strike on a vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of trafficking drugs. That action came after a pause of more than two months in the U.S. campaign against alleged smugglers.

The Trump administration is pursuing deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the U.S. to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal. Ecuador launched similar missions with the U.S. in March.

President Donald Trump has said the U.S. is in “armed conflict” with cartels in Latin America and has justified the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the United States and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing smugglers.

Dolly Parton, who was born in a two-room log cabin and rose to become the world’s wealthiest country music star with timeless hits including “9 to 5” and “Jolene,” has died aged 80 after a “brief battle with cancer.”

Her death was announced by her nephew, Bryan Seaver, in an Instagram video posted Tuesday afternoon. The musician’s publicist confirmed Parton’s cancer diagnosis to the Associated Press later in the day, but did not give further details on her illness.

“Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched. Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand,” the statement from her reps to People magazine read.

“Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly’s unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact. After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones.”

Earlier, Seaver said that Parton had asked him years ago to record the video announcing her death. He served as Parton’s head of security for more than two decades.

“Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus,” he continued. A cause of death was not revealed. However, Parton had been open about struggling with her health in recent months, forcing a slew of concert and public appearance cancellations.

Most recently, Parton was forced to pull out of attending the opening night of a new attraction at Dollywood, her Tennessee theme park last week. The singer suffered dizziness and dehydration and her doctor advised her against travel.

open image in gallery Dolly Parton photographed in London in 1977, the same year she released her first million-selling album ‘Here You Come Again’ ( Getty )

Parton became one of the most beloved singer-songwriters of all time and sold more than 100 million records globally, earning her the nickname the “Queen of Country,” over the course of her six-decade career.

She wrote more than 3,000 songs, and a record-breaking 44 of her albums reached the top 10 on the country music charts. She won eleven Grammy Awards, three Emmy Awards and was set to receive an honorary Oscar for her humanitarian work in 2026.

She was believed to be the world’s wealthiest country music star, with an estimated net worth of $500m, and became a noted philanthropist. She was known for her efforts to encourage literacy around the world through her Dollywood Foundation’s Imagination Library, and also used her money to fight the HIV/Aids crisis, fund the American Red Cross and develop a Covid vaccine.

In 2022, she was awarded the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy and commented: “I just give from my heart. I never know what I’m going to do or why I’m gonna do it. I just see a need and if I can fill it, then I will.”

open image in gallery Dolly Parton attends the opening of the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum exhibition ‘Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker’ in Nashville, Tennessee, in May 2025 ( Getty )

Born on January 19, 1946, in a two-room log cabin on the banks of the Little Pigeon River in Tennessee, Parton was the fourth of 12 children. Her father was an illiterate sharecropper who worked his way up to owning a small tobacco farm.

Parton later described her family as being “dirt poor” but credited her mother with passing on her love and deep knowledge of traditional folk ballads and her father for his work ethic. “He raised that whole family on his brains and hard work,” she wrote in a 2020 memoir. “He knew how to count money. He knew what everything was worth.”

Parton started performing when she was a child. By the age of 13, she had appeared on local radio and television in East Tennessee; performed at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville; and recorded her first single “Puppy Love.” When she graduated high school in 1964, she moved to Nashville the next day and began establishing herself as a songwriter.

open image in gallery Dolly Parton in 1980’s ‘9 to 5’. She also wrote and sang the title song, which became a number one hit and was nominated for an Oscar ( 20th Century Fox )

She released her debut album Hello, I’m Dolly in 1967, the same year she joined the weekly television program The Porter Wagoner Show. Wagoner was an established country star who mentored Parton, and they released a string of successful albums as a duo.

In 1973, Parton decided to concentrate on her solo career and wrote the ballad “I Will Always Love You” about their professional separation. The song was a hit for Parton and again for Whitney Houston, who recorded a 1992 power ballad cover that topped the charts for a then-record-breaking 14 weeks.

Parton once said that she wrote “I Will Always Love You” the same day she wrote another of her signature hits, “Jolene.” She later qualified the claim, telling an interviewer: “When we found an old tape, they were on the same cassette. That could have been a few days apart. They were certainly written within a very short span of time.”

open image in gallery Dolly Parton and Kenny Rogers had a chart-topping hit in 1983 with ‘Islands in the Stream’ ( Getty )

open image in gallery Dolly Parton, seen opening a new ride in 2010, bought an interest in a Tennessee theme park in 1986 and renamed it Dollywood ( AP )

Both songs were included on her 1974 album Jolene, which brought her to a wider audience outside of country music. 1977’s Here You Come Again was her first album to sell a million copies, and gave her a first Grammy win after almost a decade of nominations.

In 1980, Parton took on her first acting role when she was cast alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin in the subversive workplace comedy 9 to 5. She also wrote the film’s theme song, which became a number one hit, earned an Oscar nomination for Best Original Song and made her an icon to women everywhere. It was eventually adapted into a Broadway musical.

The film’s success helped Parton launch a secondary career as an actor, appearing in movies including The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas (1982), Steel Magnolias (1989) and Joyful Noise (2012).

open image in gallery Dolly Parton and Carl Dean were married for 58 years ( Instagram/@DollyParton )

Parton kept up a prolific rate of productivity throughout her life, releasing a new album at least every couple of years alongside diverse business ventures including TV specials, frozen food and her own Dollywood theme park in Tennessee. Among various rides and attractions, the park features a replica of the tiny log cabin where she was born.

She married just once – to her husband of nearly 60 years Carl Dean, a businessman who she met aged 18, on the same day she moved to Nashville. The singer once wrote she was “surprised and delighted” that while Carl talked to her, he looked at her face.

“He seemed to be genuinely interested in finding out who I was and what I was about,” she said.

open image in gallery Dolly Parton performing with Miley Cyrus, her goddaughter, at the Grammy Awards in Los Angeles in 2019 ( Kevin Winter/Getty Images for The Recording Academy )

open image in gallery Dolly Parton, seen here launching her first Imagination Library’ in the UK in Rotherham in 2007, was a noted philanthropist ( Getty Images )

The pair married two years later on May 30, 1966 in Georgia. For years they kept their relationship strictly private, with Parton telling AP in 1984: “A lot of people say there’s no Carl Dean, that he’s just somebody I made up to keep other people off me.”

Dean died in March 2025 at the age of 82. Parton said just days before her death that she neglected her own health while caring for Dean.

Parton’s health concerns first became public in September 2025, when she was forced to postpone her Las Vegas residency.

She made the announcement with a joke about her history of cosmetic surgery, writing: “As many of you know, I have been dealing with some health challenges, and my doctors tell me that I must have a few procedures. As I joked with them, it must be time for my 100,000-mile check-up, although it’s not the usual trip to see my plastic surgeon!”

Parton was then forced to miss several planned public appearances, including one at Dollywood just days before her death.

The buzziest film in China this year was shot almost entirely in a southern Chinese dialect that most Chinese viewers need subtitles to understand.

Yet “Dear You” has become China's second-highest-grossing film of the year. Now it is heading overseas, part of a broader wave of Chinese cultural exports.

“Dear You" was shot mostly in Teochew, a dialect spoken in Guangdong’s Shantou region. Set among the Teochew immigrant community in Bangkok, it tells the story of people who left China in search of work to support their families. Made on a low budget, it features a cast of mostly unknown actors.

The film provides a glimpse into the centuries-long history of Chinese migration to Southeast Asia. It has succeeded in making this little-discussed history visible to a wider audience, threading the fine needle of passing official censorship requirements, experts say, while telling a compelling story.

As of August, the movie had grossed about 269 million yuan ($40 million) at the Chinese box office. It was released in Thailand in early August after being shown in Singapore, Malaysia and Australia. It will be released in the U.S. next month.

China is increasing its soft power with cultural exports

The film's popularity comes as Chinese culture and consumer brands have been gaining global cachet — from collectible Labubu dolls to “Chinamaxxing,” a social media trend of embracing aspects of the Chinese lifestyle.

The Chinese government began promoting the film as it became a hit and prepared for its international release.

The Chinese consul in Sydney said at a June screening of the film that it “reflects the Chinese nation’s virtues of diligence, kindness, courage and unity.”

The movie aligns with Beijing’s broader goal of “telling China’s stories well,” highlighting themes of friendship, tradition and family, including motherhood and kinship, said Belinda He, an assistant professor of East Asian cinema and media studies at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

China’s ambassador to Thailand presented the film at a special screening in July and again at a red carpet event this month.

“We’re grateful to Guangdong for making such a wonderful film,” Chinese ambassador Zhang Jiangwei said at the red carpet event, which was attended by officials from Guangdong's Information Office. “Stories about ordinary people and simple, genuine emotions can be even more moving. This film is an excellent vehicle for telling China’s story well.”

Chinese migration to Southeast Asia has been ongoing for centuries

The film first resonated in Malaysia and Singapore because it showcases a history that's rarely featured in mainstream films.

Chinese migration to Southeast Asia dates back centuries, with many migrants coming from the Guangdong and Fujian provinces in southern China. Many worked as laborers in building projects in an era of Western colonial rule across much of Asia.

The film starts with a young man trying to find his grandfather, Deng Musheng, in hopes of getting a loan to repay his debts. In the family lore, there was supposedly a wealthy grandfather in Thailand, who left his young wife and children behind in China and never came back.

Using an address on an old remittance letter his grandfather had sent, he meets people who became part of his grandfather’s life in Bangkok, uncovering the mystery of why his grandfather never returned.

The film's director, Lan Hongchun, wrote in a column for the People's Daily, a state media outlet, that he grew up hearing stories from his grandmother about people she knew migrating to Bangkok, and wanted to tell these stories in film.

The film also resonates with Thai Chinese viewers

The plot revolves around “qiaopi,” remittance letters used by Chinese immigrants to send money and news back home. Many workers who could not write Chinese relied on scribes to compose the letters.

Scenes set in the centralized offices where the scribes worked, called “poy kuan,” were directly out of the childhood of 74-year-old Sathien Tuntipaiboontana.

“I connected emotionally with that part of the film quite strongly," he said after watching the first screening of the film in a Bangkok theater with his older sisters and sisters-in-law. Among them was his eldest sister, who is 89 and needed help climbing the stairs to the cinema.

Their father had immigrated to Bangkok from China in search of work, leaving behind a wife and children. He ended up remarrying and never returned to China. But Sathien’s family continued to send remittances to the family left behind in China.

Thitikorn Phanprayoon, a third-generation Thai Chinese, said he decided to see the film after hearing Teochew, the Chinese dialect he speaks at home, in the trailer. It surprised him since most Chinese films are in Mandarin. He plans to return with his parents.

“I felt like I was sitting at home," he said. “It felt like my family was performing in the movie in front of me.”

___

AP writer Fu Ting contributed to this story from Washington, D.C.

News.title: Palmer and Rogers show promise of star double act for Chelsea
News.content:
“I am very happy for Cole,” Alonso said. “I have really enjoyed seeing him play with the dynamism and the freedom and the responsibility... when Cole feels this way we have a better team and a better Cole.”

Palmer makes it look very easy in this form, capable of switching the direction of play a beat before anyone else spots the opportunity. He and his old Manchester City academy friend Rogers came off before the end, Palmer having demonstrated some discomfort chasing a ball. Asked afterwards how ready he felt, Palmer responded in kind. “Did you not watch the game? I’m only joking, I’m ready... it was a difficult season with injuries and whatnot, but through the summer and since I’ve been back I’ve worked extra hard.”

If there was an attacker to compare with him on the other side it was King, who looks even better. The 19-year-old was way ahead of Arbeloa’s two young Real Madrid imports. García toiled away and took his chance, but César Palacios struggled for any impact in a position tucked in on the left. Oscar Bobb and King gave Fulham some edge but the concern, as ever, will be where Fulham get their goals.

Arbeloa pushed his full-backs high and encouraged Sander Berge to drop deep to get on the ball in the first passing phase. The Norwegian delayed too long in challenging João Pedro for Chelsea’s third – backing off and allowing Palmer to overlap to receive the pass.

Sánchez had not been the only concern for Chelsea. Back in the team, Levi Colwill misjudged a challenge on King in the first half and was relieved that the card was only yellow. Roméo Lavia took a wild swing at Calvin Bassey and was also booked. Moisés Caicedo was not fit to play. Enzo Fernández was on the bench and would come on in the second half to the kind of reception from opposition fans to which he will quickly become familiar.

There was a grin from the Argentine at those who berated him from the home stands when he returned at half-time. Fernández worked hard to transmit a general sense that the abuse did not land, although he will be relieved that the Chelsea fans were supportive. His future still feels very much in play.

It was Palmer’s subtle ball through that gave João Pedro the chance with 32 seconds of the game played. The ball came forward immediately from Lacroix’s firm header from defence. The Frenchman delivered a very accomplished assist for Rogers’s first-half goal. Before that King had equalised. There was an exchange with Timothy Castagne, and King looked up just inside the box and decided to have a swing at it. Sánchez was close enough to grasp the ball and somehow failed to do so.

Sánchez would later push a Castagne shot in the direction of García, who stooped and nodded the ball over the goalkeeper after Palmer had scored Chelsea’s third. This second error was unfortunate, but it is the kind of thing that happens to a goalkeeper as erratic as the one for whom Chelsea’s hierarchy seem to have such patience.

News.title: This summer’s wildfire epidemic is one of the worst in decades – so why are deaths so low?
News.content:
Wildfires in Britain and Europe this year are among the worst in decades, yet direct deaths are at some of the lowest levels, according to a Telegraph analysis.

As of early August, 505,683 hectares of land have burned across Europe, forcing the evacuation of more than 360,000 people as uncontrollable flames reach major cities, towns, and villages.

The problem is global – in the US, Nevada declared a state of emergency over the weekend after a wildfire caused more than 42,000 people to evacuate their homes.

But what sets 2026 apart isn’t just the vast areas of land burned, but how few deaths have been caused by the fires.

This summer, just 14 people are reported to have died in European wildfires, the vast majority in a single blaze in Almería, southern Spain.

By comparison, more than 130 people were killed in the summer of 2017 – a toll driven largely by the Pedrógão Grande disaster in Portugal, where more than 60 people died on a single stretch of road.

In 2018, at least 100 others died in a single afternoon in the Mati disaster near Athens, despite total hectares burned that year being roughly a third of current levels.

Since the modern phenomenon of summer wildfires exploded in Europe a decade ago, the direct death toll has broadly trended downward, as the chart below shows.

News.title: Swine flu outbreak in Delhi swamps clinics and hospitals
News.content:
India is battling a surge in H1N1 flu infections, prompting the federal health ministry to step up surveillance and hospital preparedness.

The national capital New Delhi has recorded 1,777 cases this year, almost eight times the number (229) reported during the same period in 2025.

Dr Randeep Guleria, a senior pulmonologist and director of Medanta Medical School, Gurugram, says the H1N1 cases are much higher than reported.

“It’s quite likely that the reported numbers are an underestimate because they depend on how many people are tested,” Guleria said. “If you speak to patients admitted to hospital who test positive for H1N1, you often find that other members of their family have similar symptoms, although they have not been tested.”

“There is a surge and we are seeing a lot of patients. We are testing only those who come to hospital and are more seriously ill,” Guleria said.

H1N1, commonly known as swine flu, is a subtype of influenza A. It is a contagious respiratory infection that can cause fever and cough and in severe cases it can lead to pneumonia and respiratory failure.

Officials at the Indian Council of Medical Research said the rise did not mean the emergence of a new strain of the virus.

The surge comes during India’s rainy season, when seasonal influenza and other respiratory infections typically increase.

Doctors in Delhi say they are seeing more patients with high fevers, persistent coughs and flu-like symptoms, although most cases remain mild.

The H1N1 cases have been reported beyond New Delhi. The metro cities like Mumbai, Chennai and Bangaluru have reported a high number of cases, although the pattern is not uniform across the country.

Doctors in Bangaluru have reported more influenza A infections among children, with some developing pneumonia and respiratory distress.

India’s health minister JP Nadda said there was a need for continued vigilance and robust surveillance. He has asked officials to monitor unusual increases and clusters of cases and ensure hospitals could respond quickly.

“Swine flu (H1N1) can show up through symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, headache, runny nose, body aches and fatigue… If you experience these symptoms, seek medical advice at your nearest healthcare centre,” the health ministry said on X.

Delhi’s health minister, Pankaj Kumar Singh, said the capital had enough beds, doctors, medicines and medical equipment to manage the increase. “Delhi is fully prepared to deal with the present health situation,” Singh said.

India has had several waves of H1N1 since the virus emerged globally in 2009.

The infection, commonly called swine flu, became a recurring seasonal respiratory illness after the 2009 pandemic rather than disappearing from circulation.

India recorded 3,320 H1N1 cases and 14 deaths in 2025, according to Ministry of Health data.

Sports.title: Chelsea files: Sanchez’s woeful form laid bare after Fulham horror show and ‘frightening’ Cobham talent coming through
Sports.content:
SOME Chelsea fans had had enough of Robert Sanchez even before his performance at Fulham.

Now the calls for the Spaniard to be replaced, by a new top-class signing or by No 2 Mike Penders, are even louder.



Sky Sports pundits Jamie Carragher and Gary Neville agree. They have repeatedly said Chelsea will never win the Premier League with Sanchez in goal and his errors at Craven Cottage, especially for Josh King’s equaliser, were further ammunition.

And the statistics back up what they and many Chelsea supporters have felt for some time.



The current owners have spent more than £1.5billion on players in the last four years – including five goalkeepers.

At one point they had NINE senior stoppers on their books.

Sanchez, signed three years ago from Brighton for £25m, remains their No 1, despite the numbers suggesting he is not among the top PL goalkeepers..

No ‘keeper has made more mistakes leading to shots since the start of the 2024/5 season than the Spaniard’s 15.

And only Brighton’s Bart Verbruggen has been responsible for more gaffes leading to goals in the same period, with nine to Sanchez’s seven.

On Monday night, some Chelsea fans noted King’s equaliser had the lowest xG of any goal scored in the opening round of PL fixtures.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

His poor positioning and his lacklustre attempt to stop the shot were obvious.

But xG is designed to be used to identify long-term trends rather than deliver verdicts on one-off shots.

A better indication of how a ‘keeper is performing long term, in the basic business of stopping the ball going into the net, is the difference between the xG of on-target shots they face and the actual number of goals conceded, excluding own goals.

Among ‘keepers who have made 30 or more appearances since the start of last season, Sanchez’s “goals prevented” figure of 1.8 ranks ninth out of 15.

Three of those to finish above him play for clubs who, unlike Chelsea, qualified for this season’s Champions League.



Manchester United’s Senne Lammens and Manchester City’s Gianluigi Donnarumma were the top two, with Aston Villa’s Emi Martinez in sixth.

The outlier is Raya. The Arsenal ‘keeper has let in more goals than the algorithm says he should have done since the start of last season.

Since 2024/25, Raya is second to Sanchez in mistakes leading to shots. Arsenal’s defenders seem to be better at clearing up their ‘keeper’s messes than Chelsea’s.



Of course there is more to goalkeeping than can be measured by raw data.

Yet Sanchez on Monday night showed other signs of weakness. He rarely looks comfortable playing the ball short with his feet and as Fulham tried a high press, he allowed a backpass to go out for a corner.

Chelsea have insisted all summer they are happy with their goalkeepers.

Whether the Blues were linked yet again to AC Milan’s Mike Maignan, or more recently to Porto’s Diogo Costa, the message remained the same.

Chelsea have made a panic buy of a goalkeeper before and it turned out well for a while.



After error-prone Kepa Arrizabalaga made one too many mistakes, the Blues signed Edouard Mendy in September 2020.

Mendy was in goal when Thomas Tuchel led the club to its second Champions League crown the following May.

But if the current owners and recruitment team stick to their guns, there will be no new goalkeeper arriving before the window closes

In which case, Thursday’s Carabao Cup clash against Luton looks even more like the right time to give Penders a chance to stake his claim.

New manager Xabi Alonso has insisted “the pitch will decide” whether the Belgian or Sanchez is his No 1.



But if Penders did well, it would still be a big call to drop the Spaniard for the visit of former club Brighton on Sunday.

DO THE SIMPLE THINGS WELL

XABI ALONSO’s Chelsea revolution is full steam ahead, and it’s simplicity is what makes it beautiful.

After season upon season of inverted fullbacks, touchline wingers and players out of position, the most noticeable thing about Chelsea’s game vs Fulham was how everyone knew their role and stuck to it.

Fans grew sick of Enzo Maresca‘s floaty positional nonsense at times, and it feels as though those people will be in awe of Alonso’s positional excellence.

In fact, you’d be forgiven for looking at Chelsea’s average position map and confusing it just for their formation.



Below, if you compare it to Ruben Amorim‘s Manchester United side, it shows just how clear the difference is.

His plan to play a 3-4-2-1 system, as he did at Bayer Leverkusen seems clear with the players that Chelsea have signed to play specific roles, such as Morgan Rogers and Marco Palestra.

Although he did still maintain a fairly fluid shape towards the end of the game when the Blues were trying to see the game out and hold onto all three points with five substitutes on the pitch.



It’s quite a staggering difference to when Maresca, Liam Rosenior or Callum MacFarlane were in charge last season, and that clarity upon who goes where might just be the simplicity that Chelsea need to become a serious team once more.

CNG the next best thing!

CHELSEA have taken a fair bit of flak for their decision to rebrand their academy as ‘Cobham Next Gen’.

And that is to be expected – it sounds daft.

Despite that, however, insiders in the world of academy football still rate the Blues ranks incredibly highly.

Even though the club have operated under an academy transfer embargo since March, which runs until after the January window, their talent pool was this week described to SunSport as “frightening”.



After the pain of losing Rio Ngumoha to Liverpool, a review of how the academy was run was undertaken, led by Joe Shields at sporting director level.

Chelsea are now working desperately hard to ensure figures such as the highly rated Reggie Watson, 16, or Reggie Walsh, 17, do not become the next Ngumoha to leave and find first-team success at another top English club.

Walsh has even followed in the footsteps of captain Reece James by joining Wigan on loan as a teenager.



Chelsea’s depth of talent was evident on their pre-season tour of Australia and Asia, where a lot of effort was placed on keeping the youngsters engaged, with day trips out and their family involved too.

Conversations with family are a significant part of Chelsea’s work with younger players, educating them on the pathways available to players and how to navigate them.
