World.title: 11 years after decriminalisation, ganja use complicating mental health care
World.content:
AI image of a young man smoking marijuana. (Adobe stock)

Eleven years after Jamaica decriminalised ganja, the use of the substance features heavily among patients presenting with psychosis and schizophrenia. While there is currently no data establishing whether use of the herb is causing or contributing to the mental health problems, its prevalence is complicating treatment.

This is against the background of data from the National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) pointing to an increase in high-risk usage of cannabis and the potency of the substance in Jamaica, as well as an increase in admissions for psychosis and schizophrenia over the last decade.

“What we do know is that the majority of psychiatric admissions in our public hospitals are coming from psychosis or schizophrenia. And the majority of those persons do use cannabis. So, we can look at that relationship and see that it is strong,” said Director for Treatment Services at the NCDA, Dr Kristen Robinson Barrett.

Still, Robinson Barrett noted that there is little data specifically exploring cannabis-induced psychosis.

Psychiatrist at Bellevue Hospital, Dr Brian Kazaara concurred that cannabis use has a striking presence among patients presenting with mental issues, but suggested that the substance rarely causes psychotic disorders.

“We don’t have official studies performed at Bellevue Hospital regarding cannabis use among patients, but from a cursory observation I can safely say the vast majority of patients admitted to the hospital also use cannabis,” he said.

Kazaara, who previously worked at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), pointed to a survey carried out by UHWI that revealed that the majority of persons admitted to the institution’s psychiatric ward smoked cannabis.

“What studies show is that persons with common psychiatric conditions like major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders use cannabis far more frequently than persons who do not have mental illnesses,” he said.

Despite this, Kazaara explained, “Cannabis-induced psychosis is not the norm. It is rare. At Bellevue we very, very rarely see that diagnosis. I also worked at UHWI for seven years [and] rarely saw it, almost never.”

Cannabis is a psychoactive drug and can affect the way that people perceive the world, leading to relaxation, paranoia, or other effects.

“It binds to our cannabinoid receptors around our body, but particularly in our brain, and that’s how we get the effects. It tends to create effects as it relates to emotions and feelings,” Robinson Barrett said. “They might experience changes as it relates to their time perception, so things might feel slowed down… issues with their concentration, so their attention and their awareness, their reaction time will change.”

Kazaara cautions that cannabis use can muddle the treatment of mental health issues.

“Cannabis definitely complicates psychosis, because for persons who use cannabis, they are more likely to develop an earlier onset of psychosis. So it may happen earlier than if they didn’t use it. It makes symptoms worse. It makes it harder to treat,” he explained.

Jamaica has a strong culture of recreational cannabis use, and Research Analyst at the NCDA Uki Atkinson explained that while overall population use has not necessarily changed over the last decade following decriminalisation of the drug, the potential for high-risk use has.

She supported her assessment with results from the Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (CAST) which was used during surveys in 2016 and 2023.

“We were able to compare the levels of high-risk use from 2016 to 2023. In 2016, 50 per cent of the people who used cannabis in the past year were deemed to be at high risk for misusing it,” Atkinson said, noting “this has increased by 16 per cent in 2023. So, it shows not necessarily that more people are using ganja… But there’s a significant increase in high-risk patterns of use.”

In addition to high-risk usage, the potency of cannabis being consumed in Jamaica is also a concern.

According to a European study, using high-potency cannabis with a tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) concentration over 10 percent, significantly increases the risk of developing psychotic symptoms or disorders, especially with daily use.

Robinson Barrett expressed serious concern about current potency trends worldwide compared to a potency of around four per cent in the 1990s.

“As of 2024, we’re looking at potencies of 15 to 20 per cent,” Robinson Barrett indicated.

“The potency trends of cannabis in Jamaica measured between 2014 and 2020, were showing that over that decade, the cannabis potency would have moved from about one per cent to over 10 per cent across 12 parishes,” she continued. “So, we’re concerned… because we have a culture of heavy use in young age groups…it’s a very concerning picture as it relates to all young people and any other vulnerable group.”

Outside of general risks, Robinson Barrett noted that there are some who may be particularly susceptible to the effects of cannabis use, including youth.

“Generally speaking, the earlier the age of onset for any substance is going to increase your risk for addiction, and it’s going to increase your risk for its effects…for the cannabis, we’re looking at increased risk for development of psychosis, increased risk for cognitive impairment,” Robinson Barrett said.

She also highlighted people who are genetically vulnerable, or have a family history of mental illness as well as heavy users who smoke regularly.

While cannabis has many cannabinoids, Robinson Barrett explained that the main ones are Delta-9-THC, which most people know as a psychoactive component, and CBD, which can have a calming or relaxing effect.

Kazaara agreed that cannabis misuse can complicate mental health treatment.

“Yes, it does. Cannabis complicates the treatment of psychiatric conditions. For example, in the case of schizophrenia, it can worsen symptoms and also make the medication we use for it, less effective,” he explained.

In the meantime, Atkinson stressed that the NCDA was not demonising cannabis, highlighting the medicinal benefits and scope for a medicinal industry.

“We recognise the value, but we see the downside in our clients and in some of the young people who we have to treat,” she explained.

She urged that use must be balanced with ensuring that the population, especially youth and those with a predisposition to mental illness, understand the risk of use, particularly in a problematic manner.

World.title: Honorary consul to Atlanta Elaine Grant-Bryan ‘humbled’ by OD recognition
World.content:
Elaine Grant-Bryan

When Elaine Grant-Bryan settled in Atlanta in 1990, that city was long acknowledged as the mecca of black empowerment in the United States. She joined a growing Jamaican community which has made an impact in commerce and community politics.

Grant-Bryan has been Jamaica’s honorary consul to Atlanta since 2018. Currently in her third term, she has been awarded the Order of Distinction (Officer class) by the Jamaican government for service to the diaspora.

That award will be presented during the National Honours and Awards ceremony on October 19 at King’s House in Kingston.

In an interview with Observer Online, Grant-Bryan spoke of being “deeply humbled” by recognition of her work. Like New York City and South Florida, she said Jamaicans have made their mark in Atlanta and neighbouring areas such as Decatur and Stone Mountain.

“This region has grown significantly, especially after COVID-19 as Jamaicans moved from colder regions in the United States in great numbers. Our community has doubled, and many have successfully assimilated in the Georgia culture and made significant contributions to Jamaica and this region,” Grant-Bryan stated.

An educator and real estate broker, she points to initiatives started with her husband Gregory as major achievements of her tenure. These include the Elaine Bryan Foundation which drives the Jamaican Pioneer Programme and STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, Mathematics).

The pioneer programme allows Americans of Jamaican heritage to gain citizenship in their family’s homeland. Once that is secured, they increase their contribution to Jamaica’s education system by mentoring and assisting needy students.

STEAM is an enrichment curriculum she developed with her husband, a programmer and Information Technology expert. It teaches coding/programming and offers career assessments, internships, entrepreneurships, and scholarships to Jamaican students completing degrees in STEAM fields.

Empowerment was a buzz word in Elaine Bryan’s home in Kingston, where she was born to a father who was an engineer and her mother, a nurse. A past student of Excelsior and Kingston Technical high schools, she was head girl at the latter.

Staying true to her profession, education is the thrust of upcoming projects by the Elaine Bryan Foundation.

“We will continue to include additional students who are completing degrees in the STEAM fields in Jamaica. The projection for 2026-7 is to extend mentorship programmes in Jamaica, study abroad and exchange programmes,” she disclosed.

World.title: GHN adds US$19,000 to fund 38 more students in ‘Beyond the Backpack’ programme
World.content:
Beyond the Backpack

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Global Humanity Network Inc (GHN), has expanded its inaugural Beyond the Backpack Scholarship Programme to support all 48 students who applied, adding 38 one-time scholarships after initially selecting 10 students for its planned three-year comprehensive programme.

According to a release from GHN, the expansion represents an additional US$19,000 commitment beyond GHN’s original plan.

The 10 students selected through a rigorous process will receive scholarships valued at about US$2,000 annually for three years, representing an initial US$60,000 commitment. The other 38 applicants will each receive a US$500 one-time educational scholarship.

The students attend public primary schools in St Elizabeth, Westmoreland, Trelawny and Hanover.

The 10 comprehensive scholarship recipients will receive support through their remaining primary-school years and transition to secondary education. Depending on individual needs, assistance will include uniforms, footwear, school supplies, transportation, nutrition, technology, tutoring, mentorship, leadership development, academic monitoring, emergency assistance and family-school engagement.

The 38 additional recipients will receive assistance toward essential educational expenses, including uniforms, books, supplies, transportation and technology.

GHN founder, president and chief executive officer Dr Laxley W Stephenson, said the decision to expand the programme was driven by the needs revealed during the application process.

“These students are the face and future of Jamaica, and they must not be left behind,” Stephenson said. “They are not statistics or case numbers. They are children with potential, families making sacrifices, and dreams waiting for an opportunity.”

Dr Vinnett Malcolm, principal of Sheffield Primary School, said financial assistance has greater impact when combined with sustained mentorship and support from families and schools.

“Educational barriers do not diminish a child’s ability or potential, but they can prevent that potential from being fully realised,” Malcolm said.

Dr Binzie Roy Davidson, founding director and vice-president of GHN and chair of the Beyond the Backpack Fund Development Committee, said the organisation could not support only the 10 students selected for the comprehensive programme and leave the remaining applicants without assistance.

“Although we could select only 10 students for the comprehensive three-year scholarship, we could not allow the other 38 to believe that their dreams were unseen,” Davidson said. “We see you, we believe in you, and we are committed to helping you move forward.”

Davidson is appealing to businesses, foundations, philanthropic organisations, community leaders and members of the Jamaican diaspora to help underwrite the additional US$19,000 and support the programme’s long-term sustainability.

Founding director Dr Delroy Fray, OD, described the initiative as an investment in Jamaica’s national development.

“When we remove the barriers standing between a child and an education, we do more than meet an immediate need — we protect potential, restore hope, and help prepare the next generation to lead Jamaica forward,” Fray said.

The programme recognises that educational barriers extend beyond books and school supplies and is built around four pillars: Access, Stability, Advancement and Sustainability.

“A backpack carries supplies, but a child carries dreams,” Stephenson said. “When we look beyond the backpack, we see the child carrying it — the dream behind the uniform, the courage behind the smile, and the family making sacrifices that no camera will ever capture.”

GHN said individuals and organisations can support the initiative by underwriting a US$500 scholarship, sponsoring a student in the comprehensive three-year programme, donating educational resources or technology, becoming a mentor or establishing a strategic partnership with the organisation.

“The additional US$19,000 was not part of GHN’s original financial plan,” the organisation said, “but the needs identified through the 48 applications required action.”

World.title: Nigel Farage wants to scrap GDPR for the UK
World.content:
“[T]he GDPR has strangled small businesses and tech firms alike in a web of unnecessary regulation ... Ten years after the Brexit referendum we should not still be following ridiculous EU privacy laws that hurt British businesses,” Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick said in a statement.

The EU GDPR provides for a wider set of individual rights around personal data (including the “right to be forgotten”) than New Zealand's Privacy Act does.

However, Reform UK stressed in its press release that following the New Zealand model would preserve the U.K.'s EU data adequacy status, meaning personal data would still be allowed to flow freely between the U.K. and EU.

The European Commission only grants adequacy to countries that provide an essentially equivalent level of data protection to that of the EU.

The U.K. has already diverged from Brussels on privacy laws with the passage of the Data (Use and Access) Act last year, which relaxed some aspects of the U.K. GDPR in a bid to boost economic growth.

World.title: Trains between Britain and Europe on track to run every 15 minutes
World.content:
Using this new facility will allow Trenitalia to bypass capacity limits at the Temple Mills International depot in east London, where Eurostar keeps its fleet and where Virgin is also expected to do so. The U.K. regulator allocated the last space in the facility to Virgin last year.

Mark Smith, a former rail manager who runs the popular Man In Seat 61 travel website, told POLITICO: “Both contenders appear to have the ability and financial backing to make this happen, but there are many steps in a long process before any train runs. Trenitalia are in pole position with a 2029 start date, helped by having ordered trains of a type already approved for France and a continuation of an existing production line.”

Travellers check their phones while standing next to a Eurostar train at St. Pancras station in London on December 30, 2025. | Carlos Jasso/AFP via Getty Images

“I see no reason why experience in Italy or Spain should not be repeated, where competition has raised standards, increased capacity and lowered average fares. The whole market has gown, in Italy Trenitalia is carrying more passengers than it did before competition from Italo arrived. Passengers have won, the biggest loser has been short haul flights.”

Reasons to be cautious

There’s still plenty of time for it all to go wrong — as it has before.

German state railway Deutsche Bahn once planned services through the tunnel, going so far as to send a promotional train to St Pancras for a photo op in October 2010. The operator was ultimately stymied by Brexit and backed away from the idea, although it has since shown some renewed interest.

There is also room for the new entrants to revise their plans. Operators don’t necessarily have to run every service they get authorization to operate from the ORR. Each operator also needs separate authorizations in each country and for the Channel Tunnel itself, meaning there are still regulatory hurdles to clear.

World.title: Sánchez’s ministers clash over whether Madrid missed Ceuta migrant warnings
World.content:
“Our armed forces, intelligence services, and, of course, the National Intelligence Center carried out the work that was and is required of them, and shared and analyzed this information with the state security forces and the staff of the government delegation,” the minister told lawmakers, defending the work of the agents she oversees.

Robles’ statement directly contradicts the Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska’s version of events. For weeks, he has insisted the national government did not reinforce the border in Ceuta because it had no way of anticipating the sudden migrant surge.

The minister underscored this point during an extraordinary meeting of the bloc’s interior ministers on Aug. 4, in the aftermath of the influx, where he emphasized Spain’s status as a “strong, reliable partner.”

On Tuesday, Grande-Marlaska hit back directly at Robles’ statement during a press conference, insisting that neither Spain’s intelligence services nor any foreign intelligence agents had detected or warned of anything unusual near Ceuta.

“There was no report that foreshadowed what ultimately transpired on July 30,” he said, adding that it was a matter of “common sense” that any warning would have been taken seriously and handled accordingly.

After lawmakers informed Robles that Grande-Marlaska had denied her statement, the defense minister doubled down and said the country’s intelligence services had warned authorities on July 29, a day earlier than she had originally stated, adding that it was “common knowledge, public knowledge, that people were swimming into Ceuta.”

World.title: Polish prosecutors charge MEP with Holocaust denial over Auschwitz ‘fake’ claim
World.content:
The MEP was summoned as a suspect to the Kraków branch of Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance, a state body empowered to prosecute crimes related to the Nazi occupation and communist eras.

The case stems from two interviews he gave in July 2025. In one, he declared that “Auschwitz with its gas chambers is unfortunately a fake”; in another, he described accounts of their use as a “propaganda narrative” underpinning a “quasi-religious cult.”

The existence and use of gas chambers at Auschwitz-Birkenau is extensively documented. Around a million Jews were killed in the camp, along with around 100,000 Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, gay people, Jehovah’s Witnesses and criminals.

Poland sought to strip Braun of his parliamentary immunity over the remarks, and the European Parliament approved the request in March. Braun, who has a long record of antisemitic rhetoric, is already on trial over separate alleged offenses, including his use of a fire extinguisher to disrupt a Hanukkah celebration in the Polish parliament in 2023.

Braun did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.

His legal troubles come as his party emerges as a potentially consequential force ahead of Poland’s October 2027 parliamentary election. A CBOS poll published Monday, after allocating undecided voters, put Braun’s party at 10.2 percent, compared with 21.3 percent for the conservative Law and Justice party and 14.9 percent for the far-right Confederation.

PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński has repeatedly ruled out an alliance with Braun’s party. But PiS prime ministerial candidate Przemysław Czarnek has drawn a narrower line: He has said Braun himself would “200 percent” not serve in a PiS-led government, while declining to exclude a coalition with his party categorically.

That distinction could matter after October 2027, when Poland’s fragmented right may need every available seat to assemble a governing majority.

World.title: UN chief tells countries to rein in autonomous weapons
World.content:
Guterres and ICRC chief Mirjana Spoljaric underlined that targeting civilians in war is a violation of international humanitarian law, and said they fear that machines won't be able to tell the difference between combatants and non-combatants.

Both called for a ban on autonomous weapons which produce unpredictable results and anti-personnel weapons that deliberately target human beings.

The UN is set to hold a conference in Geneva in November to review its treaty on conventional weapons. Lethal autonomous weapon systems are expected to be a subject of that gathering. The UN has long been pushing countries to progress on legally binding rules.

"When we speak about AI, we want human oversight," European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters on Tuesday when asked about the Commission's assessment on whether humans should be kept in the loop of military applications.

Human oversight is a key concept of the bloc's Artificial Intelligence Act, which doesn't apply, though, to defence or security applications.

Der vereitelte Drohnenanschlag am Flughafen Leipzig/Halle hat gezeigt, wie verwundbar kritische Infrastruktur in Deutschland sein kann. World.title: French driver, 46, detained in Italy after three Akeron missiles found in van
World.content:
A routine check at the port of Bari turned into an investigation into a shipment of high-powered military equipment.

 

Italian law enforcement officers stopped a 46-year-old French citizen, named as Regis Claude Albert Normand, after he disembarked from the Superfast II vessel after it arrived from Patras.

In his van, which had French number plates, investigators found five transport containers designed to carry anti-tank weapons systems.

Inside were launch tubes and missiles, including three Akeron missiles, which, according to a technical assessment and based on information gathered so far, are to be classified as weapons of war.

The case is detailed in an order issued by judge Valeria Isabella Valenzi of the Bari court, who ordered that Normand be held in pre-trial detention.

The investigation

During the inspection, the driver produced three international consignment notes.

However, according to the findings, these documents were too vague to clarify the nature of the load.

Further checks led to the discovery of the five containers. One was empty; a second contained an inert training missile with no guidance system, propulsion or warhead. The remaining three each contained an Akeron missile.

Experts from the Italian army were tasked with determining the nature of the three missiles.

One detail that came under scrutiny during the investigation was the colour of the tubes. The containers had blue bands, which, under NATO standards, indicate training equipment with no explosive components.

According to the military, however, those bands did not appear to be part of the original markings and were said to be ordinary adhesive tape that could be easily removed.

Once the blue tape was removed, a yellow-and-black colouring scheme could reportedly be seen, indicating high-explosive ammunition designed to have a penetrating effect.

Repairs in Greece

Normand told authorities that he was a driver tasked with transporting the equipment to Greece on behalf of the defence firm MBDA. He said he had been due to deliver it to a company called Altus LSA for repair work.

His defence team submitted commercial and travel documentation, as well as an authorisation issued in 2025 by the French Ministry of Defence to MBDA France for activities involving war equipment.

The judge nevertheless said further investigation was necessary, pointing to anomalies in the provided paperwork, including different stamps and discrepancies in the dates.

According to the judge, the permits required under Italian law to transport military equipment had not been produced either during the check at the port or before the judicial authorities.

Normand said he was working as a subcontractor for a French company that also specialises in transporting military goods.

However, according to investigators, the haulage company he works for, which is registered under his wife's name, does not appear to specialise in this type of transport.

The investigation will now need to establish where the missiles came from, where they were headed, and whether their transportation was authorised.

World.title: At least 306 people infected with salmonella in Belgium in outbreak linked to eggs
World.content:
At least 306 people have been infected with salmonella in Belgium after they ate eggs, according to figures released by the Belgian Federal Agency for the Safety of the Food Chain (FASFC).

 

The outbreak has been linked to eggs produced by Laerco, a company based in Geel in northern Belgium. Salmonella was first detected at the facility at the end of April. The following month, a large-scale recall saw all eggs from the site withdrawn from the market.

Contamination spreads

At first, the contamination appeared to be confined to one of the company's four henhouses, but the number of new cases did not fall as expected.

New laboratory tests subsequently detected the bacteria in a second henhouse, before FASFC decided to halt operations at the farm and launch another recall of potentially contaminated eggs.

The products concerned were distributed throughout several major supermarket chains, including Colruyt, Delhaize, Aldi and Carrefour.

The precautionary recall has also been extended to Luxembourg, while FASFC has notified several other European countries that may have received the eggs, including the Netherlands, France, Italy and Portugal.

What is salmonella?

Salmonella are a group of bacteria that can cause a gastrointestinal illness called salmonellosis. Symptoms of infection often include diarrhoea, a fever, and abdominal cramps, while more serious cases can lead to a high fever and aches. It can also be fatal in some cases.

The bacteria, which live in the guts of many farm animals, can be passed to food products such as eggs during rearing, slaughtering, or processing.

World.title: Armenia detains former President Kocharyan on corruption charges
World.content:
Former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan and his eldest son were detained Tuesday after law enforcement officers conducted searches at dozens of locations linked to the family, the country's Anti-Corruption Committee said.

 

Armenia's Prosecutor General's Office said it initiated criminal prosecution against Kocharyan, 71, on charges of abuse of authority, bribery, and large-scale money laundering.

The office said it detained four other people besides Kocharyan and his eldest son Sedrak as part of the investigation.

Armenia's Anti-Corruption Committee said it was investigating allegations that state assets were illegally sold to private companies below market value during Kocharyan's time in office from 1998 to 2008. It further said the case included nine other people besides Kocharyan.

Former President Serzh Sargsyan, who served as Kocharyan's prime minister from 2007 to 2008 before becoming president himself from 2008 to 2018, is also facing charges for alleged abuse of power or official authority as part of the case, the committee said.

Sargsyan was summoned to the Anti-Corruption Committee headquarters in Yerevan on Tuesday.

The elder Kocharyan leads the Moscow-friendly Armenia Alliance, parliament's second-largest opposition bloc.

Bagrat Mikoyan, who heads his office, described the detentions as "yet another attack on President Kocharyan and his family" by authorities. He added that Kocharyan felt ill after his detention and was taken to a hospital.

During his mandate as Armenia's president, Kocharyan deepened Yerevan's links to Moscow, signing a declaration of "allied partnership" with the Kremlin and overseeing a significant expansion of Russian investment in Armenia's economy.

He has maintained close personal ties with Vladimir Putin. In 2021, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the two had "good relations for a very long time" and were frequently in contact.

'A signal to the Kremlin'

The raids came less than 24 hours after Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan clashed with Kocharyan's younger son, Levon — who is part of Kocharyan senior's bloc — in a fiery exchange in parliament.

During a parliamentary question-and-answer session, Levon Kocharyan accused Pashinyan of pressuring the courts and law enforcement agencies to open investigations against individuals.

Pashinyan responded by asking Levon Kocharyan where his family's wealth came from, saying any assets gained at public expense should be returned to the state.

Robert Kocharyan went on trial in 2019, accused of ordering the illegal use of force by security officers against demonstrators protesting alleged fraud in the 2008 presidential election. At least 10 people were killed in the clashes. The charges were later dropped, and the legal proceedings ended in 2021.

Analyst Alexander Iskandaryan, director of the Caucasus Institute in Yerevan, said that critics have long accused Kocharyan of corruption while in power.

Iskandaryan said the case will intensify the conflict between the pro-Russian opposition and Pashinyan's government, which is pursuing a pro-Western course and prioritising closer ties with the European Union.

"Of course, this is a signal to the Kremlin," Iskandaryan said. "Kocharyan effectively positions himself as a Russian proxy, and we see a trend where the authorities have begun to fight — intensively and by all possible means — against political forces aligned with Russia."

Pashinyan, who was elected to office on the back of a 2018 street revolution, has often portrayed himself as a man of the people and supports closer ties with the West. The 51-year-old's party was re-elected in June.

The leader of the largest opposition party — Armenian-Russian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan — was arrested last year on suspicion of calling for the overthrow of Pashinyan.

Karapetyan is the founder of Russia's Tashir Group of Companies and has an estimated fortune of $4.1 billion (€3.5bn) — close to half of Armenia's annual public budget. He built his wealth primarily in Russia and also holds Russian and Cypriot citizenship.

In his criminal trial in April, Karapetyan told the court that he had begun the process of renouncing his Russian and Cypriot citizenships to be eligible to run in the June 2026 parliamentary elections. He and his lawyers have denied all charges.

World.title: Mission accomplished for Sophie Adenot: ISS antenna installed
World.content:
The mission began at 12:27 GMT. Twenty minutes later, Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency (ESA) was once again in the vacuum of space around the ISS, accompanied by her teammate, NASA astronaut Anil Menon, mounted on the base of the Canadarm2 robotic arm.

 

The two astronauts had already spent more than six hours outside the ISS, just enough time to remove the faulty Space-to-Ground antenna, the one NASA engineers call SGANT.

That day, Sophie Adenot and Anil Menon had struggled with stubborn bolts and connectors, and the two astronauts had not had time to replace SGANT with a new antenna.

Sophie Adenot, left, and Anil Menon, right, with the now-famous antenna on 18 August during their unfinished mission. Roscosmos/Anna Kikina / NASA Site web

The aim of this second spacewalk was therefore to finish the job.

This second outing lasted 6 hours and 30 minutes. The two astronauts installed and then connected the replacement antenna. This equipment plays a key role in communications between the ISS and NASA’s control centre in Houston, particularly for the transmission of high-bandwidth data.

In all, this operation marks the 98th US spacewalk and the 283rd conducted for the assembly, maintenance or modernisation of the International Space Station.

Last February, Sophie Adenot became the second French woman to travel into space aboard the US capsule SpaceX Crew Dragon. Claudie Haigneré went before her in 1996 and then in 2001 aboard Soyuz rockets.

World.title: Mysterious, ultra-powerful AI system emerges as China closes in on the West
World.content:
A strange new AI system called Ox Alpha has created a storm of confusion among tech analysts and users alike.

 

Nobody knows who made this model, which dropped on OpenRouter as an anonymous proprietary stealth model on 20 August.

While it is not open source, it is currently offering a free preview until 27 August, after which it is yet to be determined whether the model will be chargeable or not.

Although the maker and owner of this model is currently unknown, there are suspicions of it potentially belonging to China-based Zhipu AI’s unreleased GLM-5.x series. However, these speculations have not been confirmed yet.

This has led to increased concerns about China potentially overtaking Western powers like the US in the AI race by consistently rolling out highly sophisticated and often unclaimed models.

In the past other Chinese companies such as Alibaba and ByteDance have released models without immediately taking credit for them.

This can be to bypass international export scrutiny, avoid immediate regulatory blowback and test high-capacity models without tying liability to a specific corporate entity.

Why Ox Alpha is so powerful

Coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE suggest Ox Alpha is as good as, if not better than, several top models from industry giants including OpenAI and Anthropic.

The model already boasts a token context window exceeding 1 million, and can process images, text and video content with almost unlimited usage, despite its power and current free tier.

It also has a significant output capacity of up to 131,072 tokens in a single response, allowing it to write expansive, detailed scripts.

Ox Alpha is designed for long-horizon tasks such as complex programming, production-scale data processing and sustained agentic workflows.

Its website currently states that prompts are "retained by the provider" but not used for training, though this has not been independently verified.

The model highlights the scale of China's AI ambitions, with the state treating artificial intelligence as a national and strategic priority. This allows Chinese companies to cut costs, roll out models quickly, and pivot fast when needed.

US AI companies, by contrast, often face delayed or staggered rollouts, hampered by expensive proprietary models and fast-changing export controls and chip bans.

World.title: Brazil fines TikTok owner over misuse of children's and teenagers' data
World.content:
Brazil's National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) said on Tuesday that it had imposed a fine of 153.7 million reais (€25.57 million) on ByteDance, owner of the social network TikTok, for "irregularities in the processing of data belonging to children and adolescents".

 

In addition to the fine, the Chinese platform will be required to delete data collected irregularly and, according to the statement, "ByteDance has also committed to implementing a compliance plan to improve the protection of children and adolescents on TikTok".

The platform will have to automatically apply stricter privacy settings to accounts belonging to children under 16, strengthen systems for parental supervision and introduce tighter content filters.

The Brazilian oversight and regulatory authority identified practices by the Chinese company that were not in line with the country's General Data Protection Law (LGPD) in two modes of access to the platform, specifically in relation to the feed for users with and without an account.

ANPD said it had found that the mechanisms adopted by TikTok "were not sufficient to prevent, from the outset, the improper processing of personal data of children and adolescents".

The company behind TikTok will have to strengthen parental control systems and introduce stricter content filters.

In the version without user registration, for example, TikTok will have to suspend advertising across Brazil, restrict the experience to content suitable for all ages and cut screen time to 12 hours.

In the no-login version, users will also not be able to post or watch live broadcasts.

Earlier this month, ANPD also ordered popular streaming platform Discord to suspend live broadcasts and video calls after a teenage girl was allegedly encouraged to take her own life during a stream.

The agency told AFP that an appeal lodged by Discord on Monday against the suspension is currently under review.

In recent years, Brazil has taken a tougher line in regulating social media platforms.

A recent law requires platforms to link accounts held by users under 16 to their parents' accounts and to verify the user's age.

In 2024, the platform X was blocked in Brazil for 40 days, until the social network owned by the world's richest man, Elon Musk, complied with Supreme Court orders to remove accounts spreading disinformation.

World.title: Haiti: UN chief condemns Haiti attack that killed 47
World.content:
The UN Secretary General has condemned a violent attack that left at least 47 dead and saw over 50 more kidnapped.

At least 47 people, including at least five children, were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped by armed men in Haiti on Sunday, the United Nations confirmed on Tuesday.

The incident, which took place in Kenscoff on the outskirts of the capital, Port-au-Prince, is believed to be one of the largest mass kidnappings in the troubled Caribbean country in recent years.

In a video posted on social media, a gang leader threatened to murder hostages if Haiti's National Police kill any of his men in an attempt to rescue people.

"If any of our soldiers are hurt, I will kill all of them," he said.

One resident told the Associated Press that gang members had kidnapped his brother, stepmother, stepfather and two cousins. He said his 16-year-old niece was also kidnapped and raped but managed to escape.

"I had to run over bodies," he said, recalling his own escape. "I can't sleep knowing all these people died."

Haiti: UN condemns violence

United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres condemned the attack which he said underscored the "alarming security conditions" in Haiti and amplified the need for both domestic and international security efforts.

Via a spokesman, he called for Haitian authorities to "ensure that those responsible for such attacks are held accountable," including through specialized judicial units recently established with international support to investigate mass crimes.

How the West messed with Haiti To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Strategic location targeted by gangs

Kenscoff is located around 10 kilometers south of Port-au-Prince at an altitude of around 2,000 meters.

Thanks to its cooler climate, is considered a relatively desirable residential area, while its mountainous location also makes it strategically important when it comes to control of key road connections.

Kenscoff is also close to the political institutions, embassies and banks of Pétion-Ville, a comparatively affluent suburb of the capital.

The first major attack on Kenscoff occurred in January 2025. Since then, there have been sporadic attacks in the mountains surrounding the city center.

But Sunday's attack was the largest yet, shattering the belief that security in the Caribbean country was improving.

Haiti: 'Major security test for government'

"This is a major political and security test for the government, for the police and for the international mission," said Romain Le Cour, head of the Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime.

Le Cour believes the threat of executing hostages is a trap: if the authorities don't act, they will be seen to be abandoning the captives; but if they do and more people die, the gangs will blame the state.

More than 3,050 people were reported to have been killed in Haiti between January to June, according to UN statistics released this week, while gang violence has displaced an estimated 1.5 million more.

The UN also noted that nearly 800 rapes and over 80 kidnappings were reported between April and June alone.

"These figures represent only a portion of the total number of people kidnapped," read a statement, pointing out that victims' relatives often choose to negotiate directly with the kidnappers in the belief that this approach will secure a quicker release and avoid possible reprisals.

World.title: Remembering Dolly Parton: 8 facts about the icon
World.content:
Dolly Parton was one of the world's most successful artists. On Tuesday, her family announced that she passed away at 80. Here are some important and extraordinary facts about the country music superstar.

More than 100 million records sold, 25 No. 1 hits on the US country charts, 11 Grammys and three Emmys — country star Dolly Parton was one of the most successful singers in the world. On Tuesday, her nephew Bryan Seaver announced in a video shared on Parton's social media channgels that his aunt had passed away.

"Dolly... opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent," Seaver said in the video. "She never saw a door she couldn't open, and the doors she opened made and changed history."

Here are eight facts from eight decades of Dolly Parton.

1. Cornmeal for the doctor

Dolly Parton came from humble beginnings, growing up with 11 siblings in Sevier County, Tennessee.

Born on January 19, 1946, her parents paid the doctor who assisted at her birth with a sack of cornmeal — though some sources claim it was oats.

Parton was born into a musical family and learned to play the guitar when she was 7. She gave her first performance on television at age of 10.

Dolly Parton in 1977 Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

2. No 'Dumb Blonde'

Multiple sources have reported Parton's IQ to be at least 140. Her first song, which entered the US country charts on January 21, 1967, was "Dumb Blonde." In it, she sings "this dumb blonde ain't nobody's fool." It was a bold start for her entry into 1960s show business, at the time dominated by men.

"I'm not offended by all the dumb blonde jokes because I know I'm not dumb… and I also know that I'm not blonde," she said of the stereotype.

3. Impressive parade of wigs

Across her seven-decade career, Parton loved following fashion trends — especially when it comes to hairstyles.

Her trademark platinum blonde hair, though — as mentioned above — was never truly her own. Rather than spoil her hair with bleaching, she began wearing wigs from early on. It's said her collection numbered over 350 different wigs.

Even wigs need styling: Parton, who appeared in the film 'Steel Magnolias,' visited the Broadway show in 1988 Image: Mark Lenihan/AP Photo/picture alliance

Parton never made a secret of her cosmetic surgeries. Over time, she used it to change her face and figure — but she always remained the friendly superstar with a big heart.

In 2025, Forbes magazine valued Parton's fortune at around $450 million (€387 million). She shared her wealth with people in need for decades — in particular in her home state of Tennessee, but also around the globe.

4. Promoting reading for kids

Since 1995, Parton's The Dollywood Foundation has been sponsoring books for children as part of her Imagination Library program. From the day a child is born, parents can apply to receive a book every month up until the age of 5. More than 300 million books have already been distributed in five English-speaking countries: the US, Canada, Australia, UK and Ireland.

Dolly Parton donated her royalties to good causes Image: Mark Humphrey/AP Photo/picture alliance

The program is funded by the foundation itself, government support and private donors. Recently, however, some Republican-governed states in the US have announced plans to scrap financial support for the Imagination Library. Parton, who didn't have children of her own, founded the library program in honor of her father Robert Lee Parton — who was unable to read.

Each year, the foundation also awards five university scholarships to high school graduates from Sevier County. The Dolly Parton Scholarships of $15,000 are aimed at "students who have a dream they wish to pursue and who can successfully communicate their plan and commitment to realize their dreams," as stated on the foundation's website.

5. A million dollars during COVID

In 2020, Parton donated $1 million to the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, Tennessee, where the biotechnology company Moderna was working on a COVID-19 vaccine.

On the BBC's "The One Show" in November 2020, she said of her donation: "I'm a very proud girl today to know I had anything at all to do with something that's going to help us through this crazy pandemic."

A few months later, she received the vaccine on camera and rewrote her hit-song "Jolene" to "Vaccine" for the occasion.

6. Hundreds of 'Jolene' covers

"Jolene" is one of the most frequently covered songs in pop music history. The web portal cover.info notes over 80 official cover versions — from famous artists to indie musicians. Countless other versions can be heard on YouTube and other platforms.

One of the most popular covers was the raw and gritty 2004 interpretation by US duo The White Stripes. Parton herself has recorded several versions of her famous hit — accompanied by a cappella group Pentatonix, for instance, or alongside her famous godchild, pop star Miley Cyrus. In 2016, all of them got together to perform it live together on The Voice.

7. Two world hits in one day

Parton wrote both "Jolene" and "I Will Always Love You" on the same day in 1972. When Whitney Houston covered the latter two decades later, it became an instant global hit.

You might be surprised to know that "I Will Always Love You" was never meant to be a romantic song. In fact, it was about Parton ending her professional collaboration with her mentor, country star Porter Wagoner.

Speaking with radio host Howard Stern in 2023, Parton recalled the conflicted emotions she felt when writing the song.

"How am I going to make him understand how much I appreciate everything, but that I have to go? I thought, well, what do you do best? You write songs. So I sat down and I wrote this song."

Dolly Parton at an event to celebrate the expansion of the Imagination Library of Kentucky in 2024 Image: Timothy D. Easley/AP Photo/picture alliance

Houston's '90s cover version earned Parton another $10 million in royalties. Speaking in 2021 on "Watch What Happens Live," she revealed that she invested the money into an office complex in a Black neighborhood in Nashville, Tennessee.

"I just thought, 'This was great. I'm going to be down here with her people, who are my people as well… I think, 'This is the house that Whitney built,'" she said.

8. Not the best doppelganger

Last but not least: Parton said that she once took part in a Dolly Parton drag queen lookalike contest — and lost.

On "The Ellen DeGeneres Show," Parton revealed that she had overdone her styling to avoid being recognized: She made her beauty mark bigger, her breasts larger and her hair bigger. All the contestants had to walk across the stage at a gay bar, and whoever received the most applause was declared the winner. In the end, it wasn't Parton who won.

This article was originally written in German. It was first published on January 18, 2026 and was updated upon news of her death on August 25, 2026.

World.title: US country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80
World.content:
Representatives of the country music legend told US media that Dolly Parton died after a "brief battle with cancer." Parton's career spans more than half a century and includes a wide array of smash hits.

US country music singer Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80.

Her nephew Brian Seaver announced the news in a video posted to Parton's Instagram page.

"After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones," Parton's team later said in a statement to CBS News.

Earlier in the year, Parton canceled a series of shows in Las Vegas citing ongoing treatment for health problems. Late last year, she had rebuffed rumors about her health with typical good humor, declaring in a short video, "I ain't dead yet!"

The 80-year-old singer spent almost all of her life making music and is known all over the world for a series of major hits like "Jolene," "9 to 5" and "I Will Always Love You." Her decades-long career earned her 10 Grammys and 13 Academy of Country Music (ACM) awards.

Country music icon Dolly Parton dies To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Parton's nephew say announcing her passing?

Parton's nephew and longstanding head of security Seaver said it was an "honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness," to issue this announcement on her behalf, saying she had asked him to do so long ago.

He hailed her influence both on his life and his family's but also on the wider world's.

"By her example, we believed anything was possible," he said of Parton. "She never saw a door she couldn't open, and the doors she opened made and changed history."

"My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly Parton, but so have you," he said. "She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family whether you liked it or not."

Trump pays tribute, says flags will fly at half-staff for a week

US President Donald Trump said he had called for flags around the country to be "lowered" for one week starting on Tuesday night in memory of Parton.

"Rest in Peace, Dolly!" Trump wrote on social media, describing her as "one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER."

"This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will," he wrote of a fellow famous member of the class of 1946.

Democratic Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer wrote simply: "Rest in peace, Dolly Parton -- a true legend and force for good. May her memory be a blessing."

Dolly Parton: musical tributes

The Academy of Country Music hailed Parton's "unmistakable voice, unforgettable songs, generosity and larger-than-life spirit," saying: "Her music will live on, carrying her voice and her story forward for generations to come."

Beatle Paul McCartney said Parton's "songwriting, her singing and her philanthropy were unrivaled in the world of country music" and said it is "hard to imagine living in a world without Dolly."

"There was no greater honour for me than to have her sing my song 'Let It Be' and, even though I only made a small contribution to it, I am so honored that she did it. I am so proud to have known her and admire her unique talents."

Mick Jagger of The Rolling Stones said: "What a wonderful songwriter and singer Dolly was. She brought so many people together, we will all miss her so much."

"It's hard for me to imagine the world without Dolly," said singer-songwriter Cyndi Lauper. "Dolly's heart was as big as her talent. She used her art, her fame and her money to help so many people. She was a great role model for all of us."

Who was Dolly Parton?

Dolly Rebecca Parton was born on January 19, 1946 in Sevierville into what she called a "dirt poor" Tennessee family in the US south.

She was the fourth of 12 children, growing up in the family's small shack in the Great Smoky Mountains.

From singing her first songs to chickens, Parton graduated to performing in a church, where her grandfather was a preacher.

Her debut album, appropriately titled "Hello, I'm Dolly," was released in 1967 with Parton having barely entered her 20s.

She was prolific in her output. By 1974, Parton was already releasing her 13th studio album. Entitled "Jolene," it included what would become two of Parton's most famous songs, the eponymous first track and the opening track of side two, "I Will Always Love You."

She released a staggering 49 solo studio albums in a career spanning well over half a century, concluding in 2023 with "Rockstar."

Parton was known not only for her voice, stage presence, provocative costumes and ample bust, but also as a rapier wit and a stellar storyteller on stage when she had the mic in her hand between her songs.

Sometimes this would also spill over into her creative process. On a visit to the 2014 Glastonbury music festival in the UK, performing in front of an estimated 180,000 sodden fans braving horrendous weather, she said she had composed a special rap just for them earlier that morning, called "Mud."

Catchier lines included rhymes like "Up to our bums in all this crud," while the crowd soon caught on to the chorus by the second go around — chanting "mud, mud, mud!" on her behalf.

You can read more about the iconic country music legend here: Remembering Dolly Parton: 8 facts about the icon

World.title: Grain exports stall as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russia's Black Sea ports
World.content:
Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian infrastructure on the Black Sea are disrupting grain and oil exports from the port of Novorossiysk and other key hubs.

When Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke in 2014 about Russia's motives for annexing the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, and thus violating international law, he justified it by saying: "We could not allow NATO forces to eventually come to the land of Crimea and Sevastopol, the land of Russian military glory, and cardinally change the balance of forces in the Black Sea area."

What now? Intensified Ukrainian attacks on Novorossiysk, Russia's largest commercial Black Sea port, have caused significant disruptions to oil and grain shipments in recent weeks. The Russian navy no longer dominates the region. And exporting goods via the Black Sea is becoming increasingly difficult for Russia because of Ukraine's drone strikes. It is only possible to reorganize logistics partially.

If the attacks continue at such intensity, the consequences for Russian exporters and the national budget could be significant, experts told DW.

Container ships and other vessels have also come under attack Image: Igor Onuchin/TASS/ZUMA/picture alliance

Novorossiysk major Russian hub for exports

Novorossiysk has been a major hub for Russian exports since the 19th century and even today it remains Russia's largest port in terms of cargo volume, as well as one of the largest in Europe. Up to a third of Russia's grain exports are handled through the hub, which is located close to the country's major agricultural regions. Crude oil, metals and containerized goods also pass through the port.

Recent Ukrainian maritime and aerial drone attacks have severely disrupted shipments, particularly of grain. Andrei Sisov, the head of SovEcon, a research and consulting firm specialized in agriculture, uses Telegram to follow the developments. On August 12, he posted that the Novorossiysk Bread Products Plant (NKHP ) — one of Russia's largest grain export terminals — and the Novorossiysk grain terminal had ceased operations. A day later, KSK, one of Russia's largest deep-water grain terminals, also halted its operations. Operations at a major grain terminal in Taman had already come to a standstill at the end of July. Prior to that, Ukraine paralyzed operations at the shallow-water ports of the Sea of Azov.

At the time of publication, only Tuapse, the smallest of Russia's deep-water grain terminals, was still in operation. "This means that virtually all Russian grain exports via the Azov-Black Sea basin are blocked," Sisov said.

Ukrainian drone attacks are doing consistent damage to Russian infrastructure Image: Vantor/Handout/REUTERS

Oil exports also affected

The situation regarding oil exports is not quite as dramatic but while they have not come to a complete standstill, they are frequently disrupted. According to the British news agency Reuters, the Sheskharis terminal — Russia's main oil export facility on the Black Sea, handling some 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day — halted loadings on August 14, which resumed only two days later.

According to London-based Argus Media, a global energy and commodity price reporting agency, Russia could have 45 million metric tons of wheat — Russia's main agricultural export good — for export in 2026 to 2027. However, the situation in the Black Sea, through which about 90% of shipments are usually routed, will make it almost impossible to supply the global market.

Sisov of SovEcon estimated that "many Russian producers will not survive this season, especially after several years of deteriorating financial conditions."

Because exports have come to a standstill, surplus grain will have to be sold on the domestic market, which is already putting downward pressure on prices. Even if exports were to recover over time, there will still be problems. August is usually when shipments peak and it will be difficult to deliver anything no sent this month because terminals tend to operate at full capacity during the autumn anyway.

Ukraine's desperate search for farm labor To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukrainian grain exports also decrease

The escalation of hostilities in the Azov and Black Sea regions will also be felt on the global market since Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter.

Ukrainian grain exports have also fallen sharply since there are attacks on both sides. In the past month, Russia too has stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships that are docked there.

"The disruptions have blocked out good wheat harvests in Ukraine and Russia from accessing global market," Xiaoyi Deng from Argus Media told DW. "Both have struggled to work with alternative infrastructure, such as Baltic ports (via rail) or Danube River ports but the alternatives would not be up for full replacement."

According to the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Helsinki-based think tank, the port of Novorossiysk "loaded 30% less oil than during the same period last year" in the first two weeks of August. The decline was preceded by a Ukrainian strike on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) marine terminal on July 19.

How Ukraine fights in the Black Sea without a navy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Isaac Levi, an energy analyst at CREA, pointed out that damage to infrastructure was not the only reason for shipments to fall. He said that "strikes on vessels have discouraged ships from calling at ports considered major targets." According to US business news channel Bloomberg, a Greek tanker believed to be carrying Russian oil came under attack on August 17.

"If these constraints persist through August, Russia will find it increasingly difficult to simply defer shipments and make up the lost volumes later," Levi said. "Russia can reroute barrels, but it cannot reroute infrastructure. The most plausible alternatives include the Baltic ports of Primorsk and Ust-Luga.

"But rerouting oil through the Baltic Sea ports would significantly increase transportation times and costs compared with Black Sea exports, while available capacity remains too small to replace significant volumes from Novorossiysk."

This article was originally published in Russian.

World.title: CIA director in Moscow for meetings — US media reports
World.content:
US media outlets say John Ratcliffe was in Russia to attend meetings. Flight tracking websites had earlier detected the arrival of a US military transport plane at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport.

US CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow on Tuesday, USnews outlets reported, saying he would be attending meetings.

CBS News and Axios both reported the visit, but stopped short of saying who Ratcliffe was meeting with or the topics on the agenda. CBS News quoted sources familiar with the situation as confirming Ratcliffe's trip, saying it was his first known visit to Russia as CIA chief. Axios separately cited an unnamed US official.

Earlier on Tuesday, data from Flightradar24 showed that a US military transport plane used by the US Air Force flew from Latvia to Moscow's Vnukovo Airport. The flight-tracking website later reported that the same plane departed Moscow hours later.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he did "not have such information" when asked about the arrival of a US military plane in the Russian captial.

If the reports prove accurate, it would be the first known time that a CIA director has visited Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ratcliffe's predecessor William Burns had talks with President Vladimir Putin in 2021.

Last such flight into Russia was in January this year

High-ranking US visits to Russia have become extremely uncommon amid the war with Ukraine.

The last time a military transport plane of this kind flew into Moscow was in January of this year.

At that point, it was ferrying Trump's negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner into the capital as the US tried to broker some kind of truce between Moscow and Kyiv.

That meeting, the second of two in back-to-back months, also came soon after the US abducting Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and just over a month before the war with Iran was launched.

Uptick in strikes on non-military targets in Ukraine, Russia

The US-brokered talks have slowed in the last six months, partly as US bandwidth is occupied by the war in Iran and also amid little tangible progress between Moscow and Kyiv.

Ukraine has intensified long-range attacks into Russia and started targeting its petroleum and oil industries and other contentious targets like the Wildberries online retailer in recent months.Russia has also increased its volume of attacks on civilian and non-military targets in Ukraine.

Nevertheless, both Russia and Ukraine also maintain that they would be willing to engage in negotiations under the right circumstances — albeit showing few signs of agreement on what would need to happen to facilitate talks.

World.title: Houthi strikes threaten to pull Yemen back into full-scale war
World.content:
The Iran-backed Houthis are using regional warfare to increase pressure on Saudi Arabia, while their attacks risk reopening Yemen's own conflict and disrupting shipping in the Red Sea.

Yemen is increasingly at risk of backsliding into full-scale conflict. On Monday, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militia attacked another crude oil tanker in the Red Sea off the coast of Saudi Arabia. The attack followed earlier strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure and other ships in the nearby Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The waterway connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and has served as an alternative route for oil exports from Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries affected by Iran's ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

In August, the Houthis also attacked areas under the control of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, particularly the port city of Mokha. Yemen's internationally recognized government targeted Houthi infrastructure in response.

"Mokha overlooks the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which is strategically important to the Houthis," Hisham Al-Omeisy, a Yemeni conflict analyst, told DW. "In the long term, the Houthis want to weaken the government's control over the Red Sea coastal areas and they aim for full control of the governate Al-Hudeydah [of which Mokha is a part] to continue their strategy of exerting pressure on global maritime trade," he predicted.

The current military flare-up ended four years of relative calm between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government, backed by Saudi Arabia.

However, Al-Omeisy notes that there are also two other aspects that drive the latest Houthi strategy.

Following the ceasefire in 2022, Saudi Arabia has continued to support the Yemeni government financially and militarily. Saudi Arabia also never fully lifted its air and port blockades in areas under Houthi control. Despite this, the Houthis consolidated their position as Yemen's de facto rulers. In Al-Omeisy's view, the Houthis now hope to extract additional concessions from Saudi Arabia.

"The Houthis are under a lot of pressure locally to deliver on their promises, for example, to reform the government, pay salaries and improve livelihoods," Al-Omeisy said. He therefore believes that the Houthis are using the wider Middle East war to distract from their failure to deliver in these areas by "saying that we are now busy with another war."

The Houthi strikes are also carefully timed, Al-Omeisy added. "They've learned their lessons from how Iran managed to basically dominate the Strait of Hormuz," he said, adding that the blockade of imports and oil exports leaves Saudi Arabia in a very vulnerable position.

The Houthi militia attacked the port of Mokha which is under the control of the Saudi-backed government in Yemen Image: Khaled Ziad/AFP

Saudi Arabia's balancing act with the Houthi militia

"Instability in Yemen is no longer simply a problem on Saudi Arabia's southern border," Alice Gower, director of geopolitics and security at the London-based consulting firm Azure Strategy, told DW.

"Ultimately, Saudi Arabia wants a more secure Red Sea, but also wants to achieve that without becoming trapped in another war in Yemen," she added.

"Saudi Arabia's priority is protecting the economic transformation under Vision 2030 which also explains why Saudi Arabia increasingly sees the Red Sea as one connected theater rather than separate crises in Yemen, Sudan and the Horn of Africa," Gower said, noting that Houthi attacks threaten shipping, raise insurance costs, deter investors and disrupt the infrastructure on which Vision 2030 increasingly depends.

In turn, Saudi Arabia has updated its defense policy, she also noted in a recent op-ed. "Riyadh has been focusing on building a broader security architecture that could reduce the burden of defending its maritime interests."

Earlier in July, Saudi Arabia spearheaded the creation of a multinational Maritime Defense Alliance with more than 14 countries, including Saudi Arabia's strong ally and Iran's adversary, the United States.

"The new Saudi-led maritime coalition is part of that approach as it allows Riyadh to spread the security burden, strengthen regional deterrence and counter threats across the Bab el-Mandeb, Red Sea and Gulf of Aden as part of the same security problem," Gower said, adding that it is yet to be proven to be effective.

In August, Saudi Arabia also joined a defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey, the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. However, analysts again point out that this new pact is yet to show "operational relevance."



For Mohammed al-Basha, founder of the US-based risk advisory firm Basha Report, none of these coalitions and alliances will actually help Saudi Arabia avoid being dragged back into war in Yemen. In an interview with the Financial Times newspaper he said that "they either give the Houthis $5 billion and allow them to fly directly to Tehran, allow them to dock any ship at their ports, and hope they are not going to come back in a few years and ask for $10 billion…or you use that $5 billion to support your anti-Houthi coalition of Yemenis to push the Houthis to get down from their high horse and negotiate."

Analysts say that the Houthis learned from Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz before they started their own blockade of Saudi ships in the Red Sea Image: Media Office of the Ministry of Transport - Republic of Yemen/Handout/REUTERS

Humanitarian situation depends on a peaceful roadmap

For the population, neither of these scenarios spell hope for real peace. According to the United Nations, Yemen is still suffering from one of the world's worst humanitarian crises after years of war between 2014 and 2022. More than half the population is in need of humanitarian assistance. "I urge all parties to halt immediately any actions that risk returning Yemen to full-scale conflict," the UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Türk warned in a recent statement .

"It feels impossible to imagine worse conditions for people in Yemen right now," Niku Jafarnia, Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, told DW. "And yet, renewed conflict between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition threatens to worsen conditions further," she warned.

With Yemen's humanitarian crisis already so severe, the question is whether the latest escalation in Yemen can still be contained through diplomacy.

For the Yemeni Nobel Peace Prize laureate and human rights defender Tawakkol Karman, any serious peace effort must begin by addressing the root cause of the crisis: the collapse of the Yemeni state and the undermining of its institutions.

In a recent meeting with representatives of UN Security Council member states, Karman said that in her view, the National Dialogue outcomes — reached through consensus among all Yemeni components including the Houthis, under UN auspices and with the endorsement of the Security Council — remain the most realistic roadmap for peace.

World.title: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on US goods
World.content:
Canada's government said it would impose tariffs on some 700 US goods as of next month, amid the latest trade spat between Donald Trump and Mark Carney.

Canada on Tuesday announced retaliatory tariffs against the United States , as relations between the neighbors faltered following failed trade talks last week.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government in Ottawa also announced financial support for businesses and workers impacted by the latest dispute with the Trump administration.

It listed some 700 US products that would be subject to either 15%, 25% or 50% tariffs as of September 8, in steps designed to match those announced earlier in the week by US President Donald Trump.

The US is Canada's largest trading partner, and Canada is the second largest for the US, trailing only fellow neighbor Mexico. Several such disputes have marked both of Trump's terms.

What did Canada say about the measures?

Canada's Finance Ministry said in a statement that the government had negotiated "intensively and in good faith" with the US towards a "fair and comprehensive trade agreement."

"In recent days, however, the US proposed new terms that were not in Canada’s best interest, basically, asking too much of Canada, and offering too little in return," the Ministry wrote, saying that at this point it suspended talks rather than accepting a "bad deal."

"Canada did not choose this trade conflict, but we need to respond to provide a level playing field to our businesses," it said.

Finance Ministerr Francois-Philippe Champagne described the measures as "dollar-for-dollar, rate for rate counter-tariffs," as well as a "multi-billion dollar support package [that] will protect workers, farmers, families, and businesses."

"Canada's counter tariffs will apply to products covering $27.6 billion in imports from the US and will focus on sectors such as steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics, that are most impacted by US tariffs," the ministry said, naming the same figure as the US in its announcement.

Here's what you need to know about the backdrop to this flare-up:

Washington ‌and ​Ottawa were racing to reach an agreement beforeUS President Donald Trump's steep new US tariffs, announced in July, were due to take effect

Talks broke down days after the US President announced the neighbors were close to agreeing to a trade deal

The collapse in negotiations triggered Trump's threatened 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods the next day

Why is Canada imposing new tariffs?

While the US and Canada have shared one of the world’s largest trade relationships, the recent talks signal a breakdown in relations.

"An attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States" is "not something we’re going to accept," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

"We learned during the negotiations that the Americans want to destroy our major industries, including autos, steel and aluminum," Carney said, opting for an even blunter approach in French. "That was one of the main reasons we said no. It was a bad deal."

US-Canada trade war: The cost of fighting back To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What had the US said?

Donald Trump returned to the topic of Canada early on Tuesday on social media, claiming the US was mulling renaming Lake Ontario, the only one of the five North American Great Lakes named after a Canadian territory.

"The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don't expect to doing [sic] much business with them any longer," Trump wrote.

His administration "renamed" the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America soon after Trump returned to the White House last year — a change that almost nobody besides the US government has implemented. Even US tech giant Google shows it as the Gulf of Mexico first on its maps for users everywhere but in the US.

A day earlier, Trump had threatened he would impose a 50% tariff on Canadian automobiles, car parts and steel from January 1, 2027, and took to social media to unleash a tirade against the historic partner.

Trump hits Canada with 50% tariffs in major trade escalation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"On trade, ‌and in other ways, also, ‌they ​are among the worst nations in the world to deal with. They feel entitled, and ​yet, WE DON'T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!" the US president said.

Canada relies heavily on the US as its top trading partner, with American-bound exports making up 70% of the country's total. The relationship runs both ways, too: government data shows Canada was the second-largest US trading partner in goods this year, just behind Mexico.

No further negotiations are currently scheduled.

Edited by: Rob Turner
