World.title: Regulation on recognising foreign same-sex marriages comes into force in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. All registry offices in Poland can now recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union countries, after a government regulation issued in May went into force. The decision came in response to a ruling by the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) requiring Poland to recognise such unions. Deputy prime minister Krzysztof Gawkowski expressed his “great joy, because finally in Poland we have a law that gives the right to dignity”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, warned local authorities that they will be breaking the law if they refuse to comply with the new rules. However, the mayor of one town in a conservative region has already declared that his administration will not recognise such marriages. He argues that doing so would violate Poland’s constitution, which mentions marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Od jutra polskie państwo będzie lepiej chronić godność i prawa swoich obywateli. Nowe wzory aktów małżeństwa umożliwią transkrypcję zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych z pełnym szacunkiem dla par. To koniec administracyjnej fikcji i niepewności, z którą przez lata… pic.twitter.com/mRZYkEg9W4 — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 22, 2026 Polish domestic law still does not allow any form of same-sex unions to be formed. However, last year, the CJEU ordered that the country recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other EU member states. That was followed by a similar ruling from Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA). One obstacle to implementing those decisions was that, previously, Poland’s civil registry only allowed male-female marriages to be entered. But, under a regulation issued by the government in May, the system now allows either mixed-sex or same-sex marriages. Even before that went into force on Sunday, some Polish cities, starting with Warsaw and Wrocław, had already begun transcribing same-sex marriages conducted abroad into their registries. They simply listed one spouse in the “man” section and the other as a “woman”, even though that was not accurate for one of them. But some local authorities have refused to do so, pointing to article 18 of Poland’s constitution, which states that: “Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland.” Such doubts were cited by the mayor of Zakopane, a town in southern Poland, last week when he announced that his administration did not intend to begin recognising foreign same-sex marriages after the regulation came into force. “We will not be issuing such transcriptions in Zakopane,” said Łukasz Filipowski, quoted by local news service Nasze Miasto. He argued that doing so would “not be in accordance with the constitution”, adding that, while Zakopane is “tolerant”, it “promotes the traditional family model…[as] our foundation”. Filipowski pointed to a ruling in July by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which found that the government’s regulation conflicts with the constitution’s definition of marriage. However, the government considers the TK to be improperly constituted and therefore regards its rulings as invalid. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal has ruled that a new regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage certificates to be registered in Poland is unconstitutional. The government says it will not implement the rulinghttps://t.co/xDAzLjcJQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2026 In response to Filipowski’s remarks, Kotula told broadcaster TVN that officials who refuse to recognise foreign same-sex marriages “will be breaking the law”. She said that the personal views of officials cannot “translate into what [legal] actions they take” and that the government would be monitoring the situation. Gawkowski – who, like Kotula, is a leading figure in The Left (Lewica), a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition – also warned municipalities against issuing refusals. He noted that, as well as the CJEU ruling, Polish courts have also issued orders to recognise foreign same-sex marriages. “In the end, these local authorities will lose [a court battle], so why embarrass themselves? Let’s not look for legal tricks. Let’s just implement something that has been done in other, normal countries for years,” Gawkowski told Polsat News. However, even once same-sex marriages are transcribed into Polish civil registries, there remains uncertainty about what legal consequences that will have in practice, especially given that Poland’s domestic law does not allow for any legally recognised form of same-sex union. Legal experts say that it may take years – and potentially many more legal challenges by same-sex couples – for the situation to be clarified. Separately, parliament earlier this year approved a bill, proposed by the ruling coalition, that would have granted same-sex couples in Poland certain rights normally granted to married couples. However, the law was vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Ukraine to establish new national pantheon as Poland warns against honouring massacre figures
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed a law establishing a new national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian historical heroes. While it is not yet known which figures will be honoured there, Poland has expressed concern that they will include nationalist leaders associated with massacres of Poles in World War Two. On Sunday, a Polish deputy foreign minister warned that Kyiv “will have a huge problem” integrating with the European Union if it celebrates such individuals. But Zelensky reiterated that “only Ukrainians will decide who is a hero to us”. The establishment of the pantheon has taken place against the backdrop of a diplomatic crisis triggered in May by Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. Parts of the UPA were responsible for the so-called Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards the episode as a genocide, though Ukraine strongly rejects that label. Many Ukrainians hold the UPA in high regard for the role that it played in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Poland condemned Zelensky’s decision and stripped him of the country’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. In response, the Ukrainian president announced in late June that he would seek to create a new national pantheon, because “no one will dictate which heroes we should honour”. A bill creating the pantheon was subsequently approved by the Ukrainian parliament in July, and, on Saturday, Zelensky signed it into law, just ahead of today’s celebrations of Ukrainian independence day. “A Ukrainian pantheon will definitely be established, and only Ukrainians will decide for themselves who our heroes are,” declared Zelensky at a meeting with military veterans on Saturday. “All our true heroes…who fought for Ukraine, for our independence…deserve due honour.” However, the introduction of the law only now begins the process of building the pantheon itself – where the remains of those chosen as national heroes will be reburied – and the establishment of an advisory body that will decide which figures should receive such an honour. It therefore remains unknown for now who will be included in the pantheon. However, on Sunday, Polish deputy foreign minister Marcin Bosacki warned against honouring figures associated with the Volhynia massacres. “Every nation and its government has the right to choose the heroes they deem appropriate,” emphasised Bosacki in an interview with broadcaster TVP. “However, if individuals responsible for mass crimes against civilians, such as [Stepan] Bandera or [Roman] Shukhevych, are included in Ukraine’s national pantheon, it would significantly worsen Ukraine’s relations not only with Poland but with Europe in general,” he added. Bandera was the leader of a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN-B), which in turn founded the UPA. Shukhevych was a military leader of the UPA. Both figures continue to be honoured in Ukraine, often prompting protests from Poland. 🇵🇱 Polskie MSZ ostrzegło Ukrainę przed „ogromnymi problemami” z Europą z powodu Bandery i Szuchewycza „Ukraina wie, że z tymi, którzy zabijali nie tylko Polaków, ale także Ukraińców, Czechów, Żydów i Romów, na swoich sztandarach będzie miała ogromne problemy z integracją… pic.twitter.com/hyujMppbEw — NEXTA Polska (@nexta_polska) August 24, 2026 “Ukraine knows that, with those who murdered not only Poles, but also some Ukrainians, Czechs, Jews and Roma, on its banners, it will have a huge problem integrating with Europe,” added Bosacki. However, the deputy minister also emphasised that, “strategiaclly, the interests of Poland and Ukraine remain very close” and that Poland must continuing “supporting Ukraine in defeating the aggressive Russia”. “We do not differ much with the Ukrainians, only with certain parts of the Ukrainian authorities after their absolutely erroneious decision to name a unit after the ‘heroes of the UPA’.” The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Polish government figures have previously made it clear that, if Ukraine honours figures associated with historical massacres, that will make it harder for the country to achieve its ambitions of joining the EU. In June, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz warned that “you can’t build a pantheon to those who destroy European cooperation”, and that countries seeking EU membership should “not build national identity…on events, people or systems that in some way raise objections or pain among EU partners”. Kosiniak-Kamysz declared that, just as Zelensky said no one will tell Ukraine who they can honour, “no one will tell us how to vote on the entry of any state into the European Union”. That was an allusion to the fact that Poland, like all other EU member states, can veto Ukraine’s accession to the bloc. Polish and Ukrainian media have widely quoted Poland's deputy PM as saying: “With Bandera, Ukraine will not enter the EU.” However, he did not actually speak those words. We explain what @KosiniakKamysz actually said and how it came to be misinterpreted https://t.co/S3bozRIJTA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2026 ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski seeks to switch allegiance to Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A rising US track star has declared his intention to represent Poland, the country of his ancestors. Sam Blaskowski’s personal-best 100 metres sprint time of 9.89 seconds is more than a tenth of a second faster than the current Polish national record. “I plan to make Poland the finest sprinting nation in the world. I want to win medals for Poland,” the 23-year-old told Polish broadcaster TVP Sport. Sam Blaskowski przed naszymi kamerami mówi o tym, dlaczego chciałby reprezentować Polskę! 🇵🇱 Więcej o tej sprawie 👉 https://t.co/oC8MJ4moV6 pic.twitter.com/Nw1i7YqrIp — TVP SPORT (@sport_tvppl) August 23, 2026 Blaskowski says that two of his ancestors, Franciszek and Julian, left Poland in 1905, at a time when the country was still partitioned between Germany, Austria and Russia. “My last name is Polish. But for a long time, I didn’t understand that these were my roots. Everything changed recently, because my parents and I talked a lot about our roots,” he explained to TVP Sport. He was contacted by Piotr Maruszewski, coach of the Polish sprint team, after clocking a time of 9.89 seconds in May, which is the joint-ninth-best run by anyone in the world this year. The Polish 100m record is still held by Marian Woronin, who ran 10.00 in 1984. View this post on Instagram A post shared by D3 Glory Days | D3 Running Podcast & News (@d3glorydays) Maruszewski has since been persuading and helping Blaskowski to apply for citizenship, including hiring lawyers to obtain documents proving the sprinter’s heritage. Under Polish law, people who have a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who was born in or lived in Poland after January 1920 are themselves regarded as holding Polish citizenship. That means Blaskowski’s ancestry may not be enough to qualify. However, it could be enough to convince Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who has discretion to grant citizenship to anyone he wishes. Last year, Nawrocki granted citizenship to Vladimir Semirunniy, a speed skater who fled from Russia to Poland. Semirunniy now represents the Polish national team, including at this year’s Winter Olympics, where he won a silver medal. Given that Blaskowski last represented the United States as a junior over four years ago, he is not subject to World Athletics’ mandatory waiting period for athletes transferring national allegiance. At yesterday’s Silesia Diamond League meeting in Chorzów, Poland’s biggest annual athletics event, Blaskowski told Citius Mag that he expects to be able to represent Poland at next year’s World Championships in Beijing. “I want to inspire the next generation… to make an impact on people around me, and I think the best way to do that is to go and represent Poland,” he told TVP Sport at the same event. “Not only do I have heritage there, but people [in Poland] are very aware of your talent and they give so much appreciation for our sport, and I think it’s a great place.” He added that he and his parents plan to visit their ancestors’ hometown of Sompolno in central Poland on Monday before he again competes in Szczecin on Wednesday. In Chorzów, Blaskowski came fifth in his semi-final against some of the world’s sprinters, just ahead of European champion Romell Glave. Poland’s current top male sprinter, Dominik Kopeć, finished ninth and last in 10.32. The final was won by Jamaica’s Oblique Seville in 9.83 seconds, ahead of another American with a Polish surname, Kenneth Bednarek, who was adopted as a child by a woman with Polish heritage. “The love and support I received from Poland today were truly incredible,” Bednarek wrote on social media after competing at the same event two years ago. “I’m thrilled to have run here for the first time and can’t wait to return with my mom, who has Polish roots.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kung Fu Kenny (@kenny_bednarek) Blaskowski would not be the first sprinter to switch allegiance to Poland. Belarusian runner Krystsina Tsimanouskaya received Polish citizenship in 2022, having been granted a humanitarian visa the previous year after the Tokyo Olympics. This month, high jumper Maria Żodzik, another Belarusian who was granted Polish citizenship in 2024, won silver at the European Championships, adding to another silver at last year’s World Championships. At the 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris, Poland’s athletes disappointed, finishing with just one bronze medal in track and field events and one gold and ten medals overall, the country’s worst result since 1956. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: How will the Law and Justice split affect Polish politics?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak The biggest-ever split within Poland’s main right-wing opposition party is a serious self-inflicted wound, signalling a more fragmented conservative landscape and complicating the right’s path back to power. While it provides a tactical boost for the Tusk government, there is still every chance of a conservative comeback if the right-wing parties cooperate effectively. Radical-right challengers At the end of last month, the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party, Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, saw the biggest split in its 25-year history. The rupture was the culmination of months of increasingly open and bitter factional conflict over the party’s future direction. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right. However, it lost power following the October 2023 parliamentary election, which led to the formation of a coalition headed up by Donald Tusk, leader of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party. Since last autumn, PiS has seen its polling numbers decline to the party’s lowest level of support for 15 years. At the same time, it has been challenged by two radical right competitors: the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and the ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which together began to match, or even exceed, PiS’s level of support. Responding to declining support At the heart of this conflict was a bitter clash between longtime party leader Jarosław Kaczyński and Mateusz Morawiecki, who served as PiS prime minister from 2017 to 2023 but grew increasingly impatient with the former’s dominance. Two main factions emerged centred on a bitter dispute on how the party should respond to declining support and political competition on its right flank. The hardline traditionalist-conservative faction, often referred to as the “butter-makers” (maślarze), was more Eurosceptic and advocated a clearer right-wing agenda that included pushing ahead with radical state reconstruction and promoting a conservative vision of national identity and traditional values. In their reading, PiS lost support to its right-wing competitors because it was not radical enough and the solution was to sharpen its ideological profile and double down on hardline rhetoric. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 This group gained influence in party structures and when, in March, Kaczyński designated one of its key figures, former education minister Przemysław Czarnek, as the party’s prime ministerial candidate in the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, this was widely seen as a clear signal favouring the traditionalist-conservative faction. Morawiecki and his allies in the modernising-technocratic faction, often called the “scouts” (harcerze), also had strong conservative values and at times were very critical of Poland’s post-1989 establishment. However, they advocated a strategy of stressing economic competence, pragmatic governance and boosting Polish prosperity over hardline rhetoric on moral-cultural issues as a more effective way of appealing to voters less influenced by traditional institutions such as the Catholic church. Although they were also critical of Brussels overreach, Morawiecki’s faction preferred to avoid escalating conflict with the EU and argued that PiS had to broaden its appeal to younger, urban, more centrist-conservative Poles who found radical cultural rhetoric off-putting. Programmatic differences and personal ambitions The conflict became so destabilising because, although rooted in genuine programmatic and strategic disagreements, personalities and individual ambitions also played a major role. While Kaczyński maintained formal control of the party, his advancing age escalated debates over PiS’s direction and leadership, and these tensions intensified after the party failed to translate its presidential candidate Karol Nawrocki’s surprise summer 2025 election victory into broader momentum. For his part, Morawiecki grew increasingly impatient and frustrated as hardliners sidelined him, while his supporters were afraid that they would be excluded from PiS candidate lists at the next election. These long-simmering tensions came to a head in April, when Morawiecki announced the formation of Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), a think tank-like platform focused on economic development The association was widely interpreted by Kaczyński and PiS hardliners as a direct challenge to party unity and the leader’s authority. The leadership ruled that Development Plus violated the PiS statute, which explicitly prohibits members from joining political organisations that conflict with the party’s goals. While Morawiecki insisted that it was simply a modest intra-party policy forum, by registering an organisation with dozens of parliamentarians, he gave his faction a formal institutional shell that could potentially act as a launchpad for his own rival breakaway party. Initially, Kaczyński and Morawiecki came to a compromise agreement whereby Development Plus would work within an official party expert group. However, in July the situation escalated when the PiS leadership issued an ultimatum banning members from participating in internal political factions (clearly targeting Development Plus) and instructing parliamentarians to sign loyalty declarations confirming that they were not involved in any such groupings. Most complied, but 40 parliamentarians affiliated with Development Plus refused to do so, accusing the leadership of political blackmail. Ultimately, Kaczyński announced that, by refusing to sign, Morawiecki and his allies had effectively left the party, while Development Plus framed it as expulsion over policy differences caused by “plotters” surrounding the party leader. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 An even more fragmented right The loss of 40 deputies means that PiS is no longer the largest parliamentary caucus, thus losing procedural advantages, committee control and visibility. The departing group includes many experienced and talented politicians, particularly in the economic and foreign policy fields. The split also reduces PiS’s funding, staffing, and in some regions local organisation, as well as creating the risk of demoralisation and further defections. Even if the Polish right secures a parliamentary majority at the next election, PiS’s relative influence could be greatly reduced. Although Kaczyński’s formal party leadership remains unquestioned, the split signals to the broader right that his authority is waning and undermines his claim to be the undisputed hegemon and central broker on the right; he is increasingly now one leader among several. It also further erodes the model that Kaczyński has built over many years as the main ideologue and ultimate arbiter of internal PiS factions. In earlier crises, this personal authority and control gave him leverage to keep everyone on board so that disagreements were managed internally, and even disillusioned figures usually stayed in, or returned to, the party. Indeed, by adding a fourth distinctive player, the PiS split further compounds the divisions on the Polish right that have deepened since the last election, transforming what was once a relatively consolidated “big tent” bloc into a multi-polar competitive field. For sure, polls conducted after the split show the combined right-wing vote as competitive overall, but even if this level of support remains stable, or even increases slightly, it is now divided across more options. This is significant because Poland’s proportional electoral system uses the d’Hondt counting system that favours larger groupings. It also creates the risk that smaller right-wing parties such as Morawiecki’s new grouping could fall below the 5% parliamentary representation threshold, so their votes are excluded from seat allocation. All of this makes it harder for the right to translate raw voter support into political power. Moreover, even if the right-wing parties win a combined parliamentary majority, post-election coordination becomes much more complex with four (or more) actors whose leaders’ rivalries, different priorities and historical animosities complicate forming a stable coalition government. Nawrocki’s role will be crucial In the light of this, Nawrocki has emerged as a critical unifier with crossover appeal across the fractured Polish right. His presidential election victory showed that he could attract support well beyond traditional PiS loyalists and consolidate a broad right-wing coalition, including the vast majority of voters from both Confederations. As president, he operates outside direct party control and has cultivated an image as an authoritative unifying figure on the right, which gives him much greater moral and symbolic stature than a partisan leader immersed in day-to-day machinations. Nawrocki has also used his constitutional powers and standing, including a legislative veto that the government lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority to overturn, to position himself assertively as a powerful counterweight to the Tusk administration, and is currently Poland’s most popular politician. Nonetheless, Nawrocki’s potential to act as a possible right-wing unifier and broker is limited. For sure, he can use the presidency to set a broad conservative agenda and mediate negotiations among the various right-wing groupings to secure pre- and post-election agreements. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland's largest opposition party, PiS, has called on President @NawrockiKn to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections https://t.co/Q3BFSOSfTG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 However, Nawrocki has no formal unifying mandate and his success ultimately depends on whether the various actors are willing to be led. Without broader cooperation, even his efforts will only mitigate, not eliminate, the damage from a divided right, and personal and ideological rivalries currently run deep and cannot be easily overridden. Moreover, not only is the president expected to remain formally above the fray and not engage too openly in day-to-day politics, he also lacks the control over party organisational machinery needed to micro-manage and enforce messy backroom deals. Pivotal but not transformative? Initial polling conducted since the split suggests that Morawiecki’s new grouping would likely clear the 5% threshold and enter parliament with a small-to-medium-sized fraction; according to Politico Europe, it is currently averaging around 6% support. Although this could make it a pivotal player in coalition talks, it does not suggest that the grouping can dramatically reshape the country’s political landscape. Moreover, its support appears to be drawn mainly from PiS’s traditional electoral base, so it is simply further fragmenting the existing right-wing vote rather than drawing in a significant number of new voters who hitherto supported the governing coalition parties. For sure, Morawiecki‘s project has advantages that many newcomers lack, notably its leader’s very high name recognition and a sizeable bloc of high-profile, political heavyweight allies, much larger than any previous PiS breakaway faction. His grouping immediately became the third largest parliamentary fraction, giving it visibility, funding, and organisational backbone. However, although there are some rare exceptions that usually involve major figures with significant resources breaking from established parties, it is a familiar pattern in post-1989 Polish politics for a brand new “startup” party to show an early bounce, benefiting from initial media coverage, only to fade or disappear as voters drift back to more established groupings or abstain at the next election. Sustaining momentum requires local organisational infrastructure, reliable funding, rapid professionalisation, and a clear identity, which new parties often lack. Indeed, to be successful a new startup should really attract at least 10% support initially simply because of its “newness”. Over the years, PiS breakaway politicians have established new parties that either quickly disappeared from the political scene or were eventually reintegrated into the grouping. Temporary relief for Tusk From a short-term tactical perspective, the PiS split is a welcome political gift for the Tusk government, shifting the media focus away from criticisms of its record and recent scandals and controversies. It has for example, blunted the opposition’s ability to maintain a sustained assault over a scandal involving high earnings for, and mismanagement by, a KO-connected doctor, alleged VIP access and potential patient harm at the Warsaw South Hospital, which had previously dominated the summer news headlines. The ruling coalition is likely to survive until next year's election, but its prospects are hampered by a weak domestic record, writes @AleksSzczerbiak The government has therefore made security key to its reelection narrative, but that also carries risks https://t.co/w2UeNaTwAO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 1, 2026 However, the PiS split has not resolved the deeper image and performance problems that have dragged down the Tusk government’s approval ratings. The administration struggles with perceptions of slow delivery on promises while facing a hostile president, and if these problems persist, or new controversies reignite strongly once the PiS drama cools, the government will very quickly find itself back on the defensive. The PiS split only provides temporary relief; to win the next election, the ruling coalition needs to improve its own standing, not rely on opposition mistakes. World.title: Polish NGOs urge PM’s “right-hand man” to withdraw constitutional court candidacy
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A group of Polish civil society organisations has urged a former government minister to withdraw his candidacy to become a Constitutional Tribunal (TK) judge, saying his close ties to the prime minister could undermine confidence in the court’s independence. In a joint statement, the nine organisations say that restoring the legitimacy of the court, which has been in crisis since 2015 following illegitimate judicial appointments made by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, requires not only addressing legal irregularities but also rebuilding public trust. “The existence of the Constitutional Tribunal as an organ of judicial power only makes sense if it is an independent arbiter,” they say. 🔴Wspólnie z innymi organizacjami apelujemy do dr. M. Berka o rezygnację z kandydowania do TK, a do Sejmu o wybór osoby niezależnej politycznie. Droga do praworządności to nie „odbijanie” Trybunału, ale odbudowa jego autorytetu. Przeczytajcie nasz apel, link w komentarzu ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/LPlbk39lNr — Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka (@hfhrpl) August 20, 2026 The appeal follows Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s announcement that Maciej Berek, who until recently served as a government minister and whom Tusk has described as his “right-hand man”, would be put forward as a candidate for the Constitutional Tribunal. The choice has drawn particular attention because Tusk came to power promising to “depoliticise” the court after the previous PiS government appointed former politicians as judges. “Regardless of the extent to which the tribunal has become politicised, the way to reform this institution cannot be for it to be ‘recaptured’ or ‘taken over’ by another ruling majority,” the NGOs write in the statement. The organisations, including the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, the Institute of Public Affairs and the Stefan Batory Foundation, say Berek’s close ties to the current political leadership could cause his appointment to be perceived as political, regardless of his legal qualifications or personal integrity. “Not only must courts and tribunals operate independently and impartially, but citizens must also recognise and have confidence in that independence and impartiality. This is not possible when judges are appointed whose links to the government are immediately apparent,” the organisations add. “We therefore call on Dr Maciej Berek to withdraw his candidacy in the interests of the independence of the constitutional judiciary.” The proportion of Poles who negatively assess the justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law. State pollster @CBOS_Info found 61% now hold a negative view, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017 https://t.co/P3fbTTbS5C — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 The organisations also argue that Berek’s nomination goes against a principle that the current ruling coalition sought to introduce: that anyone who has held political office within the previous four years should be barred from appointment to the tribunal. Berek was a government minister until last week. The coalition’s proposal was included in a bill approved by parliament in 2024. However, the Constitutional Tribunal itself later ruled the provision unconstitutional after former President Andrzej Duda, an ally of PiS, referred the legislation for review. “Although this law has not come into force, it would be reasonable for the Sejm to adhere to the standard it has adopted,” they said, referring to the lower chamber of the parliament, which is responsible for nominating new TK judges. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. It found that the measures "violate judicial independence" https://t.co/uBJr1bXFv4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2025 However, the selection of Berek, whose candidacy was put forward by MPs from Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has exposed divisions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from centre-right to left. “We were supposed to be different from PiS; we were supposed to do things differently, not exactly the same way,” Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s (Lewica) parliamentary caucus, told Polsat News. Paweł Śliz, leader of the centre-right Poland 2050’s (Polska 2050) caucus, said Berek would make an excellent Constitutional Tribunal judge were it not for his recent role as a government minister. “I consider him an excellent, outstanding professional; I value his experience and expertise. However, my position on this matter is unequivocal. I will not compromise my principles,” he told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The chief justice of the constitutional court has refused to accept four new judges appointed by parliament but whom the opposition-aligned president has refused to swear in. The decision deepens an unprecedented standoff over Poland's top court https://t.co/B02DKA3uBL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 9, 2026 Given that the government has a majority of just nine in the 460-seat Sejm, it would only require a small number of MPs from Tusk’s coalition opposing Berek’s nomination for him to lose the vote. Last week, Tusk said that he “understands” concerns from some coalition partners but that he would “try to convince those who have doubts”. However, even if Berek is approved by the Sejm, the law states that new TK judges must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. It remains unclear what the president would do in the case of Berek. Presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz told PAP on Thursday that “there are serious doubts” about Berek’s formal qualifications to become a Constitutional Tribunal judge. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though he was never a member of the PiS party). ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland has summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) have discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból. “Partnership requires mutual respect,” declared foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for [the] IDF’s excessive use of force[,] are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations.” Partnership requires mutual respect. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for IDF’s excessive use of force are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations. https://t.co/9H0nhiDE4H — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) August 20, 2026 The incident in question took place in April 2024, when Israeli drones struck a convoy delivering humanitarian aid from World Central Kitchen (WCK), a major international food relief NGO. The attack killed seven aid workers, including Soból. The incident caused outrage in Poland, whose government demanded that Israel fully explain the circumstances. The IDF expressed “sincere sorrow” over the deaths and pledged to carry out a “thorough and transparent” investigation. On Wednesday this week, the IDF announced that it had closed the case after determining “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation or the taking of additional measures against any of those involved in the incident”. The IDF said that its troops had identified a gunman on one of the trucks in the convoy. It also claimed that WCK had hired an armed security force to protect the convoy without coordinating that with IDF authorities and that the convoy deviated from the route previously agreed with the IDF. However, the IDF also acknowledged that it had mistakenly identified several individuals as being armed. It added that attempts to contact WCK representatives over a half-hour period while the convoy was on the move were unsuccessful. The IDF noted that, after the incident, two military officers were removed from their positions while three others were reprimanded. But it found that there was no basis for any further action. ⚖️ IDF prosecution rules on five FFAM cases: The IDF says its General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism has completed reviews of approximately 150 exceptional wartime incidents since the beginning of the war and transferred them to the Military Prosecution. Decisions… pic.twitter.com/H5g4qOu5e2 — Israel Realtime (@IsraelRealtime) August 19, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s foreign ministry issued a statement saying that it was “greatly disappointed to receive the information provided about the discontinuation of the proceedings by the Israeli military authorities”. It announced that it had summoned the Israeli ambassador in order to “communicate a critical assessment of the actions taken to date to clarify the causes and course of the tragedy”. It also noted that Polish prosecutors are still conducting their own investigation and that the foreign ministry had informed the Israeli ambassador that they “expect the Israeli side will provide the relevant Polish authorities with all necessary explanations and materials requested”. “The circumstances of the tragedy should be fully investigated and [we] do not accept that the perpetrators are avoiding legal and moral responsibility,” concluded the ministry, adding that “the families deserve adequate compensation”. We strongly condemn the Israeli military prosecutor’s account of the deaths of our seven colleagues on April 1, 2024. And we fundamentally disagree with their decision about criminal investigations into the IDF airstrikes that killed our team. Read our full statement here:… — World Central Kitchen (@WCKitchen) August 19, 2026 The IDF’s findings were also condemned by WCK itself, which called them “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. It added that, “at the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody”. The NGO repeated its demand for an independent investigation into the incident, “because the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct”. On Friday, the UK, Canada and Australia, whose citizens were also killed in the strike, issued a joint statement calling the IDF’s decision to drop the investigation “shameful” and another example of the lack of accountability for incidents in Gaza. Joint statement from the foreign ministries of Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom on Israel closing the investigation into strikes on the World Central Kitchen convoy in Gaza on 1 April 2024 ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/V3CZe286tN — Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (@FCDOGovUK) August 21, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Not Ready for Summer to End? 3 Places to Take the Kids Before August Ends
World.content:
The end of the summer holidays is in sight. While school supplies, pencil cases and sports shoes are already making their way onto shopping lists, there are still a few days of summer left to enjoy.

Before the September school routine kicks in, here are three ways to make the most of the final days of August with the family.



Letni Letna

When: 12–31 August

Where: Prague, Letenské sady

Letenské sady is taking on a new look until 31 August, transforming into a colourful festival village. The Letní Letná Festival isn’t just about evening acrobatics for adults. It also offers a programme for younger visitors called Letní Letná for Children.

From morning until late afternoon, the huge children’s tent comes alive with fairy-tale performances and other activities. Kids can take part in creative and juggling workshops, explore an interactive play area made from recycled materials or take a ride on the iconic hand-carved wooden carousel.

Most of the children’s activities take place under the festival tents, so an unexpected rain shower won’t disrupt the day.

The festival also offers a “Night Watch” childcare service for children aged four and up. Parents can enjoy the evening programme while experienced entertainers look after their children.

When: 24–29 August

Where: Liberec and the surrounding area

Fancy a trip beyond Prague at the end of August? Head north to Liberec from 24 to 29 August, when the city hosts Crystal Valley Week, a celebration of Czech glassmaking and jewellery.

This year’s theme focuses on the interconnection of cultures, with the Czech glass bead at the centre of the programme. Children can also enjoy a free ride aboard the special Crystal Tram, which has been decorated this year to resemble a long-distance train.

There are plenty of opportunities to make your own jewellery from glass beads, with workshops and craft sessions taking place throughout Liberec for both children and adults.

When: Sunday, 30 August, 11:00–19:00

Where: Prague, Ladronka Park

On the last Sunday of the summer holidays, skip cooking lunch and head to the F.O.O.D. Picnic in Prague’s Ladronka Park. The popular event returns for its 16th edition this year.

Entry to the festival grounds is free, with 120 food and farm stalls to explore, including food trucks. There is also a large children’s zone with games and creative workshops, as well as a raffle for younger visitors.

It’s a family-friendly way to spend the final Sunday of the holidays, combining food, activities and a relaxed atmosphere before the new school year begins.

World.title: Airbnb Accounts for 1 Percent of Prague’s Housing Stock, Analysis Finds
World.content:
Prague’s short-term rental market has grown into a professional business but Airbnb accounts for only a small share of the city’s housing stock, according to a new analysis.

In June 2026, around 7,878 entire apartments and houses in Prague were actively listed on Airbnb. With roughly 720,000 apartments across the capital, that represents about 1.1 percent of the total housing stock.

The situation is very different in individual parts of the city. In Prague 1, Airbnb-listed properties account for around one-fifth of all apartments, according to the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR). In Prague 2, the share is around 7 percent, while in some outer districts it is below 0.5 percent.



The concentration of short-term rentals has also changed the nature of the market. IPR data show that hosts managed an average of two apartments in 2019. By 2024, that figure had risen to three, while more than half of Prague’s Airbnb listings were operated by hosts with at least five properties.

This means short-term accommodation is increasingly being run as a business rather than as occasional home-sharing.

Prague’s housing shortage is much larger

Despite the impact Airbnb can have in central neighborhoods, the analysis points to a much bigger problem behind Prague’s housing crisis — a long-term shortage of new construction.

Since 2006, Prague has accumulated a housing deficit of more than 91,000 apartments, according to the analysis. That shortfall is about 11.5 times larger than the number of apartments currently listed on Airbnb.

Even if every Airbnb property in the city were suddenly returned to the long-term rental market, Prague would still be short more than 83,000 homes.

The accumulated construction deficit reportedly became larger than the number of active Airbnb apartments around 2009 or 2010. Since then, the gap has continued to grow.

This suggests that Prague’s housing crisis began well before short-term rentals reached their current scale.

Tourism brings other concerns

Housing availability is also not the only issue surrounding short-term rentals.

Residents in central Prague have complained about noise, disruption and visitors staying in residential buildings.

The city also collects accommodation fees from short-term stays, although payment is not automatic because apartment owners must register and pay the fees themselves.

The debate over Airbnb in Prague therefore extends beyond housing. While short-term rentals can change the character of central neighborhoods and create problems for residents, the latest figures suggest that the city’s wider housing shortage is primarily the result of years of insufficient construction.

World.title: ASEAN Plus Three Film Festival Returns to Prague for Its Fifth Edition
World.content:
The ASEAN Committee in Prague (ACP), representing the embassies of ASEAN member states, together with the embassies of China, Japan and the Republic of Korea, will host the fifth edition of the ASEAN Plus Three Film Festival (APTFF).

The festival will begin on Monday, September 7, 2026, at the Municipal Library of Prague.

Organised in cooperation with the Municipal Library of Prague, the festival will run until September 14 and feature seven full-length films, alongside a curated selection of short films from across the ASEAN Plus Three region.



Since its launch in 2022, the APTFF has introduced Czech audiences to the diverse cultures and cinematic voices of ASEAN and its Plus Three partners.

Previous editions have featured acclaimed films including Escape from Mogadishu (Republic of Korea), Father and Son (Viet Nam) and Yuni (Indonesia).

This year’s programme includes Solata: Friends Are the Family We Choose (Indonesia), Babah (Malaysia), The Beginning (Myanmar), I’m Perfect (the Philippines), 4 Tigers (Thailand), Song of the South (Viet Nam) and One and Only (China).

A selection of short films will also be screened during the opening night on September 7.

The programme includes Mbiyodo/Communal Work (Indonesia), Ninavau (Malaysia), Myanmar Be Enchanted (Myanmar), Lola Loleng/Grandma Loleng (the Philippines), Give to Getters (Thailand), Welcome to Viet Nam (Viet Nam), My Chinese Ecological Notes (China), Pukkulapottas and Hours in the Forest (Japan), and Persona (Republic of Korea).

Beyond its cultural programme, the festival is part of a broader effort by ASEAN and its Plus Three partners to introduce Czech audiences to the region, its societies and creative industries, as well as its shared identity as a community of more than 690 million people.

All screenings are open to the public and free of charge. Films will be shown in their original languages with English and Czech subtitles.

The full programme and schedule are available on the Municipal Library of Prague website.

World.title: GALLERY: Light Installation “Synapse” Coming to Florenc Metro Station
World.content:
Jan Poš light installation Synapse will go on display in the Florenc Line C metro passage at the end of September.

The artwork will track passengers’ movements and complement the existing Battle of Sokolovo mosaic. Prague city councillors approved around CZK 1.38 million in funding to complete and install the artwork.

“Synapse” is a light-based installation by visual artist Jan Poš (1996) and the winning entry in the “Light for the Metro” competition held in 2023.



The aim was to create a light artwork for the passage connecting the north and south concourses of Florenc metro station. A total of 23 artists and teams submitted proposals, with four advancing to the final stage, which was conducted as a competitive dialogue.

The five-member jury considered the artwork’s long-term maintenance and its ability to withstand demanding operating conditions.

According to Poš, the artwork, installed on the wall opposite the underpass’s main staircase, comes into view as metro passengers ascend or descend the stairs.

It becomes part of their daily journey while remaining elegantly set apart, creating a space where it can stand on its own and offer a moment of respite from the hustle and bustle.

Poš says the work’s format and style enliven and build on the Battle of Sokolovo mosaic, creating a bridge between the past and present of the city.

The artwork was originally due to be installed alongside the completion of the reconstruction of the station’s ceiling slab. Prague’s public transport operator, DPP, has been repairing the structure since 2022 due to corrosion.

World.title: Partial Lunar Eclipse to Be Visible From Prague at Dawn on August 28
World.content:
Prague residents willing to get up early on Friday, August 28, will have a chance to witness a partial lunar eclipse, with almost the entire Moon passing into Earth’s shadow shortly before it sets.

The eclipse will reach its maximum at 6:12 a.m. CEST. By then, only a narrow section along the Moon’s northern edge will remain illuminated.

In Prague, the Moon is expected to set at approximately 6:17 a.m., leaving only a few minutes to observe the eclipse at its peak.



The partial phase will begin at 4:33 a.m. As the event progresses, Earth’s shadow will gradually cover the lunar surface, reducing the bright portion of the Moon until only a thin illuminated crescent remains visible.

Astronomers at the Silesian University in Opava say observers will need an unobstructed view towards the southwest, as the Moon will be low above the horizon throughout the most important part of the event.

The eclipse follows another major astronomical event visible from the Czech Republic earlier this month, giving skywatchers a second opportunity to observe a rare celestial phenomenon within a short period.

Unlike a solar eclipse, observing the Moon does not require protective eyewear. The eclipse can be seen with the naked eye, while binoculars or a camera may provide a closer view.

For the best chance of seeing the maximum phase, observers should choose a location with a clear southwestern horizon and arrive before dawn. Weather conditions will also play a decisive role in whether the eclipse is visible.

World.title: September 19: Prague Hosts Indian Festival of Music, Food, and Community
World.content:
Prague will host its annual celebration of Indian culture, Ganeshotsav, on Saturday, September 19, at Kulturní dům Ládví.

Ganeshotsav, the festival honoring Lord Ganesha, is more than a celebration of Indian culture—it’s a way to bring people together.

Since 2021, the festival has grown into a space where Indian and Czech communities can meet, connect, and enjoy shared traditions.

The event is organised by Maharashtra Mandal, Czech Republic, a registered non-profit dedicated to promoting friendship and understanding between Indian and Czech residents.

The festival features traditional Indian rituals, music, dance, and food, and welcomes everyone to join in the fun.

Like last year, this year, the festival adds a charitable aspect: part of the registration fees will go to support non-profits in the Czech Republic.

“With this initiative, we want to contribute to the development of communities both in our country of origin and in the country that is now our home,” says the organizers to Prague Morning.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Maharashtra Mandal Czech Republic (@maharashtramandalczechrepublic)

By partnering with like-minded organisations, the festival encourages intercultural dialogue, mutual respect, and connections between diverse communities living in the Czech Republic.

Like last year, organizers will support small entrepreneurs from the Indian community who will present the diversity of Indian cuisine.

The project is called “”Our Annapoorna -The Taste of Every Indian Household”, and will offer visitors a diverse selection of traditional dishes from different corners of India.

The cultural program, featuring music, dance, and traditional rituals, will run from 5:00 PM to 8:30 PM

World.title: A Multi-Brand K-Beauty Pop-Up Is Coming to Prague This September
World.content:
A Korean beauty pop-up will bring eight K-beauty brands and K-pop entertainment to Prague’s Vltava River this September.

The HARUNARU K-Beauty Pop-up will take place aboard KVASOUL, a self-brewing boat restaurant, from September 4 to 8.



An industry preview for beauty professionals and influencers will be held on September 3.

Visitors will be able to discover, test and buy products from eight Korean brands, including GASH, ranked No. 1 at Olive Young, South Korea’s leading beauty retailer, and ilso, known for its pore-care products.

The event will also feature K-pop performances, a Random Dance Challenge, an idol-style makeup show and a dedicated selection of K-pop albums and merchandise.

The pop-up is aimed at introducing emerging Korean beauty brands to consumers and industry professionals in the Czech Republic and across Central and Eastern Europe.

Entry is free, although visitors are encouraged to register online in advance.

The event is organized by Bramasole Prague s.r.o., which operates several Korean restaurant brands in Prague.

World.title: Dancing House Marks 30 Years With a Free Weekend of Dance in Prague
World.content:
Prague’s Dancing House will celebrate its 30th anniversary with a free two-day program of dance classes, performances and workshops on August 29 and 30.

Jiráskovo náměstí, next to the landmark on the Vltava embankment, will host a temporary stage and dance floor throughout the weekend.



The program will run from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both Saturday and Sunday.

Visitors can join professional instructors for classes in bachata, street dance and Latin American dance. There will also be sessions for children, dance demonstrations and opportunities to meet and talk with instructors.

The event is open to all levels, with participants able to watch performances or take part in the classes.

Weekend program

The schedule is the same on both days until the evening finale.

11:00 a.m. – Opening

11:05 a.m. – Children’s dance class

11:50 a.m. – Talk with the instructor

12:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

12:05 p.m. – Bachata class

12:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

2:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

2:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

3:05 p.m. – Children’s dance class

3:50 p.m. – Talk with the instructor

4:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

4:05 p.m. – Bachata class

4:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

5:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

5:05 p.m. – Street dance class

5:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

6:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

6:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

7:05 p.m. – Hula Hoops performance

The closing acrobatic performance will differ each day. Saturday will feature a handstand performance, while Sunday will bring Duo ReAct.

Admission is free. Organizers will also provide light refreshments.

Completed in 1996, the Dancing House is one of Prague’s best-known examples of modern architecture. It stands at the corner of Rašínovo nábřeží and Jiráskovo náměstí, overlooking the Vltava.

The building was designed by Croatian-Czech architect Vlado Milunić in collaboration with Canadian-American architect Frank Gehry. Its curved forms and leaning towers give the impression of a dancing couple, which inspired its Czech name, Tančící dům.

The building is also known by the nickname “Ginger and Fred,” referring to American dancers Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire.

World.title: Photos: another popular Hungarian lake dries out, Bölömbika lookout shows critical conditions
World.content:
The water level of yet another Hungarian lake has fallen to a critical low, meaning visitors to the Bölömbika lookout, which has seen better days, are now confronted with a dispiriting scene of environmental devastation rather than spectacular views and abundant wildlife. Check out the latest photos in our article below.

Photo: Facebook/Madárpart Túraközpont, Kölcsönző és Kemping Photo: Facebook/Madárpart Túraközpont, Kölcsönző és Kemping

Nature horror from Hungarian lake lookout

Nature lovers visiting one of the Tisza Lake’s best-known attractions, the Bölömbika lookout, have recently been met with a deeply disappointing sight. The landscape around the lookout has changed dramatically: areas once covered by water are now dry lakebed, leaving the structure effectively standing on dry land.

The transformation is particularly striking in new photographs taken by the Madárpart Hiking Centre, Rental Service and Campsite. From the images, it is difficult to imagine that the lookout was once surrounded by water. The present condition of the landscape illustrates the dramatic consequences of the Tisza Lake’s water level falling to an exceptionally low point.

The situation is even more pronounced in the Tiszavalk Basin. The area has almost completely dried out, while the lake itself is registering an unusually low water level. Not only has the familiar landscape disappeared; the conditions that once made the area attractive to hikers and water-sports enthusiasts have also been severely compromised.

Historic drought, drying rivers and vanishing lakes

Hungary is enduring a historic drought, with water levels in its lakes, rivers and streams repeatedly falling to record lows. Lake Velence, once renowned for its thriving tourism, sporting events and festivals, is now in its final throes. Even at Lake Balaton, Hungary’s so-called “sea”, swimmers must walk a considerable distance before reaching water deep enough for a swim.

The Danube’s level was so low in July that the Paks nuclear power plant had to be almost entirely shut down. A submerged weir was subsequently built to raise the water level and ensure that sufficient cooling water could be drawn from the river during periods of extreme low flow such as the present one.

The Tisza is also exceptionally low, while one of its tributaries, the Zagyva, has dried up altogether. The same has happened to the Tarna, the Galga, the Bózsva stream, the Morgó stream, the Tápió and the Hajta. Lake Kolon, a strictly protected habitat in the Kiskunság region, had already dried out by the beginning of summer, as had Lake Bicsérd in Transdanubia and Lake Kocs in the Balaton Uplands.

If you missed: Invasive mosquito species conquering Hungary – climate change destroys our echosystem?

Not just a Hungarian problem

Lake Öreg in Tata, like the Tisza Lake, is experiencing exceptionally low water levels; the same is true of Lake Balaton and Lake Velence. The extreme conditions require swift action from the Government, as forecasts suggest that summers in Hungary will remain hot and dry as climate change and global warming intensify.

The exceptionally dry summer is not a uniquely Hungarian phenomenon. Its consequences are being felt across every area of life, from agriculture and tourism to energy production. Romania was forced to shut down its only nuclear power station because of the Danube’s exceptionally low level, while in Italy the Isonzo – a river familiar from the battles of the First World War – has dried up.

Hungarian agriculture, as we know it, is nearing the end – but researchers already have a plan

World.title: House price growth eased in Hungary – here are the latest prices
World.content:
House price growth eased in July, with the gap between average prices per square metre reaching as much as tenfold across the country, property website ingatlan.com told Hungary’s MTI news agency on Tuesday.

House price growth eased in Hungary

Monthly price growth slowed to 0.1 per cent, while the annual increase fell to 11.9 per cent. In Budapest, prices rose by 0.9 per cent compared with the previous month, although ingatlan.com said this may have represented a correction following June’s 0.1 per cent decline, MTI wrote.

According to the company’s house price index, Budapest property prices were 8.3 per cent higher than a year earlier, despite a substantial increase in supply.

The number of newly built homes listed for sale in the capital rose from 3,742 a year ago to 5,381 this year, ingatlan.com said. The median price per square metre for second-hand homes in Budapest ranges from HUF 942,000 to HUF 2 million, while prices for newly built properties in the most expensive districts are approaching HUF 3 million per square metre.

Regional differences

The housing market presented a mixed picture nationwide. Pest County stood out with a monthly price increase of 1.2 per cent in July, while the Southern Great Plain recorded a 2.9 per cent decline.

Debrecen had the country’s highest median price for second-hand homes among regional centres, at HUF 1.04 million per square metre. Szeged and Székesfehérvár were also approaching the HUF 1 million mark. Salgótarján was the cheapest county seat, with a median price of HUF 312,000 per square metre.

If you missed – Good news for homebuyers and students: vast student city and residential district could rise on Budapest’s derelict waterfront

Debrecen also led the expansion in the supply of newly built homes, with listings nearly doubling. Across the main provincial cities, supply increased by an average of close to 50 per cent.

The estate agency said current trends pointed to annual house price growth of less than 10 per cent this year. The last time prices rose at such a modest rate was in 2016.

Looking beyond price per square metre: how Budapest, Warsaw and Bucharest’s new-build home markets differ

World.title: How Hungary’s former Chief of the General Staff squandered taxpayers’ money – and must remain silent about it
World.content:
Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi served as the Hungarian Defence Forces Chief of the General Staff for one year and 328 days. During that period, one of the companies owned by the Defence Ministry, HM EI Zrt, spent around HUF 1 billion converting a luxury official residence in Dunakeszi, under the authority of Defence Minister Kristóf Szalay-Bobrovniczky. The parties remember differently who requested what, and precisely for what purpose. But Gábor Böröndi, who succeeded Ruszin-Szendi as Chief of the Defence Staff, did not move into the property. Instead, another house was rented for him elsewhere – at considerable expense.

From one luxury property to another

A curious housing decision emerges from General Böröndi’s three-year tenure. Although the luxury property in Dunakeszi had been created specifically for the serving Chief of the General Staff, and was available to him, he did not move in. Instead, the Defence Ministry rented him another luxury property in Szentendre.

One of the ministry’s companies, the aforementioned HM EI Zrt, paid EUR 2,890 a month for the rental. Between August 2023 and May 2026, this amounted to a cost of roughly HUF 36 million to the state, depending on exchange-rate fluctuations. As a rented property, however, the house never became state property.

Gábor Böröndi is no longer Hungary’s Chief of General Staff, but he remained a reservist in the rank of colonel general. Photo: Facebook/Magyar Honvédség

The Szentendre property was no ordinary home, either. It is a three-storey family house measuring 386 square metres, set on a plot of almost 1,200 square metres. It includes, among other things, a wellness area, a jacuzzi, a sauna and a three-car garage. It is currently being offered for sale for HUF 275 million. To see what the property looks like, click here.

No one knows who wanted the luxury

The case is particularly striking because the official villa in Dunakeszi was left empty. More than HUF 1 billion had previously been spent on the property. According to an earlier report by the Government Control Office, merely maintaining the villa cost the state an average of HUF 368,000 a month.

In other words, the ministry was paying to maintain an unoccupied official residence while also covering the rent on another house for Böröndi. The distance between the two towns and Budapest cannot explain the decision, since Dunakeszi lies roughly the same distance to the north as Szentendre does to the south.

One of the most unusual aspects of the affair is that Böröndi himself is not permitted to explain why he did not use the official villa made available to him. Both 24.hu and HVG contacted the former Chief of the General Staff, who is currently a serving soldier in the reserve establishment and may speak publicly only with the Defence Ministry’s permission.

PM Péter Magyar and Minister of Defence Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi. Before, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi served as Hungary’s Chief of the General Staff for almost two years. Photo: Facebook/Ruszin-Szendi Romulusz

The ministry, now led by Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, did not grant that permission. As a result, the man at the centre of the affair is unable to explain why, instead of using the Dunakeszi property that the Hungarian Defence Forces could have provided, another high-value house was rented for him in Szentendre.

The available information therefore suggests that, for three years, the state incurred costs associated with two separate properties: the maintenance of the villa in Dunakeszi and tens of millions of forints in rent for Böröndi’s house in Szentendre.

There is still no answer as to why the second property was needed in place of the official residence. Böröndi himself cannot provide one because the ministry has refused him permission to speak.

A peculiar luxury project

The Dunakeszi property, which remains state-owned, is still empty. According to Ruszin-Szendi, it was fitted out to a luxury standard because it was intended for official and representational purposes, including receiving foreign delegations, as well as serving as the official residence of the serving Chief of the General Staff.

If you missed: Leading candidates for Hungary’s “almighty” National Asset Recovery and Protection Office have presented their programmes

He himself lived there with his family for several months. But according to the Government Control Office’s report, he ordered bespoke features for the villa by email, together with his wife, including a custom billiards table, panoramic terraces and a wellness area.

An April article by Átlátszó reported that the decision to undertake the luxury project had not been made by Ruszin-Szendi. Instead, it may have been taken by “either the administrative state secretary of the Prime Minister’s Cabinet Office, the administrative state secretary of the Defence Ministry, or the board of directors of the state-owned HM EI Zrt”.

However, after annulling a final court judgment, Hungary’s Supreme Court did not release the documents requested in connection with the project. The court’s president remains András Zs. Varga, who was appointed by Fidesz and has repeatedly been urged to resign by Péter Magyar.

How Hungary’s central bank squandered EUR 30.4 million in two years — inquiry concerning luxury project begins

World.title: Hungarian National Bank cuts base rate again
World.content:
The Monetary Council of the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) decided to cut the central bank base rate by 25bp to 5.50pc at a monthly policy meeting on Tuesday.

The Council also lowered the central bank’s symmetric interest rate corridor by 25bp, bringing the O/N deposit rate to 4.50pc and the O/N collateralised loan rate to 6.50pc.

In a statement released after the meeting, the Council said inflation developments were below the baseline scenario projected in June, while the risk premium on domestic assets had remained stable. “These factors have preserved the Monetary Council’s room to manoeuvre,” they added.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Hungarian National Bank Governor Mihály Varga. Varga remained in position after the government change despite serving as Orbán’s finance minister for more than one and a half decade. Photo: Facebook/Varga Mihály

The Council noted that July inflation had slowed to 1.2pc, below market expectations as well as the forecast in the central bank’s June Inflation report. They added that CPI was set to stay under the 3pc target for the rest of the year and throughout 2027 before returning to the target in H1 2028.

“Looking ahead, Hungary’s risk assessment will be primarily influenced by expectations regarding the fiscal path and the adoption of the euro, as well as the external market environment,” the Council said.
