World.title: This town has finally realised its potential as the perfect beach getaway
World.content:
InspirationQueensland This town has finally realised its potential as the perfect beach getaway Julietta Jameson Updated August 26, 2026 — 11:27am ,first published August 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This article is part of our comprehensive guide to the Sunshine Coast, your guide to where to stay, eat and the must-see highlights. See all stories .

Common wisdom says galleries and museums are the mark of a fully formed destination. I believe it’s coffee. At least this is the conclusion I reach over a latte at Cici’s Continental Deli, a hole-in-the-wall cafe a stone’s throw from Mooloolaba Beach. It’s a cave-like refuge from all that Sunshine Coast sunshine (though of course there’s outdoor seating), with clever mid-century styling that makes it feel decades older than 2025 when it opened. The coffee is excellent, the sandwiches generous and the attitude distinctly Sunshine Coast: friendly, relaxed and chatty. Mooloolaba Beach, on Queensland’s Sunshine Coast, has come of age. The last time I was here, more than a decade ago, finding decent coffee required local knowledge. Friends who lived there pointed me in the right direction. This time I simply stumble across it. If not fully formed in the way top destinations are, Mooloolaba, I think, is at least growing up. Could it be the new Noosa, the aspirational jewel in the Sunshine Coast crown? Queensland coastal destinations have never needed museums for holiday crowds to think of them as the perfect getaway. What they need is sun, sand, surf and lifestyle.



Despite having all that, Mooloolaba has had the reputation for being a bit, well, daggy. Locals and regular holidaymakers have liked it that way. 



It’s a leap to declare all this on the back of finding a great cafe. In fact, it’s almost contradictory. Good coffee can be a gateway drug to parking problems and other conditions that make a place insufferable. The Mooloolaba Spit separates the Pacific Ocean from the Mooloolah River. But for now, Mooloolaba is having a moment, balancing lived character with contemporary sophistication – and that’s in no small part due to the new Avani Mooloolaba Beach Hotel, the first full-service internationally branded new-build hotel on the Sunshine Coast in four decades. With a young, enthusiastic staff, there’s a real sense of place at the Avani. It’s a $50 million landmark development that runs to the seaside-holiday playbook perfectly. It’s got beachy tones in a relaxed decor that pops with decorative accents and an airy sense of space. Rooms have balconies, many of which have big ocean views and beds oriented for a sunrise wake-up. The story of the site on which it sits is emblematic of the town’s change. Just a block back from the beach, hence premium real estate, it was previously an expansive council-owned ground-level carpark. Council sold off half – that became the hotel – while the other half was developed into a far more efficient multilevel parking structure.



Avani Mooloolaba’s highlight is its upper reaches. There’s a rooftop infinity pool and terrace, and Sully’s Rooftop, the hotel’s signature restaurant, eagerly patronised by locals. Later this year at street level, First Avenue Cellar & Bar will also open, joining the excellent Lobby Bar (another spot for good coffee). The Avani Mooloolaba Beach Hotel is the first new full-service hotel to hit the Sunshine Coast in 40 years. A bedroom with an uninterruped beach view inside the Avani hotel in Mooloolaba. The 180 rooms span 12 storeys in line with local height restrictions, meaning no Gold Coast-style shadows on the beach. Mooloolaba’s second luxury hotel, though, the Aria development just down the road, will be bigger, with council recently approving two extra storeys on the basis of needing additional hotel rooms in the region.



Locals worry about such incremental height creep. Up to now, though, their biggest worry amid all the change, has been the demolition of Mooloolaba’s much-loved but undeniably dated “loo with a view”, a badly placed public convenience that blocked the beach view and became a joke’s punchline. It makes way for a foreshore precinct that is currently under construction and which features boardwalks, terraced sea walls and community facilities Seafood eatery Prawn Star inhabits a couple of converted prawn trawlers and a pontoon. Those same priorities have seen Mooloolaba Wharf become a lively hub of hospitality. Too often, old wharf precincts can become Disneyfied white elephants. But here, the wharf is still in regular use for boating purposes, and the boutiques, cafes and eateries are packed with visitors and locals alike. A highlight is Prawn Star, a seafood-serving institution inhabiting a couple of converted prawn trawlers and a pontoon. A didgeridoo performance during a Salwater Eco Tours cruise. One morning, we leave the wharf with Simon Thornalley, founder of Indigenous tourism operator, Saltwater Eco Tours, for a cruise on Gubbi Gubbi/Kabi Kabi Country. His boat is a 1908 heritage-listed sailing vessel that he restored himself. It’s big on character and is a good match for Thornalley’s.



The Mooloolah River has an extensive canal network and cruising on it, we pass mansions, including one owned by the Irwins with their research boat parked out the front. Most of our admiration is for the remaining little 1960s and ’70s holiday shacks. The juxtaposition makes me reflect on what we lose to the same progress I admire. The losses to Thornalley’s people, however, are on a far greater scale and on a much longer timeline. He doesn’t dwell on it. Instead, as we munch on a morning tea, he points out birds and land forms, tells stories of the water, and as our cruise nears its end, he treats us to a didgeridoo performance. Paddling out with Saltwater Eco Tours. On a sunset cruise with Set Sail Cruises, it’s all about simply admiring the coast from both the river and the ocean. We crank up a yacht-rock playlist, pop the bubbly, and enjoy the wind in our hair and spray on our faces. In Mooloolaba there are whale watching cruises, snorkelling and diving cruises, turtle activities, canoeing, paddleboarding and kayaking adventures, and so much more. The fact it’s so jam-packed with activities is what makes it fundamentally different to Noosa, a local tells me. “Noosa’s about being seen, we’re about doing.”



At Sea Life Sunshine Coast it’s hard to argue. It’s a favourite with families but behind the penguins, seals and underwater tunnel is one of the region’s most important marine rescue operations, rehabilitating injured turtles before returning them to the ocean. It’s a reminder that, for all its growing sophistication, Mooloolaba remains closely connected to the marine environment that built it. You can admire the coast from both the river and the ocean on a boat trip with Set Sail Cruises. Then there’s the Lycra brigade. The Mooloolaba Triathlon is Australia’s second-largest triathlon event. Held annually in mid-March, the festival attracts about 9000 competitors across elite and amateur categories, with the ocean swims, sprint and cycling standard Olympic distances. For those looking to recover from all that, even wellness has become part of the town’s evolution. Once upon a time, a surf followed by fish and chips probably qualified as self-care here, and it probably still does to many. Today, visitors can alternate beach walks with infrared saunas, ice baths, massage treatments and spa rituals. Tank Bathhouse has helped introduce communal bathing culture to the Sunshine Coast, while Sauna & Ice Studio caters to the growing enthusiasm for hot-and-cold therapy. The Avani has also introduced a terrific spa to the equation. Not only are the treatments top tier, but the hotel, which runs the spa itself, has priced products competitively (rather than at the enormous mark-ups many hotel spas favour), making it a lovely retail experience as well as a healing one.



Amid the touristy restaurants with touts out the front, the ice-cream vendors and dark entryways to the plethora of short-term apartment accommodation that is the lifeblood of Mooloolaba stays, the esplanade is home to some terrific boutiques. The Wharf Mooloolaba has gelato, sushi, tacos, a bakery and plenty of atmosphere. A standout is Zambezee, where international women’s fashion brands hang next to quality local designers. Avenue J deals in exquisitely curated antique jewellery and some lovely objets d’art. Even the pharmacy has some great finds in the form of Queensland-made cosmetics, candles and hair accessories. It’s not Noosa-level retail therapy, but that pharmacy is perhaps one of the best illustrations of the Mooloolaba change: it’s locally focused with a side of sophistication, rather than sophistication first, local second. Sure, there is increasing style here: better coffee, better restaurants and better places to stay. There will be more thoughtful public spaces. But it feels like the natural evolution of a beach town that is realising its potential, while still maintaining its own unique character. And in that, there’s no need for it to be “the new” anywhere, other than the destination it is.





MORE

discovermooloolaba.com.au The writer travelled as a guest of the Avani Mooloolaba Beach Hotel.

World.title: Gawn makes All-Australian history, but Dawson’s moving speech steals the show
World.content:
Melbourne great Max Gawn has capped a record ninth All-Australian selection by being named captain, but the biggest moment of the AFL Awards came when Gawn’s Adelaide counterpart Jordan Dawson was named as his deputy. On the field, the Crows skipper had a year to remember, but off-field he endured unimaginable heartbreak with the loss of his elder brother, Jaryd. Jonathan Brown interviews Max Gawn in one of the moments of the night at Centrepiece at Melbourne Park. AFL Photos In paying tribute to Dawson, Gawn said he knew who showed the most leadership this season – the No.12 for Adelaide. “There’s a lot of captains in the team, [but] to be honest I think we probably saw one of the better captains speeches here tonight already,” Gawn said.



“I think we saw some leadership tonight. For Jordan to get up and do what he did, to speak about mental health, to lead his side through the tragedy that happened with his family, and then to show vulnerability in front of a group of strangers, that he hasn’t got it right, he hasn’t got it perfect [in] his battle right now in asking for help – that’s a captain that I want to be behind.” Just minutes earlier at Centrepiece at Melbourne Park, Dawson – this year’s All-Australian vice captain – gave a spine-tingling speech about the importance of speaking up when times are tough. View post on X “It’s been a struggle,” he said of his 2026 campaign. “It’s not easy – it’s a range of emotions. They come at different times, and for me it was just about creating a safe place within the footy club, within home and understanding that there’s going to be times where I’ll struggle to come into work, but the footy club’s been awesome in that space.



“[It’s] also me understanding that it’s OK to feel a certain type of way, and to also talk to the people that are close to me and the ones I love, and make sure we’re having ongoing conversations about how we’re all dealing with the events that’ve happened. It’s still pretty raw ... it’s always going to be hard to talk about, I think. “I just want to wish anyone who’s struggled with mental health out there, or who is struggling with mental health, to know that you are definitely loved, and the world is a better place with you in it, and that you are enough, and that we all love you, and that you have beautiful family and friends around you.” On the football front, there were several controversial omissions in the 23-man team unveiled on Tuesday night. Gawn became the first man to earn nine green blazers and was honoured to also assume the captaincy, a role Demons coach Steven King last week said he deserved. Gawn had captained the All-Australian side once before, in 2021. Record breaker: Melbourne captain Max Gawn has received his ninth All-Australian blazer. AFL Photos



Western Bulldogs counterpart Marcus Bontempelli joined a select group – also including Gary Ablett snr, Gary Ablett jnr, Patrick Dangerfield, Lance Franklin, Robert Harvey and Mark Ricciuto – to have enjoyed the top honour eight times. A record five Indigenous players were named – Wayne Milera, Jarman Impey, Kysaiah Pickett, Shai Bolton and Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera. The record had been four players in 2006, when Shaun Burgoyne, Lindsay Gilbee, Adam Goodes and Andrew McLeod were honoured. Loading The club-imposed suspension of Sydney players Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner – almost certainly all would have been selected – opened up three spots, but there were still contentious selections. Zak Butters, despite playing only 17 games because of injury, was chosen ahead of Hawthorn co-captain Jai Newcombe, and Carlton superstar Patrick Cripps, who has been integral to the Blues’ rise under Josh Fraser.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Butters declares he’s leaving Port, but he won’t get to Collingwood. Suns spearhead also on the move Port Adelaide defender Aliir Aliir was also a surprise omission, while teammate Jason Horne-Francis also had strong claims. Geelong wingman Oliver Dempsey was one of nine maiden All-Australians, the young star redefining how his role is played through his ability to push forward and kick goals. However, Dempsey was chosen ahead of star teammate Max Holmes, who was in superb touch, averaging 29 disposals, before a right ankle fracture and syndesmosis injury in July. Emerging Fremantle gun Murphy Reid donned a blazer in just his second year in the AFL, an outstanding achievement. All told, 10 players retained their spots from the 2025 team – Gawn, Bontempelli, Dawson, Wanganeen-Milera, Pickett, Jordan Clark, Harris Andrews, Bailey Smith, Zac Bailey and Nick Daicos.



The full list of club representation was: Adelaide (two), Brisbane Lions (three), Collingwood (one), Fremantle (five), Geelong (two), GWS (one), Hawthorn (two), Melbourne (two), Port Adelaide (one), St Kilda (two), Sydney Swans (one) and Western Bulldogs (one). The selection panel included AFL CEO Andrew Dillon (chair), Eddie Betts, Simon Black, Jude Bolton, Abbey Holmes, Glen Jakovich, Laura Kane, David Mundy, Joel Selwood and Greg Swann. Meanwhile, Daicos, now a three-time All Australian, was crowned the AFL Players’ Association most valuable player for a second time, capping a fine season in which he polled 147 votes – a new benchmark. Daicos, having averaged a whopping 35 disposals per game, beat Bontempelli (109 votes) and Gawn (99) to the honour. He also won the award in 2024. He surpassed Richmond champion Dustin Martin’s previous benchmark of 122 votes in 2017.



“We are incredibly proud of what he has achieved and even more so for the way he approaches his game in all phases. On-field and off-field, Nick sets the standard at our club and is a wonderful leader. We want our program not just to develop great players, but incredible people and Nick really represents that,” Magpies coach Craig McRae said. St Kilda co-captain Callum Wilkie claimed the inaugural AFL Coaches Association defensive player of the year. Wilkie finished the home-and-away season with 42 votes, ahead of Brisbane’s Andrews, Sydney’s Tom McCartin and Geelong’s Connor O’Sullivan, who each polled 30 votes. Dockers star Reid and St Kilda’s Max Hall shared the AFLCA’s best emerging player award.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Australia, UK, Canada urged to consider probe into Zomi Frankcom killing; Tributes pour in for country music legend Dolly Parton
World.content:
Commissioner Virginia Bell acknowledged frustration among the Jewish community over the antisemitism royal commission’s failure to make the investigation into circumstances leading to the Bondi massacre public, but has defended holding closed hearings into the event as a criminal case against one of the gunmen continues.

Bell proposed the release of confidential aspects of her interim and final reports, much of which addressing the drivers of the attack and what may have prevented it, once criminal proceedings against Naveed Akram, accused of orchestrating the Bondi massacre with father Sajid on December 14, are complete.

“I am conscious that many members of the community, and particularly members of the Jewish community, must find it frustrating that a royal commission established in the aftermath of the Bondi Hanukkah attack has not been seen publicly to be investigating what led to the attack and whether it might have been prevented,” Bell said.

“The commission has had to take care to conduct its inquiry in a way that does not occasion prejudice to pending criminal proceedings, and this has necessitated examination of the third term of reference, which relates to the attack being conducted in closed hearings.”

Confidential aspects of the reports addressing national security are expected to remain sealed regardless of the outcome of the criminal investigation.

World.title: Axed by Abbott, backed by crowdfunders: How Amanda McKenzie keeps finding hope in a crisis
World.content:
From tech-platform shutdowns to defining national moments, the climate chief shares how public anger outpaced government policy – and how there is enormous power in telling better stories.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Amanda McKenzie – climate wunderkind, activist for hope and Climate Council chief executive – and her husband and two young children came down with COVID-19 recently, she got out the roller skates. She and her husband unearthed some jigsaw puzzles, turned their living room into a makeshift roller rink, and told the kids to have fun. Then, they went back to work in their home office. As she tells this story over lunch, I’m struck by two things. First, it says a lot about their commitment to community that McKenzie and her husband chose to lock down their family at home for a week, regardless of whether they were still symptomatic. And second: living in McKenzie’s house sounds like a hoot. We’re meeting at Patsy’s, a tranquil up-market vegetarian wine bar in Melbourne’s inner north, where almost all the produce prepared in the kitchen is grown in the owner’s regenerative farm in Victoria’s Central Highlands. McKenzie has nominated this lunch spot, which seems an almost too-perfect choice to interview one of the most senior women in Australia’s environment movement.



Zucchini flowers with almond crema and salsa al dragoncello at Patsy’s. Ruby Alexander “I’m quite a utilitarian eater, but my husband has a very bougie, foodie vibe, so he’s made me more of a foodie,” she says. “I think if I was just left to my own devices, I’d be just eating a salad … premixed leaves with sun-dried tomatoes or something.” Today, McKenzie eschews wine in favour of a pot of English breakfast tea, while I order a hibiscus spritz mocktail. It is a bougie wine bar, after all. McKenzie has lived almost half her life in the public eye, although she isn’t necessarily a household name outside environment circles. Her first leadership role came 20 years ago when, aged 23, she co-founded the Australian Youth Climate Coalition with fellow law graduate Anna Rose. The pair hit the ground running, growing a fledgling coalition of 27 youth groups to a national organisation numbering 100,000 members three years later. Anna Rose (left) and Amanda McKenzie pictured at their offices in Sydney in 2009. Peter Rae Back then, as she travelled around organising meetings and strategic campaigns, McKenzie often found herself the only woman in the room. There were many who underestimated this young woman and the importance of the message she was trying to convey.



“At that time, it was a ‘future issue’,” she says. “I talked about [the impacts on our] kids and grandchildren, and it strikes me now, these kids I was talking about 20 years ago, they’re here: they’re eight and five, and experiencing the impacts already.” Related Article Antarctica ‘It’s beginning to look a lot like the future’: Fears over sudden loss of sea ice Without intending to, it was former prime minister Tony Abbott who lit the fuse that propelled McKenzie into making her life’s mission the fight against climate change. In 2011, she joined the fledgling Australian Climate Commission as a senior communications adviser, determined to shift public debate on Australia’s changing climate. The commission was established by former prime minister Julia Gillard and led by Professor Tim Flannery. It was designed to provide independent advice on the science of climate change, and was announced as public alarm grew about climate change, fuelled by back-to-back La Nina weather events, and on the heels of the 1997-2010 millennium drought.



In its first report to government, The Critical Decade, commissioners warned that climate change “risks have never been clearer, and the case for action has never been more urgent”. Julia Gillard, then prime minister, received the first Australian Climate Commission report from chief Tim Flannery (left) and report author Will Steffen at Parliament House in 2011. Andrew Meares Less than two weeks after the Coalition came to power two years later, the commission’s time was up. In one of his first acts as environment minister, Greg Hunt phoned Flannery to tell him the commission would be axed, as part of the Abbott government’s commitment to scrap the carbon tax. “So very quietly, I’d just gone to the commissioners and said, ‘if we started a new thing, would you be up for it?’ And Tim Flannery was like, ‘Yes, let’s do it!’” After Hunt’s announcement, the commission issued a “relatively neutral response”, McKenzie says, stressing the importance of science to Australian democracy. Flannery held a press conference in which he praised Hunt’s “gracious” conduct in their conversation. Four days later, they officially launched The Climate Council, with founding commissioners including Flannery, the late Professor Will Steffen, Professor Veena Sahajwalla, Gerry Hueston and Professor Lesley Hughes.



“It just went crazy, as soon as it hit the media in the morning,” McKenzie says. “We did a bunch of radio, we started to do some TV news. Some of the newspapers had it. And then it started this big viral moment crowdfunding campaign. Professor Will Steffen addressing the media during a doorstop interview at Parliament House in Canberra in 2013. Alex Ellinghausen “Within that first day, we raised $500,000 and by the end of the day, Twitter [now X] thought we were buying followers, so they shut us down. PayPal thought we were money-laundering, so they shut us down because we’d raised money so fast ... It was this cyclone of activity.” They raised $1.3 million within the first week – more than the previous Climate Commission’s budget – from more than 15,000 people for whom Abbott’s cuts to climate commitments felt like attacks on science. Since then, the principle that “we should base our democratic debate on evidence”, as McKenzie puts it, has driven the way the Climate Council operates. Another element of the Climate Council’s approach is something akin to intentional hope.

World.title: The political genius of Dolly Parton, the great unifier
World.content:
CultureMusicVale Opinion The genius of Dolly Parton, the last great unifier in a divided nation Cory Alpert Former White House staffer August 26, 2026 — 11:39am

August 26, 2026 — 11:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The machinery of American politics sorts everything that it sees. Every moment becomes a litmus test, where every cultural symbol is judged as either MAGA or its opposite. Artists, companies, cities, sports, and even beer get assigned into these categories. A political age consumes everything it touches. Dolly Parton was one of the last major exceptions. Photo: Marija Ercegovac She managed a high-wire act of being entirely herself, a vision of American individualism done right, a preacher who could build a congregation without demanding conversion – where its members could briefly see a piece of shared humanity in each other in their shared appreciation of the woman we Americans knew as Saint Dolly.



Her first big break on the country music stage was as the “singing girl” on The Porter Wagoner Show. During her first performance, the audience booed her during the commercial break. They were angry at the change that this brash, blonde starlet with an unusual voice represented. Related Article Vale Country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80 The show allowed her star to rise, and eventually she set out on her own. Her break with Wagoner, then the kingmaker of country music, is what inspired Dolly to write I Will Always Love You. It’s a song about leaving someone you love but refusing to hate the person you’re leaving behind. The way that Dolly left Porter became the blueprint for a career as the last great unifier in American politics. Later in her life, when Porter was left poor at the end of his career, she bought his music catalogue and gifted it back to him. By the time she built her empire, she understood how fragile the kind of fame she had developed could be. In her flock were conservatives and liberals, evangelicals and atheists, drag queens and NASCAR drivers.



Gallery Gallery icon 7 images Vale Dolly Parton in Australia All the while, she refused to endorse anything while embracing everyone. Some of that instinct had been trained into her by country music’s famously possessive fans. When Dolly crossed into pop, she told TV talkshow host Larry King that she was worried that she was leaving those fans behind. But she told them that she wasn’t leaving country music. She was taking it with her. For many artists, that act would feel like cowardice, to never state your beliefs – to just shut up and sing. But Dolly Parton was anything but a coward. Instead, she was fearless about defining herself and refused to define anyone else.



In a 1984 interview with Andy Warhol, the painter told her that she could be a great preacher. She replied, “What do you mean? I am a great preacher.” Related Article Vale Dolly Parton wrote more than 3000 songs – but we’ve picked her top 10 What she preached was nothing short of American individualism done right. The internet today is flooded with her quotes and Dollyisms, using her very body to grant permission for her fans to become whatever ambitious, sequinned thing they are capable of becoming. Her only demand in return for that permission was to afford everyone else the same privilege. In the same interview, she talked about being a star, as finding your own place and shining within it. It does not require a big stage or a big wig. In Dolly’s universe, there was room enough for everyone to shine. Where I grew up in the rural South, imagination could often be hard to come by. Our school system was so underfunded that parts of it became known as the Corridor of Shame.



It’s the same world that Dolly grew up in. Her father couldn’t read, and the hard, patient life of the mountains of East Tennessee did not afford much possibility beyond those hills. Related Article Vale Beyond the wigs, there was always Dolly Parton’s wondrous wit and wisdom As Dolly’s star grew, she sent that possibility back. She sent books to every child in her home county until they were five years old. The program slowly expanded across the South, then across America. Last year, the Imagination Library delivered its 2 millionth book in Australia alone. Across the world, more than 300 million kids have gotten books – for many, it was the only way they would receive them. She was giving children the resources to decide who they might become. America often mistakes individualism for abandonment. The version that Dolly preached was that each of our lives belong to us, but she could give us each something that could make it larger.



Faith without works is dead, after all. The congregation of Dolly does not agree on every point. Dolly became the great unifier by creating a church big enough for everyone to find room for themselves. To love Dolly was to stand alongside people with whom you share little, and to understand that they have as much right to their place as you do. Dolly gave all of us a place where we could be different together. Cory Alpert is a PhD researcher at the University of Melbourne looking at the impact of AI on democracy. He previously served the Biden-Harris administration. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Trump is clutching at straws and the world knows it
World.content:
BusinessThe economyMiddle East at war Opinion Trump is clutching at straws and the world knows it

Ambrose Evans-Pritchard August 26, 2026 — 11:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Trump administration is hallucinating again. The United States’ “economic D-Day” against Iran will exhaust political consent in Washington for this ill-conceived war long before it forces Iran’s Revolutionary Guard to capitulate. It draws out the spectacle of Donald Trump’s aimless flailing in a region that neither he nor his close advisers begin to understand, further convulsing the global energy, food and commodity markets and further eviscerating US strategic credibility. Even if Trump turns the dial up to 11, he may not get the response that he wants. AP The plan to mount the “single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary” requires also mobilising China, Russia, India, Turkey, a resentful Europe and the world’s major financial centres in a joint campaign to throttle Iran, a country that has already learned to live with 2200 separate US sanctions. The US Treasury could plausibly have pulled off such a feat 10 to 15 years ago, when it was able to crush nations by the “boa constrictor” method, using all the tools of the world’s dollarised financial system. But that supremacy relied on a tight-knit phalanx of democratic allies – or what we used to call the West. Such a world no longer exists, and China cannot be pushed around any longer.



US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has threatened the economic obliteration of any country that declines to enlist as foot soldiers in America’s quarrel. “If you insist on doing business with them – either transferring money, buying their oil, doing seaborne ship transport – the US government will put its full might and force toward enforcing against you,” he said. Related Article Analysis

Middle East at war The White House says this is the Iran endgame. We’ve heard that before Such hubris is courting fate for a nation that depends on constant inflows of capital from these same countries to fund its twin deficits and that already has to pay punitive interest rates to sell its bonds. The US Treasury made a Faustian pact by issuing so much short-term debt. The trap is closing. Bessent must roll over or fund almost $US6 trillion ($8.4 trillion) every three months in a hostile market. The budget deficit was $US432 billion for the single month of July, up 48 per cent from the year before.



Trump has a solution for this and a warning for any bond investor who declines to feed his appetite. “We have many types of intervention. The ultimate intervention is our military. And if we have to use that, we will,” he said. Does he intend to parachute the 101st Airborne into London’s Canary Wharf and Singapore’s harbour district to cart off pension fund managers in shackles for interrogation at Guantanamo? The move draws out the spectacle of Donald Trump’s aimless flailing in a region that neither he nor his close advisers begin to understand, further convulsing the global energy, food and commodity markets. AP It is normal to dial up pressure by starting with economic sanctions before escalating to killing people. Everybody can see that Trump is doing it the other way round because killing has comprehensively failed. The world can see that the US is overstretched, lacks sufficient military power to enforce its will, has exhausted two-thirds of its Patriot interceptors and “virtually all” its surface-to-surface (ATACMS) missiles, and has denuded its defences in the Far East. It can see that the US lacks the stomach for a full ground invasion of Iran and anything short of that is whistling in the wind.



Iran can see all of this too. The regime has survived a bombing campaign and the assassination of 180 members of its leadership. Sanctions are almost laughable at this juncture. Related Article Middle East at war US military top brass dispatched to aircraft carrier rocked by talk of crumbling morale Iran’s land border stretches for 5900 kilometres across seven countries, most of them either friendly or cynically transactional. The frontier rises in an arc from Pakistan to the Eurasian heartland around the Caspian Sea, then down the other side to Turkey and the entire eastern side of Iraq. It is impossible to sustain a goods blockade. The International North-South Transport Corridor already runs as a rail freight link from Russia through Central Asia to Iran. The maritime route via the Caspian does a booming trade as well. Russia cannot export much grain through the Black Sea right now because of Ukrainian drones, so it is exporting what it can to Iran and through Iranian proxies to the wider Middle East. Ergo, a) Iran will have enough food for itself even if its economy is in dire straits and b) Iran will gain strategic leverage as a grain conduit to a region facing serious food stress.



China currently buys 90 per cent of Iran’s oil and in return China sells it machinery, vehicles and electronics, including sensors and engines for Iran’s Shahed drones as well as propellants for its ballistic missiles. China will not let the US dictate how and with whom it may trade. It has gone to some lengths to demonstrate this objection. The world knows that an overstretched America lacks the capability and stomach for a full invasion of Iran. Getty Images If Washington imposes secondary sanctions on Chinese banks and entities, Beijing has a rich menu of retaliation, starting with curbs on critical minerals. Bessent has demonstrated by his actions that he fears rising US bond yields. Beijing knows this, and if it wants to rattle his cage, it can play a few hedge fund tricks of its own by weaponising $US4 trillion of dollar assets held by the Chinese central bank, the state-controlled commercial banks and the giant state-policy banks.



If the US does impose secondary sanctions on Chinese banks, it will have to do the same to European banks that do business with China, otherwise the financial blockade breaks down. But the European Union now has its blocking statute aimed at forbidding its own companies from complying with US extraterritorial sanctions or submitting to US coercion. Iran has a say in the matter too and may choose to hold Trump’s feet to the fire, exploiting the window between now and the midterm elections to cause commodity havoc while always staying just below the threshold of total conflagration. It is normal to dial up pressure by starting with economic sanctions before escalating to killing people. Everybody can see that Trump is doing it the other way round because killing has comprehensively failed. “If the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported, neither through the Strait of Hormuz nor from anywhere in the Persian Gulf,” said Mohsen Rezaee, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. That too is bluster, but it is closer to the truth than the US cares to admit. Iran still controls the Strait of Hormuz and has a second partial stranglehold over the Red Sea via its Houthi allies.



It still has a sufficient arsenal of drones and missiles hidden in mountains to strike commercial shipping at will and enough to inflict serious damage to the energy infrastructure of the Gulf states. The rest of us are condemned to months of mounting stress in the global hydrocarbon markets as storage falls to critically low levels and even greater stress in the markets for diesel, petrol and jet fuel. Despite Trump’s assertions, Iran still controls the Strait of Hormuz. Getty Images The refined petroleum products that we consume are trading today at levels equivalent to crude oil prices of $US140 to $US160 a barrel. The IATA jet fuel index is $US170 in Europe and $US165 in the US.



Wholesale diesel costs $US185 in New York harbour and $US180 in Rotterdam, and it is diesel that fuels farming, trucking, construction and swaths of the industrial economy on both sides of the Atlantic. Natural gas prices in Europe are trading this week at €69 ($112) per megawatt-hour, higher than the panic peak at the onset of Trump’s Iran war. European inventories are disturbingly low for this time of the year, and Britain has almost no safety buffer. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will face his first big crisis if this northern winter proves harsh. These commodity costs are becoming embedded in the global supply chain, are already visible in rising bond yields and will soon be visible in rising inflation and the cost of living. It is hard to see any way out of this impasse, since Trump has only two options: either to accept defeat on Iranian terms, which become more exigent by the week, or to mobilise the US for a long, bloody and costly war that consumes his presidency and may also end in defeat. He shrinks from both.

World.title: Jaws bares its teeth with more high-grade Canadian gold for Manhattan
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Jaws bares its teeth with more high-grade Canadian gold for Manhattan Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 26, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Manhattan Gold Corporation has delivered another round of strong, broad gold intercepts from its Jaws prospect in Nunavut, Canada, with drilling extending the known mineralised system by more than 150 metres to the southwest. The latest results from the company’s maiden drill campaign at its Hook Lake project include a significant 25.9-metre hit grading 1.59 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 89.92m, which housed a richer 6.1-metre core at 3.62g/t gold. This follows on from the stunning interval announced last week of 41.15 metres running at 4.66g/t gold from just 83.82m downhole at the project. Manhattan Gold’s Hook Lake project area in Nunavut, Canada. Other notable intersections from this second batch of assays included 35.05m at 1.23g/t gold from 124.97m, with a 9.14-metre slice of 2.52g/t, and 22.86m at 2.37g/t gold from a shallower 74.68m. The latter intercept contained a particularly spicy 1.52-metre section grading a hefty 26.8g/t gold. The results land at a time when Canada’s vast northern territory of Nunavut is proving to be a hot address for gold explorers. Home to mining giant Agnico Eagle’s 6.7-million-ounce Meliadine operation, 225 kilometres to the northeast and one of Canada’s largest gold mines, peers such as B2Gold and Fury Gold Mines are also advancing programs, underlining the district-scale appetite for new ounces. With the gold price recently pushing higher to more than US$4600 (A$6400) per ounce, any exploration success is getting a serious second look from the market.



‘The Jaws system remains open along strike and at depth.’ Manhattan Gold Corporation technical advisor Eric Sondergaard Manhattan says the latest intercepts from its Jaws target are returning thicker, higher-grade results than those recorded in nearby historic drilling from 1988, suggesting the company’s modern exploration approach is already paying dividends and adding material upside to the historical data. Manhattan Gold Corporation technical advisor Eric Sondergaard said:“Drilling at Jaws continues to deliver multiple broad gold zones with higher grade internal cores, led by 25.90 metres at 1.59g/t gold. Drill results including JWS26005 and JWS26006, also highlight the material upside compared to historic drilling by revealing thicker and higher-grade intercepts when compared to the nearest 1988 drillholes.” Jaws, the most advanced target at Hook Lake, hosts a non-JORC foreign estimate of 3.4 million tonnes at 2.38g/t gold for 285,000 ounces of gold, defined by drilling in the late 1980’s. Manhattan’s current program has been designed to confirm and potentially expand on that historic work. Notably, the company’s work has also recalibrated the geological map. Manhattan says its new drilling has shifted the interpreted position of the gold-bearing main shear zone 20m to 30m northwest of where historic records had placed it, providing the company with a sharper geological model for follow-up drilling. The revised geometry of the orebody provides a much stronger basis for follow-up drill targeting and may open up previously under-explored zones.



With the rods still turning at Jaws, Manhattan is looking at a bigger picture for the deposit. The company has assays pending for a further 12 drillholes, including a key hole that tested below the footprint of all historic drilling at Jaws, opening up the possibility for new mineralisation lurking below. The pending results also include the first-ever drill tests of the company’s Spectre and Lotus prospects. Spectre is a high-grade volcanogenic massive sulphide target where historic drilling in 1974 returned impressive polymetallic hits including 10.51 metres at 2.91 per cent copper, 6.70 per cent zinc, 95.67g/t silver and 1.04g/t gold. The Lotus prospect, described as a “Jaws-style” gold target, has never been drilled despite rock chip sampling in 2025 returning high-grade results of 8.01g/t gold and 2660g/t silver. With drilling at Jaws continuing to deliver broad zones of gold, a historic resource to build upon and a pipeline of assays from both extension and new discovery targets, Manhattan doesn’t look short of catalysts. As the company continues to piece together the puzzle at Hook Lake, punters will likely be watching closely for what the drill bit uncovers next. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: A loo with a view and no railings on ‘an impossible site’ in Sydney
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWArchitecture A loo with a view and no railings on ‘an impossible site’ in Sydney Julie Power August 26, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Holland House in Sydney’s Middle Cove was as famous for its architecture as it was for a ballet performed on the cantilevered terrace that hovers 12 metres above rock and bush. The balcony had no handrails. The cliff top home on an impossible site at 31 Rembrandt Drive was designed by one of Sydney’s most divisive architects, Neville Gruzman, and is now on the market for the first time in 40 years and with balustrades for safety. “Gruzman was a Sydney sensualist,” said Tone Wheeler, who was among the first of dozens of architects to visit the first open house. He was referring to Holland House’s changing floor levels, its rich materials and the sunken lounge near a copper fireplace.



Holland House, 31 Rembrandt Drive, Middle Cove Domain Inspired by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright and Japanese architecture, Gruzman was known for over-the-top mid-century homes. He catered to clients like the Hollands who liked to entertain, and weren’t afraid of the cost or making a big statement. (Having confidence to sit on a toilet in front of a wall of glass helped, too.) Holland House, c 1962, by Sydney architect and former Woollahra mayor Neville Gruzman is on the market. Julie Power At 165 square metres, the three-bedroom home now being marketed by The Agency is about 100 square metres smaller than most new builds.



The house, set on an 859-square-metre block, is not heritage listed, though it is included with other homes by Gruzman on Docomomo Australia Modern Register. Gruzman, the mayor of Woollahra in 1996, was known for being litigious, initiating 30 cases in 40 years. After his death, fellow architects described him as a stirrer, and a man who made loyal friends and mortal enemies. Like the Sydney homes he designed, he was complex, unusual, and difficult to categorise. Reviewing the Hollands new home in 1967 for Australian Home Journal, architect Basil Beirman wrote that its success on one of the most difficult sites he had seen gave his “jaded architectural palate a stimulating lift”. Beirman loved everything, except the lack of railings. They “might be acceptable at three or four feet [a metre] above the ground, but [at] 30 or 40 feet was not.” “Hand-rails might spoil the terraces aesthetically, and balustrades spoil the view. But if the owners share, even a little, my dislike of standing so high without any apparent safeguard, I don’t think it will be long before they do something about it,” he wrote.



Wheeler said Gruzman would take an idea and then push it to excess. Holland House’s design was “dramatic and relentless with the entire eastern wall covered in windows.” Gruzman designed a dressing room for his wife Margot at their Darling Point home that was wall-to-wall mirrors. The dressing room that architect Neville Gruzman designed for his wife had mirrors everywhere. Louise Kennerley The late architect Bruce Rickard, said every Gruzman design was different yet had several elements in common. “They have a beautiful spatial flow, the living areas all face north, and they are exquisitely detailed.” Gruzman thought he was Sydney’s best architect, bar none, said Wheeler. He was also quick to criticise others, including Harry Seidler – considered one of Australia’s greatest – and launched a personal attack on Wheeler at one stage.



He famously liked to compare himself with Wright, and was proud that Opera House designer Jørn Utzon had said the living room in his family home was the best in all of Australia. To his fans, Gruzman was one of Sydney’s most innovative post-war architects. A book on great Sydney homes said Holland House was built on “an impossible site” so steep that it was virtually a cliff. Its wraparound windows created the impression of a fully transparent Japanese screen. At night, it was transformed into a glowing lantern. The view from the toilet and bath is spectacular, said Julie Power, pictured, but the view of the bathroom from the deck outside is probably less attractive. Nicky Catley Look no handrail. In a file photo, the terrace seems to float about 10 metres above the bush next to sheer cliff. The former Gruzman family home at Oswald Street, Darling Point.

World.title: This town has finally realised its potential as the perfect beach getaway
World.content:
InspirationQueensland This town has finally realised its potential as the perfect beach getaway Julietta Jameson Updated August 26, 2026 — 11:27am ,first published August 26, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This article is part of our comprehensive guide to the Sunshine Coast, your guide to where to stay, eat and the must-see highlights. See all stories .

Common wisdom says galleries and museums are the mark of a fully formed destination. I believe it’s coffee. At least this is the conclusion I reach over a latte at Cici’s Continental Deli, a hole-in-the-wall cafe a stone’s throw from Mooloolaba Beach. It’s a cave-like refuge from all that Sunshine Coast sunshine (though of course there’s outdoor seating), with clever mid-century styling that makes it feel decades older than 2025 when it opened. The coffee is excellent, the sandwiches generous and the attitude distinctly Sunshine Coast: friendly, relaxed and chatty. Mooloolaba Beach, on Queensland’s Sunshine Coast, has come of age. The last time I was here, more than a decade ago, finding decent coffee required local knowledge. Friends who lived there pointed me in the right direction. This time I simply stumble across it. If not fully formed in the way top destinations are, Mooloolaba, I think, is at least growing up. Could it be the new Noosa, the aspirational jewel in the Sunshine Coast crown? Queensland coastal destinations have never needed museums for holiday crowds to think of them as the perfect getaway. What they need is sun, sand, surf and lifestyle.



Despite having all that, Mooloolaba has had the reputation for being a bit, well, daggy. Locals and regular holidaymakers have liked it that way. 



It’s a leap to declare all this on the back of finding a great cafe. In fact, it’s almost contradictory. Good coffee can be a gateway drug to parking problems and other conditions that make a place insufferable. The Mooloolaba Spit separates the Pacific Ocean from the Mooloolah River. But for now, Mooloolaba is having a moment, balancing lived character with contemporary sophistication – and that’s in no small part due to the new Avani Mooloolaba Beach Hotel, the first full-service internationally branded new-build hotel on the Sunshine Coast in four decades. With a young, enthusiastic staff, there’s a real sense of place at the Avani. It’s a $50 million landmark development that runs to the seaside-holiday playbook perfectly. It’s got beachy tones in a relaxed decor that pops with decorative accents and an airy sense of space. Rooms have balconies, many of which have big ocean views and beds oriented for a sunrise wake-up. The story of the site on which it sits is emblematic of the town’s change. Just a block back from the beach, hence premium real estate, it was previously an expansive council-owned ground-level carpark. Council sold off half – that became the hotel – while the other half was developed into a far more efficient multilevel parking structure.



Avani Mooloolaba’s highlight is its upper reaches. There’s a rooftop infinity pool and terrace, and Sully’s Rooftop, the hotel’s signature restaurant, eagerly patronised by locals. Later this year at street level, First Avenue Cellar & Bar will also open, joining the excellent Lobby Bar (another spot for good coffee). The Avani Mooloolaba Beach Hotel is the first new full-service hotel to hit the Sunshine Coast in 40 years. A bedroom with an uninterruped beach view inside the Avani hotel in Mooloolaba. The 180 rooms span 12 storeys in line with local height restrictions, meaning no Gold Coast-style shadows on the beach. Mooloolaba’s second luxury hotel, though, the Aria development just down the road, will be bigger, with council recently approving two extra storeys on the basis of needing additional hotel rooms in the region.



Locals worry about such incremental height creep. Up to now, though, their biggest worry amid all the change, has been the demolition of Mooloolaba’s much-loved but undeniably dated “loo with a view”, a badly placed public convenience that blocked the beach view and became a joke’s punchline. It makes way for a foreshore precinct that is currently under construction and which features boardwalks, terraced sea walls and community facilities Seafood eatery Prawn Star inhabits a couple of converted prawn trawlers and a pontoon. Those same priorities have seen Mooloolaba Wharf become a lively hub of hospitality. Too often, old wharf precincts can become Disneyfied white elephants. But here, the wharf is still in regular use for boating purposes, and the boutiques, cafes and eateries are packed with visitors and locals alike. A highlight is Prawn Star, a seafood-serving institution inhabiting a couple of converted prawn trawlers and a pontoon. A didgeridoo performance during a Salwater Eco Tours cruise. One morning, we leave the wharf with Simon Thornalley, founder of Indigenous tourism operator, Saltwater Eco Tours, for a cruise on Gubbi Gubbi/Kabi Kabi Country. His boat is a 1908 heritage-listed sailing vessel that he restored himself. It’s big on character and is a good match for Thornalley’s.



The Mooloolah River has an extensive canal network and cruising on it, we pass mansions, including one owned by the Irwins with their research boat parked out the front. Most of our admiration is for the remaining little 1960s and ’70s holiday shacks. The juxtaposition makes me reflect on what we lose to the same progress I admire. The losses to Thornalley’s people, however, are on a far greater scale and on a much longer timeline. He doesn’t dwell on it. Instead, as we munch on a morning tea, he points out birds and land forms, tells stories of the water, and as our cruise nears its end, he treats us to a didgeridoo performance. Paddling out with Saltwater Eco Tours. On a sunset cruise with Set Sail Cruises, it’s all about simply admiring the coast from both the river and the ocean. We crank up a yacht-rock playlist, pop the bubbly, and enjoy the wind in our hair and spray on our faces. In Mooloolaba there are whale watching cruises, snorkelling and diving cruises, turtle activities, canoeing, paddleboarding and kayaking adventures, and so much more. The fact it’s so jam-packed with activities is what makes it fundamentally different to Noosa, a local tells me. “Noosa’s about being seen, we’re about doing.”



At Sea Life Sunshine Coast it’s hard to argue. It’s a favourite with families but behind the penguins, seals and underwater tunnel is one of the region’s most important marine rescue operations, rehabilitating injured turtles before returning them to the ocean. It’s a reminder that, for all its growing sophistication, Mooloolaba remains closely connected to the marine environment that built it. You can admire the coast from both the river and the ocean on a boat trip with Set Sail Cruises. Then there’s the Lycra brigade. The Mooloolaba Triathlon is Australia’s second-largest triathlon event. Held annually in mid-March, the festival attracts about 9000 competitors across elite and amateur categories, with the ocean swims, sprint and cycling standard Olympic distances. For those looking to recover from all that, even wellness has become part of the town’s evolution. Once upon a time, a surf followed by fish and chips probably qualified as self-care here, and it probably still does to many. Today, visitors can alternate beach walks with infrared saunas, ice baths, massage treatments and spa rituals. Tank Bathhouse has helped introduce communal bathing culture to the Sunshine Coast, while Sauna & Ice Studio caters to the growing enthusiasm for hot-and-cold therapy. The Avani has also introduced a terrific spa to the equation. Not only are the treatments top tier, but the hotel, which runs the spa itself, has priced products competitively (rather than at the enormous mark-ups many hotel spas favour), making it a lovely retail experience as well as a healing one.



Amid the touristy restaurants with touts out the front, the ice-cream vendors and dark entryways to the plethora of short-term apartment accommodation that is the lifeblood of Mooloolaba stays, the esplanade is home to some terrific boutiques. The Wharf Mooloolaba has gelato, sushi, tacos, a bakery and plenty of atmosphere. A standout is Zambezee, where international women’s fashion brands hang next to quality local designers. Avenue J deals in exquisitely curated antique jewellery and some lovely objets d’art. Even the pharmacy has some great finds in the form of Queensland-made cosmetics, candles and hair accessories. It’s not Noosa-level retail therapy, but that pharmacy is perhaps one of the best illustrations of the Mooloolaba change: it’s locally focused with a side of sophistication, rather than sophistication first, local second. Sure, there is increasing style here: better coffee, better restaurants and better places to stay. There will be more thoughtful public spaces. But it feels like the natural evolution of a beach town that is realising its potential, while still maintaining its own unique character. And in that, there’s no need for it to be “the new” anywhere, other than the destination it is.





MORE

World.title: 'Sweetest boy': Wellington Zoo euthanises chimp critically injured in fight
World.content:
Wellington Zoo has euthanised one of its chimpanzees after he sustained critical injuries in a fight.

In a post on social media, the zoo said 11-year-old Kitwe was euthanised on Tuesday.

"We farewelled 11-year-old Kitwe the chimpanzee after he sustained critical injuries during a fight in the Chimp troop," it said.

"His condition was assessed by the Primate and Veterinary teams, and the decision was made to euthanise him due to the extent of his injuries."

Supplied / Wellington Zoo

The zoo said fights and displays of aggression were not unusual and a "natural part of chimp life".

However, it didn't make Kitwe's death any easier and the whole team was feeling the loss.

"We will be monitoring the troop to see how they settle over the next couple of weeks."

Wellington Zoo said Kitwe was born at the zoo in 2014 and named by world-renowned primatologist and conservationist Dr Jane Goodall.

"He was extremely sweet-natured with zookeepers and loved training.

Supplied / Wellington Zoo

"His favourite meal of the day was dinner but generally he loved food no matter what it was - he made the best excited food noises and always had to let everyone else in the troop know when there was food around."

The zoo went on to say Kitwe enjoyed playing with 4-year-old chimp, Akida, and had "endless patience" with him.
